Gifted, charismatic and passionate amid highs and lows - Keegan obituary

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:00:33 GMT

Kevin Keegan is arguably the most beloved figure in Newcastle United's history for his deeds as player and manager

Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, was one of football's most charismatic and influential figures in a career of many chapters that took him from superstar player to elite manager.

While some may remember him best for his ill-fated reign as England manager, he will rightly be much more celebrated as a world-class player at Liverpool and Hamburg, captaining England, and shining latterly at Southampton and Newcastle United, before becoming arguably the most beloved figure in the Tyneside club's history.

Keegan revived Newcastle's fortunes as a player before carrying the Geordie nation with him on a thrilling ride as manager, first by taking the club back into the top flight, then delivering a magnificently entertaining team that challenged for the highest honours - even if they ultimately fell short.

His time at Newcastle will also be recalled for his infamous "I will love it if we beat them" TV outburst aimed at Manchester United boss Sir Alex Ferguson as Newcastle's 12-point lead in the 1995-96 title race evaporated - but the unconditional love the Geordies felt for Keegan was never diluted.

Keegan's career was a reflection of himself.

He was hugely gifted, honest, decent, hard-working and emotional. There were highs and lows, but the positivity and vibrancy he brought made him a cherished figure.

This video can not be played

Keegan scores double to inspire Liverpool to 1974 FA Cup final win

Born in Armthorpe near Doncaster, Keegan came to then Liverpool manager Bill Shankly's attention playing more than 100 games for Scunthorpe United, sitting on a bin outside Anfield while the legendary Scottish boss and Scunthorpe counterpart Ron Ashman finalised one of the all-time great bargains of a £35,000 deal in 1971.

Keegan was regarded by some observers as simply a hard-working player who made himself great through sheer grit and determination. The initial assertion was correct, but he was much more than that.

Shankly, not one to knowingly undersell his players, told Keegan within a fortnight of arriving at Liverpool that he would play for England.

The new signing scored on his Liverpool debut on the opening day of the 1971-72 season against Nottingham Forest at Anfield, a scruffy finish set up by John Toshack. It was the start of a beautiful football relationship with Liverpool as well as with the Welshman.

Keegan scored twice in Liverpool's 1974 FA Cup final win against Newcastle at Wembley, but was sent off there three months later in the Charity Shield

Their almost telepathic partnership - a classic "big man, little man" combination - was even put to the test on television.

They gelled to such an extent that Granada TV's groundbreaking Friday magazine show Kick Off had Keegan and Toshack sitting back to back, trying to guess the colour and shape of a card the other was holding.

Such was their success rate some thought telepathy actually was at work - but the pair later revealed there was a mirror in the studio and they could see the other's cards.

Keegan was the spearhead of Shankly's second great side, in total winning three league titles, the European Cup, FA Cup and the Uefa Cup twice under his Scottish mentor and then his successor Bob Paisley.

He was instrumental in all of those triumphs, scoring twice in the 3-0 victory against Newcastle in the 1974 FA Cup final. His first prompted the famous line from BBC commentator David Coleman: "Goals pay the rent - and Keegan does his share."

In the subsequent Charity Shield against league champions Leeds United, Keegan was sent off after a flare-up with Billy Bremner, who was also dismissed, with both leaving the Wembley pitch shirtless. Johnny Giles had been the instigator, landing a blatant right hook on the Liverpool player, but was not sent off.

Keegan was outstanding as Liverpool won the European Cup in his final game for the club by beating Borussia Monchengladbach in Rome

In the 1972-73 Uefa Cup final against Borussia Monchengladbach, Keegan scored twice in the first leg at Anfield, a game played at the second attempt after a thunderstorm 24 hours earlier caused the match to be abandoned after 27 minutes.

The rearrangement allowed Shankly to recall Toshack, who had been left out of the initial match, and he and Keegan tormented the Germans in a 3-0 victory, Liverpool subsequently winning 3-2 on aggregate.

When the trophy was won once more against Club Brugge three years later, this time under Paisley, Keegan scored a vital goal in Belgium, the second leg finishing 1-1 to ensure a 4-3 aggregate victory.

Even off the field, Keegan's competitive spirit burned, taking part in BBC TV's Superstars series in 1976, which allowed athletes from different sports to compete against each other.

Keegan, however, suffered elbow and shoulder injuries when he fell off his bicycle. It was a rare fall from grace.

He also tried his hand - or voice - in the music business, releasing a single in 1972 titled It Ain't Easy.

Remembering Kevin Keegan

This video can not be played

1980 - Keegan leads Hamburg to European Cup semi-final win over Real Madrid

Ever ambitious and eager to test new horizons, Keegan announced midway through the 1976-77 season that he would leave Liverpool at the end of the campaign.

It brought some criticism from supporters, but was another example of deception never being part of Keegan's character, allowing Liverpool time to line up Kenny Dalglish as his replacement.

He went out on the highest high in his final game, running the great German defender Berti Vogts ragged as Liverpool won the European Cup for the first time, beating Borussia Monchengladbach 3-1 in Rome.

Keegan left having scored 100 goals in 323 appearances.

There was talk of a move to Real Madrid, but in the end his destination was Hamburg, where he was a major success as they won the Bundesliga in 1978-79, though disappointment followed when they lost the European Cup final to Nottingham Forest the following season.

Keegan confirmed his world-class credentials at Hamburg, winning the Ballon d'Or in 1978 and 1979.

Hamburg was a surprise choice when Keegan left Liverpool, but after early struggles to win over team-mates, he became hugely popular, not just with his club but in the country, where they appreciated the Englishman's down to earth approach and his willingness to integrate.

This video can not be played

Watch: Popular and passionate - Kevin Keegan's memorable football career

It all added to Keegan's status as a global superstar, one of the most marketable sportsmen around, not just seen on the pitch but in adverts and advertising hoardings worldwide.

He famously did an advert for Brut aftershave with British boxer Henry Cooper, as well as the "Green Cross Code" road safety campaign.

While in West Germany, Keegan had another crack at music with the track Head Over Heels In Love. It peaked at number 31 in the UK, but climbed to number 10 in the German charts.

Keegan returned to England in 1980 with a shock move to Southampton, showing his enduring quality by winning the Professional Footballers' Association player of the year award in 1982.

He did not win trophies at The Dell, but was still a player of the highest class in Lawrie McMenemy's team, built around experienced stars such as Keegan, Alan Ball and Saints' great Mike Channon.

Keegan, seen here with his former Liverpool team-mates Ray Clemence and Phil Thompson, was captain of England's 1982 World Cup squad but was only fit enough to feature as a substitute in their final game, so full-back Mick Mills took the armband

Keegan won 63 England caps over a period lasting almost a decade, scoring 21 goals and captaining the side 31 times.

It was a slow burner after making his debut in a World Cup qualifier in Wales, even including a physical assault by security men at Belgrade airport in summer 1974 when England arrived for a friendly against Yugoslavia under caretaker boss Joe Mercer.

There was horseplay at the luggage carousel, resulting in the perfectly innocent Keegan, one of the highest-profile players in the squad, being taken away to a side room, where he was punched and kicked. He was released, going on to score a late equaliser in a 2-2 draw.

Keegan briefly walked out of the England squad after being dropped for a home international against Wales in 1975, but returned after talks with manager Don Revie.

It summed up an England career that never fulfilled its potential.

England failed to qualify for the 1974 and 1978 World Cups, then when Keegan captained England at the 1980 European Championship in Italy, they did not progress from the group stage.

He was captain again at the World Cup in Spain two years later, but a chronic back injury - for which he left the camp to seek treatment from a specialist in Germany - meant he did not play until the last 26 minutes of England's second-round game against Spain.

Keegan uncharacteristically missed a simple headed chance, the game ending goalless to send manager Ron Greenwood's side home.

He was left out of Greenwood's successor Bobby Robson's next squad, and never played for England again.

Keegan was instantly worshipped by Newcastle's fans after arriving as a player from Southampton

Keegan felt Southampton, even under the shrewd management of Lawrie McMenemy, did not match his ambition so he signed for Newcastle - then in the old Division Two - for £100,000 just before the start of the 1982-83 season.

It was the start of a love affair when Keegan scored on his debut against Queens Park Rangers.

Newcastle were promoted to the top flight in 1983-84, but Keegan announced he would retire at the end of that season, a decision prompted by getting caught by Liverpool defender Mark Lawrenson when clean through in an FA Cup third-round tie at Anfield which his old club won 4-0.

In typical Keegan fashion, he felt he had lost a vital yard of pace so it was time to go, leaving St James' Park after a final game, his testimonial against Liverpool, still dressed in his Newcastle kit while he was whisked away by helicopter.

Keegan moved to Spain with his family vowing never to enter management, but on 5 February 1992, almost eight years after his final game as a player, Keegan returned to Tyneside.

This video can not be played

'I'm proud of it' - Kevin Keegan reflects on some of his career highlights

Keegan's management trademark was all-out, thrilling attack, with his former Liverpool and Newcastle team-mate Terry McDermott at his side and charismatic chairman Sir John Hall shaping the off-field strategy.

He had initial differences with Hall over transfer cash, prompting another classic Keegan quote when he said: "It's not like the brochure."

Matters were quickly resolved and soon Newcastle were on their way.

Having saved Newcastle from relegation to the third tier, Keegan inspired them to promotion to the Premier League, finishing only behind champions Manchester United and Blackburn Rovers in 1993-94 with goals and creativity provided by strikers Andy Cole and the returning Peter Beardsley.

Cole was sold to Manchester United in a surprise move in January 1995, Keegan famously standing on the steps outside St James' Park to explain the decision to unhappy fans.

The peak of Keegan's reign, along with the biggest disappointment, came in 1995-96 when Newcastle, strengthened by the addition of high-class stars such as Les Ferdinand and David Ginola, moved 12 points clear in the title race, only to squander the advantage to Manchester United.

Keegan will remain an iconic figure with the "Toon Army", Newcastle United's fanatical fanbase

There were two enduring images of Keegan as glory escaped his grasp, head bowed as Liverpool scored in stoppage time to win 4-3 in an all-time Premier League classic in April - before that tirade aimed at Ferguson.

Ferguson questioned whether Leeds and Nottingham Forest would try as hard against Newcastle as they would against Manchester United - and after a win at Elland Road, Keegan exploded.

His broadside ended with the never-to-be-forgotten quote: "I will love it if we beat them. Love it."

Sadly for Keegan, Newcastle did not.

Some felt Keegan's time at Newcastle never recovered from that crushing blow, but his charisma and the call of home helped England's top marksman Alan Shearer reject Manchester United to make a world record £15m move from Blackburn that summer.

Shearer's debut ended in a 4-0 loss in the Charity Shield to the club he turned down, revenge exacted spectacularly with a 5-0 win at home in the Premier League two months later.

Keegan then stunned Tyneside on 8 January 1997 by resigning, saying in a short statement: "I feel I have taken the club as far as I can."

He returned to the game the following September as Fulham's chief operating officer, eventually taking over as manager and leading the Cottagers' journey back to the First Division.

And then came England.

Keegan was appointed England's caretaker manager for a four-game period after Glenn Hoddle was sacked in February 1999.

He initially insisted he did not want the job and would return to Fulham, but the warm reception he received when England beat Poland 3-1 at Wembley in his first game pulled on his emotions.

However, by his own admission, Keegan proved an ill fit for the greater tactical nuances of international management, publicly admitting: "If it's a 0-0 draw in the Ukraine you want, then I'm probably not your man."

England qualified for Euro 2000 with a two-legged play-off victory against Scotland, but the campaign was a dismal failure.

Keegan's side were beaten 3-2 by Portugal in their first game after leading 2-0 inside 17 minutes. Germany were beaten by a single Shearer goal, but a calamitous 3-2 loss to Romania, having led 2-1, sent England out.

Keegan carried on, but criticism was mounting against this passionate, yet sensitive man.

Keegan resigned as England manager after defeat in a World Cup qualifier against Germany in the final game at the old Wembley Stadium

He resigned in dramatic fashion in October after England lost their opening World Cup qualifier to Germany in the final game played at the old Wembley Stadium before it was demolished and rebuilt.

The conversation, in which he told then Football Association executive director David Davies he was going, took place in a Wembley toilet, with a rain-soaked Keegan then going on television to admit: "I just don't feel I can find that little bit extra you need at this level to find a winning formula."

It was the most brutal recognition of his own shortcomings.

Keegan could not resist the lure of the game, however, succeeding Joe Royle as Manchester City manager after relegation from the Premier League in May 2001.

His commitment to exciting attacking football remained, signing entertainers such as Eyal Berkovic and Ali Benarbia. City were promoted as First Division champions after scoring 108 league goals.

Adding quality like France striker Nicolas Anelka, City finished ninth in the Premier League, Keegan also inspiring more remarkable memories.

In an FA Cup fourth-round replay at Tottenham in February 2004, City came from 3-0 down at the interval, with midfielder Joey Barton sent off at the end of the first half, to win 4-3 through Jon Macken's late winner. A month later they handed out a 4-1 beating to Manchester United.

While Keegan had indicated his intention to retire at the end of the 2004-05 season, he instead left by mutual consent in March 2005.

Keegan's return as Newcastle United manager in 2008 swiftly turned sour and he never returned to the game.

Tyneside was overcome with joy and excitement when Newcastle United owner Mike Ashley announced Keegan's return as manager in January 2008.

It was an ill-starred pairing, Keegan resigning after only eight months following differences with Ashley and Newcastle's hierarchy, including his former England player Dennis Wise, who was executive director.

Keegan was unhappy at his lack of control, saying: "I've been working desperately hard to find a way forward with the directors, but sadly that has not proved possible.

"It's my opinion that a manager must have the right to manage and that clubs should not impose upon any manager any player that he does not want."

He added: "I have been left with no other choice than to leave", and later won damages from the club for constructive dismissal.

It was his final farewell to football, but he remained beloved by the 'Toon Army', as well as at Anfield, his standing as a person and respect for his work in football illustrated by the outpouring of affection and goodwill when he released news of his illness.

What will Rogers bring to Alonso's Chelsea?

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:57:39 GMT

Rogers made three starts and a further four substitute appearances for England at the World Cup

Chelsea's £117m move for Aston Villa forward Morgan Rogers was a genuine transfer window shock, but how did they do it and what does it mean for the rest of the squad?

On Monday, Rogers returned from the United States, having featured for England at the World Cup, to undergo a medical in London and sign a six-year contract with an option for a further year.

It had been widely expected that Rogers, who was Villa's most prized asset, would be available only for an English transfer record fee, but many expected Arsenal to be the frontrunners.

However, Chelsea had been tracking Rogers for more than two years and had quietly made him their top attacking target. They moved quickly after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina out of his desire to focus on the World Cup.

On Thursday, after the 2-1 loss, a combined effort involving the club's sporting directors, head coach Xabi Alonso and co-owner Behdad Eghbali helped secure a deal. Even Chelsea captain Reece James was making the club's case from within the England camp, while those close to the negotiations say Cole Palmer was also aware of developments as, in Rogers' words, "one of my best friends in life".

It was a well-planned operation involving figures across the club and resulted in Rogers being signed in under 48 hours.

The deal was underpinned by the strong relationship between Chelsea co-owner Eghbali and Aston Villa owner Nassef Sawiris, with the agreement being finalised on Saturday afternoon, shortly before Rogers took to the field in England's bronze-medal victory over France.

After the deal was agreed, Arsenal were offered the chance to match the bid but they informed Villa they were committed to their lower valuation and were willing to let him join Chelsea on those terms.

They will now consider alternative targets, including Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Bournemouth's Junior Kroupi.

Although Chelsea had tracked Rogers for more than two years, the clubs had previously discussed a potential deal during the 'Profit and Sustainability swaps' of 2024.

One option explored was Nicolas Jackson reuniting with his former Villarreal manager Unai Emery, before Ian Maatsen moved to Villa Park and Omari Kellyman joined Chelsea.

Yet Chelsea's move also represents a recalibration of their transfer tactics.

In April and his last interview, Eghbali accepted Chelsea needed "to add more ready-made players at this part of the project, to take (it) to the next level, to be consistent over time," adding: "You tweak a model, you improve, you learn from mistakes."

Rogers and Palmer have been friends since their Manchester City academy days

Palmer first performed his 'cold' celebration in December 2023 after scoring two goals in a 3-2 win at Luton.

He has since taken ownership of the celebration, literally, registering a trademark for it with the UK Intellectual Property Office after scoring two goals against Luton.

However, it was first meant as a tribute to Rogers as he performed the celebration after a goal for Middlesbrough against West Brom.

It was after moving from his local club West Brom to Manchester City that Rogers first struck up a friendship with Palmer. Both were 16 and soon starred in attack for City's FA Youth Cup-winning under-18 side in 2020.

Joining Chelsea should ease Rogers' transition. He already knows Levi Colwill and Reece James through the England set-up, while Tosin Adarabioyo, Jamie Gittens, Romeo Lavia and Liam Delap all came through City's academy system.

That English contingent forms a substantial part of the club's leadership group, alongside Enzo Fernandez and Moises Caicedo.

There is, however, the more important issue of football and where Rogers fits into the team, especially given Palmer is a similar type of player.

Rogers was among the players selected by England manager Thomas Tuchel ahead of Palmer for this summer's World Cup, but their versatility means they can play either together or in each other's position.

One source suggests Rogers will primarily play on the left, with Palmer operating centrally as a number 10. That would leave Estevao Willian, Pedro Neto and new signing Geovany Quenda competing for places on the right and Jamie Gittens as his understudy.

Chelsea are likely to use a back four at times next season, but they are also exploring a back-three system, which Alonso used to devastating effect when winning the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024.

That could allow Palmer and Rogers to play together as dual number 10s, while wingers would be asked to operate in deeper wing-back roles. The Spaniard is considering several tactical options before the start of the season.

Chelsea had a number of problems last season, one of which was a five-game goalless run under former head coach Liam Rosenior, which led to his sacking.

Rogers contributed 14 goals and 12 assists in 55 appearances last season and would add further firepower.

Looking at the wider squad, and assuming winger Alejandro Garnacho is sold as planned, Chelsea would currently have six attackers competing for three forward positions in a season without European football. In addition, they have five senior strikers - Joao Pedro, Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap, Emmanuel Emegha and Marc Guiu - on the books.

It is clear that the squad needs trimming after last season's 10th-place finish, particularly given Chelsea can play a maximum of 51 matches if they reach both domestic cup finals.

It's not just about keeping players happy - Chelsea must also sell players to keep the books balanced.

The £117m fee represents a substantial outlay on top of the £47m spent to sign full-back Marco Palestra from Atalanta, as well as the potential arrivals of defenders Pep Chavarria from Rayo Vallecano and Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace.

In addition, midfielder Valentin Barco is expected to join from Strasbourg, though Chelsea have yet to confirm the deal.

It took a league-record £300m in player sales last season for Chelsea to comply with the Premier League's financial rules, which are due to move from a Financial Fair Play-based system to a squad cost ratio model this summer.

Uefa, however, represents the biggest obstacle to Chelsea's continued spending after fining the club £26.7m for breaching its rules last summer, while Villa were also fined and are under the same scrutiny, which led to Rogers' sale.

Chelsea were again found to have breached European football's governing body's regulations this summer, but the financial picture improved significantly, resulting in a fine of just £2.6m. Most of that amount will be waived if the club continues to improve its finances.

With five new signings expected this summer, Chelsea will want to sell or loan out at least a dozen players from the 37 senior options on their books, and for as much money as possible, to keep their accounts healthy.

They have already sold Marc Cucurella to Real Madrid, Andrey Santos to Manchester United, Tyrique George to Everton and Jimmy-Jay Morgan to West Bromwich Albion for a combined fee of more than £120m.

Generating transfer income has become increasingly important for Chelsea, who lag behind their traditional big-six rivals in commercial and matchday revenue, while also falling behind in broadcast income after missing out on Champions League football in three of the past four seasons.

Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:48:53 GMT

The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

The eight-week inquest will also examine what state agencies knew, or ought to have known, about Sara's safety in the run up to her murder.

Surrey County Council has previously apologised for what happened and said it had taken "robust action" to address earlier findings.

Sara's father and stepmother both attended the hearing via video links from prison.

Senior coroner for Surrey, Richard Travers, said he would consider holding the inquest with a jury at the next hearing.

Batool said she wanted to give evidence at the inquest, which will not take place until April 2027.

Sara's father did not have legal representation and at one point began criticising evidence his former partner wished to submit.

The coroner told him: This is not a re-trial, we are not going behind any findings that were made by the criminal court, I am not interested in the comments you have to make on any documents."

Sara's uncle, Faisal Malik, was found guilty of causing or allowing Sara's death and jailed for 16 years.

Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK?

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:43:55 GMT

Andrew and Tristan Tate are facing a bid by British prosecutors to have them extradited from the US to the UK after authorities issued 38 new charges against them.

US Marshals arrested the brothers in Miami on Saturday after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) brought new charges, including rape and offences related to sex trafficking, against them.

Andrew, 39, and Tristan, 37 - who came to global fame via social media - have previously denied any wrongdoing.

The dual British-US citizens were taken into custody and are set to appear before a federal court as prosecutors launch legal proceedings to have them sent to the UK.

Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Andrew Tate first rose to fame after an appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother in 2016. He only lasted six days on the programme, before being removed following the emergence of a video that appeared to show him attacking a woman.

He said at the time that the footage had been edited and was "a total lie trying to make me look bad".

Now, the former kickboxer boasts more than 10 million followers on X, formerly Twitter - and a worldwide profile. He has appeared in countless videos, flaunting an ultra-luxurious lifestyle of fast cars, private jets, and yachts.

Tate was banned from the social media platform for saying women should "bear responsibility" for being sexually assaulted, but has since been reinstated.

Tristan is Andrew's younger brother.

The CPS said on Sunday that Andrew was being charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

Tristan's new charges include two counts of rape, one count of sexual assault and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

The alleged offending is said to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017.

Andrew now faces a total of 42 charges in the UK and Tristan faces 17 charges, after CPS had pursued other charges last year.

"These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven," Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the CPS, said.

The brothers have been based in Romania, where they are also under criminal investigation. In 2024, Bedfordshire Police secured European arrest warrants for the pair to have them returned from Romania when proceedings against them there conclude. They deny all allegations against them.

The brothers have been able to travel to the US since travel restrictions against them in Romania were lifted in early 2025.

A US Department of Justice spokesperson said the arrests were "pursuant to extradition proceedings".

The UK and the US are parties to treaty that allows the extradition of people in relation to alleged offences punishable under laws in both countries by at least one year in prison.

For a UK case, the CPS prepares a request which is certified by a judge. The final request is sent to be considered by the Home Office, which then forwards the extradition request to the relevant state through usual diplomatic channels.

The decision to accept the extradition request is taken by the US State Department. The request will then be considered by the US courts, with a final decision made by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

A lawyer who represents the Tates, Joseph McBride, said on X that the brothers have court "first thing" on Monday US time.

In a statement released after the brothers' arrest on Saturday evening, McBride said "the world knows Andrew and Tristan are innocent".

"Their enemies know it best of all. That is exactly why they have been attacked," McBride continued, describing the new UK charges as a "political hit".

He said the new charges were designed to counter a defamation action filed by the brothers in the US.

"We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain's political dirty work," he continued.

Durham Law School Associate Professor Gemma Davies said there was a clause in the US-UK treaty that prevents extradition for political offences, adding lawyers for the Tates could argue the allegations are politically motivated.

"However, it's very rare extradition between the UK and US is refused on those grounds," Davies said, adding the test would be subject to a high threshold.

She said it was "relatively rare" for an extradition request between the two countries to be refused given the strong working relationship between authorities.

"It's fairly common to extradite between the two, which means it's well traversed from a legal perspective, and we are two countries that have fairly similar legal systems in terms of criminal justice," Davies said.

But Bill Bowring, Emeritus Professor of Law at Birkbeck College, University of London, said the ongoing proceedings in Romania were a "major complication".

He said he had not "seen a satisfactory answer" as to why the CPS was now pursuing extradition from the US after a Romanian court ruled in 2024 the pair could only be extradited from that country after the conclusion of their separate case there.

The BBC has requested comment from the CPS in relation to its position on the Romanian proceedings.

Davies said that if the CPS was successful, the extradition could still take months, with any appeal delaying the process by about a year, "if not more".

Newcastle, Liverpool and England legend Keegan dies

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:38:28 GMT

Keegan both captained and managed England

Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75, seven weeks after he revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, his family have confirmed.

One of English football's most decorated players, Keegan enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career.

He later went on to manage Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Keegan revealed he had stage four cancer in June, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January, after he had "further evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms" in hospital.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather," it continued.

"The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Newcastle United paid tribute, describing Keegan as "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history".

The club statement added: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him."

Liverpool, for whom Keegan played for between 1971 and 1977, said Keegan's "indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on".

Hamburg said football had lost one of its "defining figures" and they would always "cherish" his memory, while Fulham said Keegan "forged a strong connection" with the fans, who would "forever hold wonderful memories" of his short time at the club.

Keegan's first club, Scunthorpe, described him as "one of the best players of his generation", with an "inspirational demeanour" and "brilliant personality".

England and Manchester City both offered their condolences to the Keegan family, with the latter describing him as "one of the most iconic and fondly remembered figures in English football".

The Three Lions will celebrate Keegan's life when they host Spain in a Uefa Nations League match at Wembley on 26 September.

This video can not be played

Watch: Popular and passionate - Kevin Keegan's memorable football career

Gifted, charismatic and passionate amid highs and lows - Keegan obituary

As a player, Keegan won major honours with Liverpool, claiming three league titles, the European Cup, two Uefa Cups and the FA Cup over a six-year spell.

He helped Hamburg win the Bundesliga and won back-to-back Ballons d'Or in 1978 and 1979. He remains one of only four English players to have won the award to date.

On the international stage, Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 games for England between 1972 and 1982, and went on to manage them from February 1999 until October 2000.

Keegan is one of the most transformational figures in Newcastle's history - the mastermind behind 'The Entertainers', who challenged for the Premier League title in 1996.

This video can not be played

Keegan scores twice to inspire Liverpool to 1974 FA Cup final win

Such is his status, current head coach Eddie Howe even reached out to Keegan when he got the Newcastle job in 2021 to try and get the inside track on the club and the mindset he needed to succeed.

Keegan guided the club to promotion to the Premier League in 1992-93 before leading them to second place in 1995-96.

He led England to Euro 2000 before resigning in October following a World Cup qualifying defeat by Germany at Wembley.

Keegan managed City from 2001 to 2005, then returned to Newcastle for an eight-month spell in 2008.

'I'm proud of it' - Kevin Keegan reflects on some of his career highlights

Former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer: "My hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy, Boss."

Prince William, Patron of the Football Association: "Incredibly saddened to hear of the passing of Kevin Keegan. A truly remarkable footballer and manager who inspired generations with his talent, passion and love of the game.

"Above all, he will be remembered as a kind and generous man. Our thoughts are with his family and all who knew him."

Former Newcastle forward Faustino Asprillia: "Today is a day I never wanted to see. I am absolutely heartbroken to hear of the passing of Kevin Keegan.

"Kevin wasn't just a football manager to me - he was the man who introduced me to the Premier League and made me fall in love with the beautiful city of Newcastle. Through his passion, belief, and love for the game, he inspired so many people, myself included."

Ex-Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher: "One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies and goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

"One of the most important men in making LFC what it is today."

BBC Radio 5 Live senior football reporter Ian Dennis: "Really sad news. He had such a magnetic character. He was mesmeric as a player and a person. This is really sad news. Condolences to his family, friends and former colleagues.

"Everything he did, he put his heart and soul in to everything."

Ex-Liverpool striker John Aldridge: "The great Kevin Keegan has passed away. He gave me great joy in my teens as a huge LFC fan, and the saying says never meet your heroes? Well I did! Roger Hunt and KK, and they surpassed everything I thought they were as people. Our thoughts are with all his family. God bless, Kevin. YNWA."

Former Liverpool defender Mark Lawrenson: "He had time for everybody. You wouldn't say that he was completely gifted as a footballer but he worked like stink to get himself even better and quicker. He was such a lovely man. It's a very sad afternoon.

"Opposition supporters would actually clap when he came on the pitch which is very seldom to do."

Ex-Newcastle striker Mick Quinn: "I knew Kevin didn't have long left and was getting a daily bulletin of his health in recent days.

"Sadly he has passed, it was a privilege to worship him as a kid playing for Liverpool then to get to work with him professionally and get to know him personally. R. I. P Kevin."

League Managers Association chief executive Richard Bevan OBE: "Kevin Keegan stands among the most decorated and iconic figures in English football history. He will be remembered with immense respect, admiration and affection."

Former Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft: "Kevin Keegan, one of the superstars of our game, has passed away. For us who discovered football in the 70s he was 'the one'.

"Later I had the pleasure to meet him, and he was such a nice and passionate guy. One part of his legacy will be that generations adored him regardless which team you supported. RIP."

Ex-Tottenham centre-back Ramon Vega: "So sad. What a player and what a character as a manager! Kevin, you brought quality and greatness to the game. Thank you. R. I. P."

Hamas names Khalil al-Hayya as new overall leader

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:02:31 GMT

The Palestinian armed group Hamas has elected Khalil al-Hayya as its new leader, according to a statement.

He replaces Yahya Sinwar, who was killed by the Israeli military in Gaza in October 2024.

Hayya, who already headed the movement in Gaza from exile, was widely seen as representing the more hardline faction that emerged from the devastating war with Israel that began almost three years ago. He was a close associate of Sinwar and is seen as continuing the political line going back to the late Ismail Haniyeh.

As the chief negotiator for Hamas, Hayya gained international prominence by leading the group's delegations at indirect ceasefire talks, meeting mediators in Egypt and Qatar.

He had recently taken on greater responsibility for Hamas's diplomatic and political strategies.

In September 2025, the 65-year-old survived an Israeli air strike that targeted a meeting of Hamas leaders in the Qatari capital, Doha. Five lower-level members of the group, including one of his sons, were killed along with a member of Qatar's security forces.

Israel's prime minister said at the time that it targeted the Hamas leaders because they had organised the attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war.

Another two of Hayya's sons were killed in previous Israeli attempts on his life in Gaza, while a fourth was killed ​in an Israeli air strike in Gaza in May.

Hayya's election as head of Hamas's political bureau followed two rounds of voting, with members apparently split between competing visions for the future direction of the group.

The first round was inconclusive, with former political bureau chief Khaled Meshaal narrowly winning more votes than Hayya, but failing to pass the required threshold, according to a well-informed Palestinian official familiar with the election.

Under Hamas's internal rules, a candidate must secure at least 36 votes from the 69-member electoral college to be elected outright.

It is understood that the second round run-off was decided by a first-past-the-post vote.

Hamas is going through one of the most difficult periods in its history.

The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK, the US and many other countries - has been severely weakened by the Gaza war, during which much of its senior military and political leadership has been killed, its governing structures dismantled, and large parts of the Palestinian territory have been destroyed.

The leadership contest has exposed a widening strategic divide within Hamas over its future.

Meshaal, who previously led the movement for decades while in exile, is associated with Hamas's traditional leadership.

His supporters have argued that Hamas should draw lessons from the war, move away from a strategy centred primarily on armed confrontation, and adopt a more pragmatic political approach while preserving the movement's core objectives.

However, supporters of Hayya successfully argued that Gaza's leadership, having borne the brunt of the conflict, should now lead the movement. They want to remain firm against pressure to make major concessions, particularly over the issue of disarmament.

Since it agreed a ceasefire deal with Israel last October, Hamas has refused to give up its weapons without a guaranteed political path to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. Hamas complains that there is a lack of security guarantees against continuing Israeli attacks and emerging rival armed groups.

About 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage in the 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel.

Israel responded by launching a massive military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,280 people have been killed, including 1,158 since the ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

Separately, in a letter to MPs in June, Ofcom said it would examine the findings of Channel 4's review into welfare on the show, and would "urgently" consider whether any further action is required.

At the time, the watchdog called the allegations exposed by Panorama "shocking and deeply disturbing".

Earlier this month, BBC News revealed that a cast member from the show had been arrested on suspicion of rape following the Panorama programme.

The individual is not being named; nor is the alleged victim. Anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.

Billed as a "bold social experiment", Married at First Sight UK - known to many as MAFS - sees single people agree to "marry" total strangers, after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.

The UK version, which has been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

In May, Channel 4 pulled all episodes of the show from its streaming service just hours ahead of the transmission of the Panorama investigation.

No decision has yet been made on whether to broadcast the latest series of the show, which has already been filmed.

The broadcaster has commissioned a review into contributor welfare on the show, which is due to be finished later this summer. However, it only intends to publish "a summary of findings", rather than the full report.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, have previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading.

Rare identical quadruplets born in Australia

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 12:57:32 GMT

An Australian woman has given birth to rare, naturally-conceived identical quadruplets after a pregnancy described as "extremely high risk" by the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital.

The four girls, who were delivered via caesarean section at 28 weeks and four days on 14 July, were monozygotic quadruplets - where a single fertilised egg splits into four embryos.

The hospital said the girls' mother, 34-year-old Jenitar Na'amoana, and her husband Jortham, already had four children and were taken by "immense surprise" when told to expect quadruplets.

Dr Alexa Bendall, who cared for the mother from the start of her pregnancy, estimated identical quadruplets occur "at one in every 15 million pregnancies" and said "but to share the same placenta - this is unheard of".

Bendall, who is a maternal foetal medicine specialist and obstetrician, said such a pregnancy was very high-risk, with the hospital admitting Na'amoana as an inpatient at 25 weeks so she could be monitored.

"We always said that if we could get her to 28 weeks, we would be doing well," Bendall said.

"So the fact that we've got four beautiful, healthy babies born at 28 weeks and four days is incredible and we're very happy to be a part of it," she added.

"Jenitar has taken everything in her stride from day one... she has somehow dodged every complication and risk for both herself and her babies," Bendall said.

The newborn girls have been named Emily, Harriet, Catherine, and also Alexa, after Alexa Bendall, who described it as "a beautiful tribute".

The babies will stay in the hospital's neonatal intensive care unit until they grow to full term and are "currently doing extremely well", Bendall added.

The parents' other children are between one and 10 years old and the mother has recently launched an online fundraising campaign to help buy a van with at least 10 seats.

In a message alongside the fundraiser, which has already received over A$37,000 (£19,261) in donations, Na'amoana wrote: "Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges we never could have imagined."

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, with doctors estimating the odds at about one in 700,000 births.

Hunter-gatherers introduced fish to a mountain lake 7000 years ago

New Scientist July 19, 2026

Hunter-gatherers transported brown trout into the mountains of Norway at least 7000 years ago so they could be harvested during summer foraging trips into the highlands.

That is the only possible explanation for how fish could have populated isolated mountain lakes that had been covered by a kilometres-thick ice sheet for tens of thousands of years, says Axel Mjærum at the University of Oslo, Norway.

Ancient DNA may rewrite the story of Iceland’s earliest settlers

“This is the oldest documented example of human-mediated translocation of fish in the world,” says Mjærum.

Advertisement

Until around 8400 years ago, Lake Tesse, at an elevation of around 850 metres, was covered by the Fennoscandian ice sheet, leaving an ecological blank canvas once it retreated.

Yet before it was transformed for hydropower storage in the 1940s, Lake Tesse was regarded as one of the richest brown trout waterways in Norway, yielding 9 tonnes of the fish annually.

Subscriber-only newsletter

While it has long been suspected that humans had a hand in establishing the brown trout population in Lake Tesse, we had no idea how long ago this happened.

Alternative ideas have included transportation by birds or natural migration of fish and eggs upstream. But most Norwegian mountain lakes, including Lake Tesse, only had brown trout until recently, and geographical features such as large waterfalls make natural dispersal upstream impossible.

Mjærum and his colleagues studied the partially buried remains of elaborate wooden fish traps, discovered in 2022 when the lake level was lowered.

Radiocarbon dating showed that the oldest trap dated from around 4950 BC. By correlating the recovered wood with the pine tree ring chronology available for the central Scandinavian mountains, the team was also able to precisely date some of the posts that were part of the younger traps.

One came from a tree felled between spring 2669 BC and winter 2669-2668 BC, and another 12 years later during the winter of 2657-2656 BC, demonstrating that the traps must have been maintained to keep them in good working order.

“Therefore, it is possible that this form of trap fishing was ongoing in Tesse during much of the period between 5000 and 2650 BC,” says Mjærum.

The surprising origins of Britain’s Bronze Age immigrants revealed

The transport of fish into the lakes is an early example of people managing the environment to provide food, centuries before the advent of farming in Scandinavia. There is evidence that fish farming began even earlier in other parts of the world, including channels and traps for catching eels built in Australia 8600 years ago.

How people transported the fish is unknown, but they may have used waterskins. People probably stayed in the mountains for part of the summer season, hunting reindeer and fishing, but spent the winters in the valleys or along the coast where the climate was milder, says Mjærum.

“A good and predictable food supply also made longer stays possible, not only for hunters aiming for big game, but for whole family groups,” he says.

Inhaling high-dose CO2 clears Alzheimer’s proteins from the brain

New Scientist July 20, 2026

Inhaling high levels of carbon dioxide intermittently for half an hour flushes proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease out of the brain, a small study has found. Exposure to the gas changes how blood vessels in the brain constrict and dilate while we’re awake, mimicking activity that occurs during deep sleep. This then turbocharges the glymphatic system to remove the build-up of waste products that could cause harm.

A 2025 study suggests the same approach could help with Parkinson’s disease, by clearing the protein alpha-synuclein. “If you have any condition that is due to or exacerbated by any sort of accumulation of waste, this could be something beneficial,” says Sephira Ryman at the University of Texas at Austin.

Alzheimer’s, stroke, depression: The preventative power of sauna

The brain’s waste-disposal, or glymphatic, system is comprised of a network of channels surrounding blood vessels that collect waste fluid released from brain cells. It is most active during deep sleep, when slow brain waves drive blood vessels to dilate and constrict about once every 30 seconds.

Advertisement

“This dilation and constriction essentially serves as a pump that clears waste from the brain,” says Ryman, who presented the results last week at the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference in London.

To mimic this pumping while people are awake, Ryman and her colleagues made use of the fact that breathing raised levels of carbon dioxide causes blood vessels to temporarily dilate, as the body tries harder to get rid of the gas and supply more oxygen to tissues.

The team recruited 12 people, of whom eight had no signs of cognitive impairment and normal levels of tau, a protein that can misfold and form tangles in Alzheimer’s disease. The four other participants had elevated levels of a form of tau in their blood, suggesting high levels in their brain, and three had mild cognitive impairment.

Free newsletter

All the participants had their brains scanned while wearing a mask that switched between delivering air made up of about 0.05 per cent carbon dioxide – like the amount we inhale with every breath – to 5 per cent carbon dioxide. This switch happened every 35 seconds for half an hour.

The researchers found that intermittent exposure to high carbon dioxide levels caused the brain’s blood vessels to pump as they do during deep sleep, driving the glymphatic system.

The team also collected blood samples before and after the half-hour session. Fifteen minutes later, levels of a form of the protein called beta-amyloid – which is similarly found in healthy brains but forms clumps during Alzheimer’s disease – had increased in the blood of all the participants. “This suggests this neurodegenerative marker was being cleared more out of the brain,” says Ryman.

The intervention also seemed to boost the clearance of tau, but only among those with signs of cognitive decline. This may be because this group had more tau in their brains in the first place, says Ryman.

Boosting the brain’s waste-disposal system is increasingly showing promise for Alzheimer’s disease, with a study now suggesting that a novel approach eases brain deficits and symptoms associated with the condition

But an around an hour after the intervention ended, the amyloid and tau-clearing benefits had returned to baseline. Further studies need to explore whether this has an impact on Alzheimer’s disease risk or progression in the long-term, and how often you’d need to do it, says Vincent Tay at Changi General Hospital in Singapore.

“We just don’t know yet whether targeting clearance with an approach like this really is going to affect cognitive decline,” says Jeff Iliff at the University of Washington in Seattle. “The interesting thing though is that stimulating these [glymphatic] clearance mechanisms is not specific to amyloid, but it can help clear amyloid, tau, alpha-synuclein and inflammatory molecules, so you could imagine the approach could have a much wider effect on the brain, and could have a much broader application that transcends Alzheimer’s disease.”

Safety also needs to be monitored long-term, although none of the participants experienced any side effects. The researchers could also explore delivering the intervention via a portable device at home, says Ryman. This may be preferable to existing ways of boosting the glymphatic system, which typically involve drugs, she says.

A mathematician has cracked an 87-year-old conundrum with the help of AI and announced the solution unceremoniously in a tweet. The finding is the most difficult mathematical problem yet solved by AI, say experts.

Levent Alpöge at Harvard University wrote on X on 19 July that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

The Jacobian conjecture – which suggests that a certain type of mathematical function would also work in reverse – was formally set out by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939. It was also on an influential list of 18 fiendishly difficult problems for mathematicians to tackle in the 21st century drawn up by Stephen Smale in 1998.

Advertisement

Alpöge did not respond to New Scientist’s request for interview, but said in his tweet that part of the work was down to his “close friend fable”- seemingly referring to AI company Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5. Alpöge thanked Fable for working during the World Cup final.

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Free newsletter

Abhishek Saha at Queen Mary University of London says AI’s recent advances in mathematics, such as the OpenAI model that recently cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, have been surprising, but this latest finding has stepped things up significantly.

“Probably this is the biggest conjecture that AI has played a significant role [in proving or disproving] so far in mathematics,” he says. “This is a pretty big deal. AI has [made] remarkable progress in the last year.”

The single line of mathematics posted by Alpöge was simple to verify and many mathematicians have already done so, says Saha. Now the big question is how it was done.

“There are some problems that are very hard to solve but once a solution is there, they are relatively easy to check. So this is like that,” he says. “I don’t know how he did it, what exactly was the prompt to give Fable, because if one were to search everything, it wouldn’t quite work, so obviously there was some insight also which is not currently published.”

Saha says both the appearance and the nature of the result is a surprise. “People have been trying to prove it [the Jacobian conjecture] because it sounds, intuitively, very true. I don’t think that many people have been trying to disprove it. And now we have this one-sentence counterexample,” he says.

Mathematicians solve 125-year-old problem to unite key laws of physics

There are still open questions, says Saha. For example, this new counterexample disproves the conjecture with three variables, but a version with two variables could theoretically still be true.

Chris Bowman-Scargill at the University of York, UK, says mathematicians have in some ways already adjusted to the shocking new capabilities of AI, but there is a difference between finding counterexamples that disprove conjectures and building whole new branches of mathematics, which still requires human creativity.

“If you look at Fermat’s last theorem [which was solved by Andrew Wiles in 1994], you had to create a hundred pages of new mathematics – you had to build a whole big theory in order to solve a conjecture,” says Bowman-Scargill. “And often the interesting stuff in maths isn’t ‘oh, we’ve ticked off this conjecture, yay’, it’s more the stuff you have to build along the way in order to solve the conjecture.”

“I think [AI] has sort of proven that it can do this, so you’re now like, OK, what next?,” he says.

Ivan Fesenko at Westlake University in China believes what comes next is increasingly capable AI models that will solve ever more complex problems, disrupting the field as they go.

“Right now, AI can already produce master’s degrees in mathematics. In one year, they will produce PhD degrees in mathematics. And then the question arises, do we really need so many mathematicians around if AI can do such things so nicely?” says Fesenko. “So basically we’re talking about fundamental change in mathematics.”

How to maximise the mental health benefits of your vacation

New Scientist July 20, 2026

Like many people, I spend much of my time at home fantasising about my next holiday. During the trip itself, most of my stresses seem to melt away, and I return feeling optimistic and energised.

Each time, I am determined to integrate those feelings into my day-to-day life, but I am almost invariably disappointed. Within a couple of weeks – sometimes less, depending on how much time I have to spend on the London Underground – I become the same irritable and frustrated person that I always was. And so, I start dreaming about my next escape.

As I planned a recent trip to Madrid, I wondered whether I was foolish to hope that my travels would offer anything more than temporary relief.

Advertisement

Why you need to future-proof your brain in middle age and how to start

Delving into the psychological literature, though, I was relieved to see that the answer is a resounding no. Growing evidence explains the specific ways that our holidays can increase our wellbeing and, crucially, the types of activities that will offer the greatest restoration, based on the ancient Greek principle of eudaimonia: “human flourishing”.

“Instead of thinking only about where you are going to travel, you can think about what psychological experience you want the vacation to provide, and try to create that experience,” says Nanxi Yan, a psychologist at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

A serious consideration of holiday psychology has been a long time coming: until recently, psychologists studying wellbeing had mostly focused on the benefits of relaxation and leisure activities more generally. There have been plenty of studies on reading, for instance, while the research on vacations was patchy. As a result, they failed to capture the distinct opportunities for a mental reset that holidays can afford away from the daily grind. “From a psychological perspective, that separation is quite important,” says Yan.

Consider a recent review of the literature, published last year. Analysing the results of 32 different studies, Ryan Grant at the University of Georgia has shown that the average mood boost begins before we have even left home, as the anticipation of a trip builds. Those good feelings remain highly elevated for at least 21 days after we have returned home and may not return to the baseline for a further three weeks.

If you, like me, struggle to feel those longer-lasting benefits, it may be because you have been focusing on the “wrong” kind of happiness. Behavioural scientist Graeme McLean at the University of St Andrews Business School in the UK argues that we should distinguish between hedonic wellbeing, which concerns enjoyment and pleasure, and eudaimonic wellbeing, which concerns “personal growth, sense of purpose and meaning”.

“On holiday, hedonic wellbeing might come from lounging on a beach, enjoying nice food or staying in a lovely hotel,” he says. “Eudaimonic wellbeing might come from the sense of achievement in completing a challenging hike, learning about a new culture or forming connections with fellow travellers.”

Free newsletter

Studying 462 holiday-makers, McLean and his colleague Mohammed Aldossary at King Faisal University in Saudi Arabia found that the boost in hedonic wellbeing faded pretty quickly, whereas the eudaimonic feelings lingered for at least eight weeks. For this reason, he recommends planning holidays that combine both elements – pure relaxation alongside the kinds of activities that feel more purposeful.

Yan agrees. “Travel can also expose people to novelty, different cultures, new activities and different versions of themselves,” she says – and it is here that the biggest benefits lie. “These experiences may help people not only feel rested, but also feel more alive, connected and reflective.”

So, what can we do to achieve it? Based on the available research on both hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing, Yan and her colleagues distilled the key elements to think about (see below).

You don’t have to include every single element, but you may benefit from reflecting on the list and deciding which are most significant to you. “For example, if relatedness is very important, you might want to prioritise meaningful time with family, friends or a partner, rather than trying to do too many activities,” says Yan. To maximise autonomy, “it helps to build in freedom and flexibility”, she says. “A vacation that is too tightly scheduled can become another source of pressure.”

Mastery, meanwhile, might involve attending an art class or learning to scuba dive, and the need for novelty might encourage you to try to experience a whole new culture, rather than returning to a familiar destination.

That may take more serious attention than you currently pay to your travel plans. “Do not treat vacations only as time off. Think about what kind of psychological needs the vacation can satisfy,” says Yan. The hard work may pay off immediately. “Our research showed that merely anticipating an upcoming vacation can boost wellbeing, so the planning and looking-forward phase has value in itself,” says McLean. “It’s better to book early!”

If you are worried about protecting your purse strings, rest assured that you can glean many of these benefits from shorter trips – in fact, the greatest relief may come from just five or six days away. Nor do the activities have to be exceptionally luxurious: in Grant’s meta-analysis, physical exercise proved to be one of the best predictors of enhanced wellbeing, and that can be achieved through long walks or visits to outdoor gyms.

You may not even have to leave your home city, provided that you take those psychological needs seriously enough and don’t simply spend the time catching up on other responsibilities. When planned correctly, taking some time off at home can still be beneficial, says Yan. “For example, people can create boundaries around work, avoid routine chores during the holiday period, try new local activities, spend quality time with others, visit nearby nature or create small rituals that make the time feel different from ordinary life.”

Whether you are travelling abroad or staying at home, you should try to find ways to immerse yourself in the memories of the experiences after your break has ended. Along these lines, McLean also found that using virtual-reality headsets to return to the location of their holidays significantly prolonged the wellbeing benefits experienced by his study participants.

We can’t all afford this technology, of course, but he suggests some lo-fi alternatives. “Deeply engaging with holiday memories – perhaps through journaling about the experience in vivid detail, creating a rich photo or video montage that you actively revisit, or even planning a return trip to the same destination – might tap into similar psychological pathways, though this would need further research to be confirmed.”

In our efforts to keep our brains healthy, how do we know what is working? Helen Thomson explores a new generation of tests that can reveal whether our efforts are paying off

“The underlying factor is about re-engaging psychologically with the vacation experience in a rich, immersive way,” says McLean. You are unlikely to get this from passively scrolling through your photos; it needs your full attention.

Attempting to put all this into practice on my trip to Madrid, I made a greater effort to chat to locals in Spanish, maximising my sense of autonomy and mastery; attended a concert by one of my favourite singers, an experience that was imbued with meaning; and visited the city’s botanical gardens, which helped me connect to nature.

It has now been six weeks since I returned, and the warm glow remains. My sunnier mood may be slowly fading, but it hasn’t yet been extinguished. Now, I’m dreaming of my next trip.
