Hannah Spencer’s proposal for maximum workplace temperatures (Green MP Hannah Spencer to introduce bill on maximum workplace temperatures, 12 July) highlights an increasingly urgent issue for employers and policymakers alike. While legislation may help provide clarity in the future, businesses should not wait for a maximum legal limit before acting to protect workers.

Extreme temperatures can have a serious impact on worker health and safety as they can impair concentration and increase fatigue, both of which raise the likelihood of accidents.

The law already requires employers to provide a reasonable indoor workplace temperature. Bosses are also required to assess workplace risks and take reasonably practicable steps to protect people. For hot weather, this can include amending work schedules, moving physically demanding tasks to cooler parts of the day, providing shaded rest areas and free access to drinking water, and relaxing dress codes where appropriate.

The debate over a UK maximum workplace temperature is an important one. But workers need protection now, not after new legislation has worked its way through parliament.

Good employers will recognise that safeguarding staff during heatwaves is not simply about compliance; it is also about preventing harm and demonstrating a genuine commitment to a safe, healthy and productive workforce. Wet paper towels and ice pops are inadequate. Our education system needs to build climate resilience – and fast.

Climate action plans, required in schools by the Department for Education, are helpful. But, while there are pockets of good practice, the country needs a more systematic approach. School leaders and teachers require clear, practical and detailed guidance to take the best action against extreme weather.

We can learn resilience from other countries experiencing record-breaking temperatures. In India and Pakistan, where we offer climate literacy courses, Cambridge researchers have studied how school buildings are using techniques like natural vegetation to cool school spaces and protect academic attainment. Since Covid, Cambridge OCR has been calling for a more resilient and flexible approach to assessment.

In June in Bonn, I spoke on a UN climate conference panel with Unicef on loss and damage caused by climate change. My message was that if we invest in resilient education systems, we will not only help children recover from crisis but enable them to shape their own futures. The UK is in crisis too, and education must be factored into practical adaptation plans.

Young, old, midlife – whatever your age, gender or sector, the unemployment crisis is hitting us all. The only way through it is together

The personal experience of long-term unemployment is one people rarely share, for completely understandable reasons. There’s a bit of superstition that saying it out loud will bed it in, and there’s always one person in 100 who will choose to explain away the misfortune as your own personal failing.

Even if they’re clearly in the grip of superstitions of their own – trying to ward off your fate for themselves – it’s hard not to take criticism personally in such a personal situation. The conventions of human interaction are that you shouldn’t really mention a cloud unless you have a silver lining handy. For instance: after the financial crash in 2008, I remember hearing a couple interviewed on the radio who had both been made redundant when the private school they worked for closed down. After describing months of fruitless job applications, the wife ended saying they’d been able to spend much more time in their allotment, and she reckoned their rocket yield alone had saved them a small fortune. That, I thought, is a remarkable and yet probably universal commitment to looking on the bright side.

So when someone breaks the omertà – as Stacey Duguid did on Instagram three weeks ago – the conversation explodes like any that’s been waiting a long time to happen.

Duguid, 52, after a varied and high-achieving career in fashion and journalism, has spent more than a year sending out 150 job applications, many of which don’t even get replies. When she said that out loud, thousands of women messaged her with similar experiences. Accordingly, it has been taken as an “older woman” or, more bluntly, a perimenopause story, which is borne out by the data – 30% of women aged 50 to 64 are economically inactive in the UK, against 22% of men – but I’d want to see more field work before I’d settle for hormones as the main reason.

Age-wise, this is also peak time for the “sandwich years”. They’re called that to describe a person trapped between childcare and elderly parents, and the term is not especially accurate, since childcare and end-of-life care are as different from one another as two bits of bread are similar. But as euphemisms go, it works, because what could be more practical and manageable than a sandwich?

By contrast, keeping regular working hours while remaining available for the sudden and irregular crises that attend the end of a life is completely impossible. My sister quit her job while our mum was dying, and it was only because she did that I didn’t have to. In other words: yes, the gender split makes sense, but no, more HRT probably isn’t the silver bullet, and don’t even start looking for a lining. This is a silver-free scenario.

For many at the start of their careers, things are just as bad. Government analysis last month insisted that entry-level positions were declining in line with the rest of the job market, but the general feeling that AI is wiping out starter jobs is backed up by research. The sectors worst hit are the most AI-friendly – software engineers, accountants, legal assistants, data analysts. A year ago, figures showed new graduate vacancies had dropped by a third since the arrival of ChatGPT. Applicants themselves describe the harrowing experience of being rejected in less than the time it would have taken for any human to read their application – in other words, by AI.

This creates a pipeline problem for employers, who will eventually land in a world where there’s no one to fill the middle tier of their staff hierarchy with the experience of having done the grunt work at the bottom. But being able to say “serves you right”, not even to a person but to a sector, lacks some quality of emotional satisfaction.

Can ageism be the issue, in a system that punishes the workforce at both ends, and traps everyone who has a job in a terrorised, scarcity mindset? Is AI really on the brink of making all human endeavour obsolete, or have AI companies just made some vast claims for it that shortsighted employers are choosing to believe, ultimately at their own expense? We’ll never find out in generational or gender silos, and the code of silence isn’t helping, either. It’s important to keep your skills updated, the employment coaches always say – the trait this modern world demands is openness. Only in talking about worklessness does it become clear: it’s not a you problem, it’s an everyone problem.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Ensure children can play outside independently

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 16:26:47 GMT

Urban transport policies and residential design need to respect outdoor play as a vital necessity for children, says Ellen Weaver

In the brilliant Swiss research cited by Lenore Skenazy (If you want your kids to thrive this summer, don’t just turn off their phones – open your front door, too, 15 July), young children playing unsupervised was culturally accepted and normal. The children in the Swiss study who did not play outside independently were prevented from doing so by traffic.

Yes, we need to relieve parents of the horrendous pressure of cultural expectation that children will always be supervised, but parents can’t open their doors for children to go out and play in traffic. Urban transport policies and residential design need to respect outdoor play as a vital necessity for children.

The Swiss research proved that playgrounds don’t meet children’s needs for play. In the study, the parents of children who couldn’t play out where they lived frequently took them to playgrounds. Nevertheless, those children were significantly limited in their personal confidence, cognitive development, social abilities, and fine and gross motor skills, compared with children who played out by their homes, where the amount and quality of play was far greater.

You recently reported that UK children will be one of unhealthiest generations in decades. In much of the rest of Europe, it is still normal for children to go places without an adult taking them. Children meet up with friends to play in public spaces without anyone calling the police – no wonder they’re much more active, confident and healthy. The consequences are disastrous and enormously costly when we prevent children from access to sufficient free play and independence.

Tech companies must be made to end harmful, addictive content, but we shouldn’t be surprised that children play virtually when so often they cannot actually play where they live. Andy Burnham should join the dots, take play seriously and appoint a minister for children. Ellen WeaverHartland, Devon

Burnham pledges to end rough sleeping in England in first speech as prime minister

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:55:21 GMT

Additional £340m over three years allocated to get people off the streets ‘at the earliest opportunity’

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham has promised to end rough sleeping in England in his first pledge as prime minister, allocating an additional £340m over three years as he seeks to replicate the homelessness schemes he rolled out in Greater Manchester.

Speaking in front of Downing Street immediately after becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would try to get people off the streets “at the earliest opportunity”.

The announcement was welcomed by homelessness campaigners, who say the pledge can be met with enough money and political will.

The prime minister’s critics, however, greeted the promise with scepticism, pointing out that despite having set out a similar goal as Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham had overseen four years of rising street homelessness.

Burnham said on Monday: “On my first day as prime minister, I’m announcing this government’s commitment to finally end long-term rough sleeping across the UK at the earliest opportunity.

“We’ll get to work immediately, bringing together national and local government with the investment needed to get it done.”

Officials said the government would now put an extra £340m into its homelessness strategy – equivalent to £113m a year – which would come from unused parts of the housing department’s budget.

They said the money would pay for 1,200 new homes and help support 3,000 people over five years.

The money comes on top of £3.5bn, the previous government’s allocation for its homelessness strategy, which ministers said at the time was designed to halve the rates of long-term rough sleeping.

Steve Reed, the housing secretary who oversaw that strategy, was sacked from his post on Monday as Burnham began the process of putting his cabinet together.

Burnham’s promise, which the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn had planned to announce if elected prime minister, aims to emulate the success of the “Everyone In” policy which the government briefly enacted during the Covid pandemic.

It also echoes a pledge he made when he was running for the Greater Manchester mayoralty in 2017, when he promised to eliminate rough sleeping in Manchester within three years if elected.

After he won that election, he had some early success with his homelessness policy, both with his rough sleeping programme, known as A Bed Every Night, and his broader scheme to tackle long-term homelessness, called Housing First.

In his first five years as mayor, rough sleeping dropped by two-thirds, which supporters say showed the merits of corralling different parts of government around the same aim.

Those in Manchester at the time say Burnham was able to use his position as mayor to force greater collaboration between different councils and government bodies to tackle the problem.

For example, he made the 10 councils under his jurisdiction share data so that someone who was rough sleeping in Bolton, for example, could also be tracked if they came into central Manchester during the day.

He also made sure landlords did not evict tenants because of relatively minor misdemeanours, which experts say is a major cause of street homelessness.

Shabnum Mustapha, a former official at the Greater Manchester mayoralty, said: “In the early days it was hard, trying to bring together a bunch of statutory agencies and organisations which have been working on this problem for decades and decades.

“But by taking a big tent approach, working with different councils, other parties and organisations such as faith groups, he had a lot of success.”

Critics, however, point out that in each of the past four years, rough sleeping has risen, so the level is now three-quarters of what it was in 2017.

Supporters say rates were difficult to keep down after the national government ended its pandemic support schemes. His opponents, however, accuse Burnham of having taken his focus off one of his foundational policies.

James Cleverly, the shadow housing secretary, said: “His record in Manchester showed initial success, then failure once his focus shifted. It looks like he’s taking money from local projects to fund this announcement, so lots of the country will be disappointed.”

No tears from Keir as Burnham strolls into No 10 with the clock already ticking

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:34:13 GMT

Rapid turnover of prime ministers continues as UK gets another promise that, this time, things will be different

UK politics live – latest updates

Not another one. It would be no surprise to find out that overseas tour companies now include package holiday visits to watch the UK’s rapid turnover of prime ministers. “Come to London to watch the motorcade nearly run over a group of fancy dress soldiers playing a Bon Jovi medley just outside Buckingham Palace.” Two years is a long time in the lifetime of a UK leader. Liz Truss was in and out in seconds. Our buy one, get one free prime minister. In Britain, we sure know how to Dance Me to the End of Love.

Still, practice makes perfect and we now have the handover of power nailed to a T. Everyone knows exactly what they are doing. Even King Charles, who is now on to his fourth prime minister in as many years. Though presumably he’s moderately pissed off about having to go to Buckingham Palace for 90 minutes to do the business. I guess he has to take the rough with the smooth. After all, he’s managed to get his subjects to pay for its upkeep even though he can’t be arsed to live there.

At about 10.30am “Hot Podium Guy” – actually, it’s a lectern – appeared in Downing Street to set things up for Keir Starmer’s farewell speech, and a while later a large crowd of former cabinet colleagues, No 10 staff and friends and supporters began to assemble in a semi-circle outside the front door. Then out came Keir with his wife, Vic. Both smiled and looked almost relieved that it was all over. An end to months of speculation followed by a weeks-long protracted exit.

Sometimes these events are emotional for the outgoing prime minister. But there was no sign of any tears. Keir can now enjoy the next six weeks of the summer with his family, safe in the knowledge that no one is going to wake him at three in the morning with the news that Donald Trump has just started a third world war.

Instead, he chose to keep his speech short and sweet. To say that his work was done. That he was leaving the country in a stronger and fairer place. Which is probably true. Just not strong and fair enough for us to have noticed and for him to have been able to persuade us.

But that’s part of Keir’s personal tragedy. He governed and led in the dullest of prose, unable to construct a narrative that could take you with him. Yet no matter how many of these prime ministerial send-offs I see, they are never not affecting. It’s like seeing someone being airbrushed out of history in real time. You can almost see them disappearing in front of your eyes. First they live in colour before rapidly turning to sepia and by the end they are barely even a pencil outline. Keir who?

And now even his legacy won’t be his to control. Anything bad that happens in the next three years will be blamed on him. And anything good, Andy Burnham will claim as his own. It was always thus. Keir ended by thanking everyone for joining him on his journey. The British people, colleagues and family. Though presumably not Peter Mandelson. He probably wishes he had never met Mandy. “I leave with good grace and a smile,” he said. And he did. There was no Boris Johnson temper tantrum. Rachel Reeves looked a bit glum, mind. Inside No 10, Larry the Cat sharpened his claws and scratched another notch into the back of the door. His sixth.

With that, Keir got into the car and headed off to Buck House to take his leave of the king. And it was time for Fiona Bruce and “senior” – is there really a junior? – royal reporter Daniela Relph to talk pure bollocks for the best part of an hour and a half. The role of royal correspondent must be the most thankless job in journalism. Years wasted having to infer meaning from a new hairstyle or who gets to sit where. So we were breathlessly told that Keir would be arriving at the “luggage door” – who doesn’t have one of those? – before being taken to the Chinese dining room. Presumably soon to become sponsored and renamed the KFC dining room.

A while later, Keir left, soon to be replaced by Andy and his wife, Marie-France. “He will be kissing the king’s hand,” said an overexcited Daniela, “though of course he won’t actually be kissing the king’s hand.” I mean, who really gives a flying fuck? Next we were told that Andy might have been dreaming about this moment for a while. Where’s Sigmund Freud when you need him? “Andy got 35 minutes with the king. A little longer than Keir.” I’m sure Keir will be devastated.

Back in Downing Street, Andy’s old muckers were beginning to assemble, Keir’s having been hurried off the premises. There was the former Everton footballer Peter Reid, the eco entrepreneur Dale Vince and the mayor of Liverpool city region, Steve Rotheram, who was holding his grandson. Monday is his day on the babysitting rota. There was no getting out of it. Not even to see a mate become prime minister.

Then the arrival of Andy at his new address. Hugs and kisses for various people in the crowd – a special one for his mum – and then he walked towards the microphone. The lectern had long since been put back inside. Andy was going to do this speechlet from the heart, with no notes. That should give Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch something to think about. Life is about to get a lot more difficult for the opposition parties.

Steve Bray had been banned from using his PA machine – he’s had a habit of wrecking every Downing Street speech – but you could still just about hear him singing Beethoven’s Ode to Joy from outside the gates. But Andy wasn’t bothered.

This was to be short and sweet. Mainly a precis of what he had said when he became leader of the Labour party on Friday. A mention that people were fed up with a politics that produced seven prime ministers since 2016. He would do things differently. Be better. They all say that. But he sounded more persuasive. A poet with imagination in his heart, who could connect.

He would give the country some breathing space from the cost of living. Starting from tomorrow. It wasn’t clear what he meant, but it sounded good. He would end rough sleeping. Something he had failed to do in Manchester. Good for him for not having given up on it. Though still a hostage to fortune.

“I will give it my all,” he said. It was the time for common purpose and positivity. Good luck with that. You could hear the country reply: “We’ll be the judge of that.” You’ve got a couple of years, Andy. The clock is ticking.

What’s left after this World Cup? A kind of messy hope

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:20:52 GMT

Kazakhs cheering Uzbeks, Bengalis wild for Argentina … This tournament was once a playground for nationalism. Now it shows how flimsy that allegiance is

It’s the World Cup final, so you pick a side. And don’t worry if you happen to be part of the 98.9% of the human race that is neither Spanish nor Argentinian – just make something up. Maybe you like the Spain kit. Maybe you’ve always been an admirer of Lionel Messi. Maybe you’re still raw about the Falklands or Diego Maradona, maybe you disagree with the Pedro Sánchez government’s stance on Palestine/Israel, maybe you once ate a dodgy empanada on your gap year. Nobody needs to see your working. Only two rules really apply: be partisan and be quick about it.

The MetLife Stadium on Sunday night was a melting pot of colliding incongruities and temporary identities. The former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson was wearing an Argentina shirt. The comedian Trevor Noah wore a Spain shirt. Indeed, ticket sales data suggests that an overwhelming proportion of the crowd was American. The most consequential fixture in international sport was, as it turned out, little more than a grand cosplay for the New Jersey leisure market.

And beyond the final, perhaps this has been one of the hidden stories of the World Cup: the gradual reimagining of national allegiance as a kind of single-use consumer brand. For six weeks, the entire nation of Bangladesh went crazy for Argentina. A group of central Asian friends in north London put aside their internecine rivalries to cheer for Uzbekistan. The Arab diaspora swung firmly behind Morocco and Egypt as the tournament progressed. Leftwing progressives who revile the cross of St George when painted on a mini-roundabout were suddenly daubing it on their cheeks.

All of which upends what we have been told for decades about the World Cup, and international sport in general. A tournament that should in theory be the ultimate playground for nationalism has in fact demonstrated the very opposite: the increasing fragility of nationhood as an idea. What the social psychologist Michael Billig termed banal nationalism – the subliminal everyday symbols of nationhood – has now become so banal as to be in essence disposable. If national identity is now something that can be slipped on and off as easily as a football shirt, then what use is it, really?

We live in an age where the boundaries of nationhood are both ever-more piercingly evoked and ever-more hazily defined. Again, football illustrates this confusion better than almost any other human endeavour. Across western Europe, far-right voices preach the doctrine of nationalism while reviling their own national teams for having too many black players. In Colombia and Brazil, many leftwing fans have chosen to spurn the national team shirt as a result of its appropriation by rightwing populists.

This is before we even address the teams themselves: in many cases not so much cogent expressions of national identity or even recognisable products of a system as they are snapshots of a sprawling diaspora at a particular moment in time, splintered on multiple planes by globalisation and migration, assembled out of convenience and expediency. Forty of the 48 competing nations contained a player born overseas. Only one member of the Curaçao squad was actually born on the Caribbean island. The Cape Verde squad that held the eventual champions, Spain, to a heroic 0-0 draw in the group phase featured more players born in Rotterdam than in the country’s capital.

And so the modern World Cup serves two abrupt functions. First, it forces us to confront the idea that most of us have multiple identities cutting across or even against national boundaries, that everywhere is the product of everywhere. Second, it interrogates the criteria by which we pledge allegiance to a country, a process that most of the time lies latent and unspoken, only bursting to the surface in the form of an urgent binary question: “Who do I support for this game?” The historian Eric Hobsbawm’s famous quote about football gestating an “imagined community of millions” takes on a subtly different resonance when you realise that very often this is a community with no defined borders or polity, a community that for 90 minutes draws its number from every corner of the planet.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Weirdly, this is a phenomenon that has become neither exclusively left- nor right-coded. If nationalism was long regarded as the preserve of the populist right and internationalism as the preserve of the intellectual left, these days the picture is far more nuanced. Today’s rightwing agitators are as likely to pledge allegiance to Donald Trump or wave an Israeli flag as they are to champion the country they’re actually from. The Trump administration has consistently demonstrated greater solidarity with white South Africans than with Black Americans. Across the English-speaking world, conservative outlets freely make alliances across national borders and appeal to abstract concepts such as “Judeo-Christian values” or “western civilisation” while denouncing and dehumanising many of their fellow citizens as traitors and scum.

Football’s role as a nation builder is often overstated. France’s World Cup triumph in 1998 was hailed as a vindication of the country’s multiethnic identity, but four years later it sent Jean-Marie Le Pen into the final round of the presidential election. Argentina’s 1978 victory on home soil generated a surge of popularity for the country’s military dictatorship, but by 1983 it had collapsed. England’s run to the European Championship final in 2021 did not, for all the good vibes and open letters, arrest our wider descent into gutter politics and culture war.

But occasionally it can hold up a mirror. And perhaps what this World Cup reflects back at us is a kind of messy hope: that a world of hardening physical borders is doomed to disintegrate on contact with reality. That for all the flags and pageantry, nationality is ultimately little more than a brand, a consumer choice, a piece of content – a mask anyone can happily wear for six weeks, and shed just as easily.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

A pioneer and a superstar, Kevin Keegan’s achievements were extraordinary

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:02:51 GMT

The former England manager may be remembered by many for his ‘I’d love it’ rant in 1996, but that should not obscure the remarkable nature of his football career

Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, is the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, was the star of Liverpool’s first European Cup-winning team, a messianic figure at Newcastle United as a player and coach, forging a team so memorable that Fifa’s president wrote to commend him, and was the captain and then manager of the England men’s national team. And yet, as Keegan would ruefully reflect, he will principally be remembered by many for an emotional outburst that precipitated Newcastle’s historic failure in a Premier League title race, a TV interview which presaged the coming era of the modern game.

Keegan’s “I’d love it” rant of April 1996, directed at Alex Ferguson, became a meme before the modern meaning of the word and social media even existed, repeatedly played on Sky Sports and becoming indelibly marked in the minds of multiple generations, many not even born when it occurred. It frequently tops polls as the most memorable moment in Premier League history and foreshadowed an era where digital clips and personality narratives would dominate football coverage.

There is a danger, however, of reducing Keegan’s life to a series of ever-more emotional explosions, of which there were many, such as his punch-up with Leeds United’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield. For that would obscure the extraordinary nature of his achievements and the fact he was arguably the most charismatic modern English footballer; more eloquent than David Beckham and Paul Gascoigne and more passionate than Bobby Moore. He had a rare gift for inspiring players and almost everyone who interacted with him at his best came away uplifted.

Still, Keegan’s meltdown on TV, where he took issue with Ferguson’s supposed “mind games” in suggesting Leeds players would go easy on Newcastle during a tight title run-in with Manchester United, became a defining moment. “Strangers shout ‘love it’ to me from car windows,” wrote Keegan in his autobiography. “Autograph hunters tell me they would ‘love it’ if I could sign their pieces of paper. When I go to charity events I am often asked to sign photographs showing me in that classic pose: headphones on, finger jabbing, blazing eyes. Those pictures tend to be auctioned for a lot more money than the ones where I am playing for England or any of my clubs.”

Keegan claimed to be relaxed about the characterisation, skewed though it was, perhaps because more than any English footballer before he had maximised football’s commercial and media opportunities and accepted the respective bouquets and brickbats that ensued. Even before that meltdown, he would be best remembered by many in the 1970s for his excruciating bike crash on Superstars, a TV show which pitted athletes from different sports against each other in unfamiliar disciplines. Sprawled across the cycle track, Keegan’s bare flesh was ripped red raw by the gravel. Most remember the drama but few recall that, showing characteristic pig-headed determination, he got back on the bike, bloodied and bandaged, for a rematch, which he won before winning the entire contest.

Keegan was born in Armthorpe, Doncaster, to Doris and Joe, a war veteran Durham miner who had migrated south in search of work at Markham colliery. His upbringing echoed Monty Python’s Yorkshiremen sketch, only his memories were authentic, a throwback to a different century. Their terrace house “had a detached outhouse where we washed. Our bath was an old zinc tub and the toilet was at the foot of the garden and we never had electricity until I was 10 and we moved into a council house in Balby.”

Keegan’s ascent to the peak of the game’s elite was unforeseen, few recognising his talent early on, most dismissing him as too small. He always credited Sister Mary Oliver, the nun who ran his Catholic primary school football team and who refereed with a crucifix around her neck, as being as important to him as a mentor as Bill Shankly was. “Kevin’s football must be encouraged,” she wrote in a school report, which gave him immense self-belief.

Doncaster Rovers rejected him and he started work at Peglers Brass Works at 16, playing for their football team but only in the reserves and also for a pub team on Sundays, where he fortuitously played against a Scunthorpe scout, Bob Nellis, who got him a trial at the struggling Third Division club. Keegan referred to himself as a “mongrel” and “weasel” and the “least-talented” Ballon d’Or winner, and despite impressing at Scunthorpe it was still a major shock when Shankly, the man he regarded as a second father and progenitor of his success, took him to Liverpool. Shankly told him: “You’re not just a great player – you’re one of the great players!” It seemed an unlikely boast but Keegan scored on his Liverpool debut and was never dropped thereafter. He would inherit from Shankly comparable motivational skills.

1951 Kevin Keegan is born on 14 February in Armthorpe, near Doncaster.

1968 Begins playing career at Scunthorpe United.

1971 Signed by Bill Shankly for Liverpool at age of 20, initially as a midfielder.

1972 Makes England debut against Wales in November.

1973 Liverpool win the league; Keegan scores twice in Uefa Cup final win over Borussia Mönchengladbach.

1974 Scores twice as Liverpool beat Newcastle 3-0 in the FA Cup final. His first England goal comes against Wales.

1976 Liverpool win the league title and Keegan scores in each leg of Uefa Cup final win against Club Brugge. His celebrity is such he appears on the TV show Superstars, and famously crashes his bike during one of the races.

1977 Another league title for Liverpool, who also win their first European Cup, a 3-1 victory over Mönchengladbach. Keegan moves to Hamburg for £500,000, nearly double the German transfer record.

1978 Wins Ballon d’Or.

1979 Wins Ballon d’Or again as Hamburg secure their first German ‌championship title in 19 years, and first in the Bundesliga era.

1980 Captains England at Euros but they are knocked out in the group stage. Leaves Hamburg to join Southampton for two seasons.

1982 Transfers to Newcastle in the Second Division. Plays final match for England, after 63 caps (31 as captain) and 21 goals.

1984 Helps Newcastle secure promotion in his second season, then retires from playing. Across his club career, he scores 204 goals in 592 ‌appearances.

1992 Takes first coaching role as manager of struggling Newcastle in February. Danger of relegation to the Third Division is averted.

1993 Leads them to the First Division title and promotion to the Premier League in his first full season in charge.

1994 Newcastle finish third in Premier League.

1996 Newcastle finish second in the Premier League, ​despite leading for most ​of campaign – by 12 points at one stage. Season includes famous “I would love it if we beat them” comments when discussing rivals Manchester United on Sky Sports.

1997 Leaves Newcastle and takes over at Fulham for two seasons.

1999 Takes charge ​of England national ‌team in February.

2000 Coaches England at Euro 2000 where they beat Germany but still go out in the group stage. Resigns in ​October after a 1–0 loss to Germany in World Cup qualifying.

2001 Takes over at Manchester City.

2008 Returns to Newcastle but lasts eight months after tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley.

Though reclusive, Keegan also had a streak of extrovertism, embracing every aspect of the game’s growing commercial opportunities, from his famous Brut advert to appearances on Top of the Pops, where his single Head Over Heels in Love reached the top 40. Though he enjoyed standing out, he admitted he would never have got away with his trademark bubble perm in the old-school Liverpool dressing room. His wife, Jean, whom he met on the waltzers at the Doncaster St Leger horse racing meeting when she was 16 and he was 19 and to whom he remained married for life, burst into fits of laughter when she first saw it. He had the last laugh, the hairstyle inspiring alarming copycat versions across the football world.

Keegan remained true to what he considered to be his working-class, mining roots, declaring himself a Labour man, annoyed that a staged photo of him feigning to kiss then prime minister Margaret Thatcher on the cheek was interpreted as support for economic policies which had ravaged heavy industry. He was more at home playing head tennis with a later PM, Tony Blair, to whom he was close enough to host at his home for dinner.

Keegan inherited two mantles from Britain’s greatest players of the 1960s. As George Best, the original footballer sex symbol of the modern era, lapsed into alcoholism and increasing unreliability, Keegan became the more wholesome and dependable commercial face of the superstar footballer in Britain, inundated with deals. For England he effectively became Moore’s successor as captain but at a time when the national team was in decline from his predecessor’s World Cup-winning heights. For Keegan, as the sole outfield world-class player, it was a heavy burden to bear as they missed out on successive World Cup finals.

His first major tournament for his country was the ill-fated 1980 European Championship and his World Cup career amounted to 20 minutes in 1982, a campaign which was disrupted by a back injury and where “my only contribution was a dreadful miss against the host nation to send us home. That moment is probably the only moment of my England career that people remember now.” It would prove to be his last game for England at the age of just 31.

More notable features of Keegan’s England career were his courage in defying IRA death threats to play against Northern Ireland in Belfast, then walking out on the team when Don Revie dropped him shortly afterwards and being arbitrarily beaten up by Yugoslav custom officials prior to a game in Belgrade, a horrific and wholly underserved ordeal that sparked an international incident. His frustration was best summed up in a story he told about the great Dutch player Johnny Rep. Surveying an England team at Wembley in 1977, Rep turned to Keegan and said: “Kevvy, you have problems here: this is the worst England side I have seen.” The Netherlands won 2-0 and, as Keegan recalled, could have scored at will.

Keegan was a pioneering player, negotiating release clauses, unheard of at the time in England, at Liverpool and Hamburg, allowing him to leave if a club met a £500,000 fee, thereby controlling his moves. Leaving Liverpool at what was assumed to be their peak – he had just helped them win their first European Cup in 1977 – to join a team sixth in the Bundesliga was demonstrative of both Keegan’s single-mindedness and capacity to challenge himself. He also quadrupled his salary, reflecting the economic state of English football at the time.

Hamburg was not an initial success. Jealous teammates held meetings to get him kicked out of the club and, according to Keegan, refused to pass to him. His nadir came at Christmas 1977 when, in a festive-season friendly, unhappy at his plight and frustrated with over-physical treatment from the Lübeck defender Erhard Press, Keegan punched him on the jaw and subsequently knocked him out, receiving an eight-week ban as punishment. Yet, a year later, he won his first Ballon d’Or and went on to lead Hamburg to their first Bundesliga title since 1960.

Keegan embraced Germany, learning the language and was nicknamed “Mighty Mouse”, a tribute to his astonishing strength given his diminutive size. His first daughter, Laura, was born there but his finale, a European Cup final that would have sealed Hamburg’s place in history, was a sad one, ending as it did in defeat to Nottingham Forest. Having won three league titles, two Uefa Cups, an FA Cup and European Cup at Liverpool, the Bundesliga title would be the last trophy Keegan ever won. He was just 29 years old.

Keegan made a typically unconventional choice in joining Southampton, a promising yet small-market team under a talented, persuasive manager in Lawrie McMenemy. Keegan propelled them to a top-six finish and qualification for Europe, but they faded to seventh in the second season and Keegan, disillusioned, made a decision that would define the second half of his professional life.

Newcastle were in one of their periodic financial and footballing crises and in the old Second Division when, with money from brewers Scottish & Newcastle, they persuaded him to join in 1982. His father’s links to the north-east and reverence for Newcastle players such as Jackie Milburn were an emotional pull on Keegan, but one that cost him his England career. The manager, Bobby Robson, didn’t feel it appropriate to pick a second-tier player for England and Keegan, still captain and by far the most iconic national team player, learned from the press he had been “dumped”. He felt “betrayed, hurt and humiliated”.

Crowds doubled at St James’ Park with Keegan’s arrival and Newcastle were promoted as champions in Keegan’s second season, 1983-84, by which point he had already decided to quit playing at the age of 33. Typically impulsive, it was when Mark Lawrenson outsprinted Keegan to dispossess him during an FA Cup tie at Liverpool that he decided he would finish his career at the end of the season.

Keegan and family, which now included his second daughter, Sarah, born in 1982, decamped to his Marbella villa and, other than periodic business deals and discussions about a long-held dream to launch a Soccer Circus, he embraced retirement. Yet endless rounds of golf failed to satisfy. The family had moved back to his Hampshire home when Sir John Hall, a dynamic north-east businessman, called in 1992, begging Keegan to help Newcastle avoid relegation to the third tier and potential liquidation. Despite having watched no football for years, Keegan accepted. He threatened to quit after a few games but stayed to keep Newcastle up and promptly announced that he wanted to build a dynasty to rival Liverpool and challenge for the Premier League title.

Most considered that quixotic and yet Newcastle won promotion to the Premier League as champions and with judicious youthful signings such as Andy Cole and Rob Lee, and veteran players such as Peter Beardsley, they came third and sixth in the top flight. So great was his authority, Keegan could even placate angry fans on the steps of St James’ Park when the club sold Cole to Manchester United.

With that money the club signed David Ginola and Les Ferdinand and won nine of their first 10 games in 1995-96, often in thrilling fashion, establishing a seemingly unassailable 12-point lead by January. But a crucial defeat at home to Ferguson’s United in March 1996 and the Scot’s repeated use of psychological barbs seemed to weigh heavy on Keegan as his team’s form disintegrated. A dramatic yet debilitating 4-3 defeat at Liverpool led Sepp Blatter to write to Keegan but the sight of him slumped over advertising hoardings as Liverpool scored a last-minute winner suggested the toll was too much.

Keegan eventually cracked, denouncing Ferguson in his famous TV interview. “You can tell him now, we’re still fighting for this title and I’ll tell you, honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it!” United won the title with four points to spare.

Keegan initially seemed determined to rebuild as the club signed Alan Shearer for a world-record £15m and they beat United 5-0 at St James’ Park that autumn, but Keegan quit soon after, outraged that a city banker preparing the club for flotation had issued him an ultimatum to sign a contract. Football’s new era seemed untethered from the idealistic foundational values imbued in him by Shankly.

Keegan seemed done with football until the now-disgraced Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed used speculative talks about his much-vaunted Soccer Circus to persuade him to become chief operating officer and eventually manager of Fulham in the third tier. He almost seemed at his happiest as the club accelerated to promotion, but his time was interrupted by a national crisis when Glenn Hoddle was sacked as England manager for making offensive comments about disabled people. The clamour for Keegan to take over was indicative of his popularity with ordinary fans. However, it proved a decision he came to greatly regret, taking in a humiliating Euro 2000 group-stage exit and ending with him resigning in the toilets after an ignominious defeat against Germany in England’s last game at the old Wembley Stadium. It was, he conceded, a job beyond his abilities.

That said, Keegan was happy to take on Manchester City in the old First Division, getting them promoted to the Premier League as champions with 99 points. He remained at the club for four years, an almost unprecedented period of stability at the club at that time. When he finally left City he seemed to be done with coaching and finally launched his Soccer Circus in Glasgow, though it closed after a few years. Yet there was to be one last comeback at Newcastle under the ill-starred ownership of Mike Ashley, which proved a disaster and lasted just eight months.

The idea that a high-minded, old-fashioned football manager schooled by Shankly could coexist with a modern businessman as ruthless as Ashley and his cast of minions running the club always seemed improbable. When he walked away from the job, eventually winning a lengthy and bitter constructive dismissal claim, it was to be Keegan’s last act in football. So acrimonious was the departure that he was only able to return in disguise to attend a function at the club.

The current regime made clear Keegan was always welcome back at St James’ Park. That was after his stage four cancer had been revealed in a series of speaking engagements in May 2026, one of which in Newcastle was, in retrospect, a heartfelt farewell to the fans to whom he had always felt closest. After that draining but exhilarating evening Keegan’s associates reported that he was in high spirits, energised by the reconnection with the fans who loved him most.

It was to prove Keegan’s final goodbye. Football, as he observed, had given him everything except for a happy ending.

Barking mad: why would someone spend £28,000 on a home spa for their dog?

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:49:00 GMT

The UK is a nation of animal lovers. But the rise of ‘barkitecture’ has taken it too far, with people investing in outdoor showers, whirlpool baths and ergonomic feeding stations for their faithful friends

Name: Barkitecture. Age: 27 years old. Appearance: Plush provisions for posh pooches.

It’s 27 years old? That’s hardly newsworthy. Well, there was Fred Albert’s 1999 book Barkitecture, about upmarket kennels. And then there was the 2020 Quibi platform show Barkitecture, where a Bachelorette runner-up made kennels for celebrities. Also, the Guardian has covered the term before.

So my point stands. But wait, the term has mutated.

Into what? It no longer covers just kennels. It is now about redesigning your house beyond all recognition in order to pamper your pet.

I need specifics. How about outdoor hot water showers for your dog? Or an ergonomic feeding station, so your pet doesn’t have to bend its neck to reach its dinner? Or a calming pheromone dispenser to keep your dog happy?

That’s just what I’ve always wanted – a lazy, stoned dog. I suppose I had better not mention the rise of the £45 doggy dryrobe, then.

Oh, for God’s sake. Dogs are working animals. And you’re a working person. Do you want to be hosed down with freezing water and eat your food off the ground every day? Do you want to wander around naked?

That’s different. I’m a human. Well, suck it up, because barkitecture is the new norm. The interior designer Laura Stephens told the Telegraph: “In high-end homes, dog showers are as essential as somewhere to put muddy boots … I’m seeing a lot more demand for dog beds too, and I’ve just designed an under-stairs cupboard for a cat with a built-in feeding station.”

So much for the cost of living crisis. That’s it. Treating your pet as lavishly as possible is a sign of a large disposable income.

This isn’t actually about the animals, is it? Of course it is. Everyone loves their pets. But if you can show your neighbours that you have enough money to love your pets more than they do, then that’s an added bonus.

Well, I do love being obnoxious. In that case, may I introduce you to the £3,000 Wet Pets hydro spa dog whirlpool bath, featuring antimicrobial walls and adjustable mood lighting? Or the £670 custom-built “Balmoral” Chesterfield-style leather dog bed?

Good lord. How about a shepherd’s hut that has been converted into a dedicated high-end dog spa? Yours for just £28,000.

Won’t all this spoil your pets? Yes, you’re completely right, your cockapoo is far less likely to help you track prey across the wild expanses if it has a warm shower once a week, isn’t it? I unreservedly apologise.

Do say: “Rover, walkies!”

Don’t say: “Once you’ve finished your massage, obviously.”

Who are India’s Cockroach Janta party and why are they staging protests?

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:28:48 GMT

Explosion of anger over education system and youth unemployment has led to movement’s rapid rise

Tens of thousands of Cockroach party protesters defy police with Delhi march

The Cockroach Janta party (CJP) might have started out as an online joke, but – driven by millions of discontented young people in India – it has swiftly grown into one of the most unexpected challenges to the powerful rightwing government of Narendra Modi.

The CJP was founded in May by Abhijeet Dipke, 30, an Indian national who recently graduated from university in the US. Enraged to hear comments made by the chief justice of India, who compared the country’s unemployed youth to “parasites” and “cockroaches” during a supreme court hearing, Dipke jokingly put out a call on social media: “What if all cockroaches came together?”

The response was overwhelming. Dipke built a website and social media accounts for a satirical Cockroach Janta party – a poke at Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) – complete with a biting manifesto taking aim at the government and a tagline: “A political party for the people the system forgot to count.”

Within two weeks, the CJP’s Instagram page had more than 22 million followers, overtaking the BJP. The Modi government, highly intolerant of criticism, attempted to block its social media accounts on national security grounds but was not successful.

As the CJP began to mobilise support, Dipke focused the movement on a burning issue for many of India’s millions of students: leaks of medical entrance exams, which have repeatedly been sold to the highest bidder.

The pressure on students to succeed is cripplingly high: more than 2 million students compete for just 130,000 places. Many families spend their life savings and get into high levels of debt to pay for their children to be coached for these notoriously gruelling medical exams, known by the acronym NEET. More is now spent in India on private tuition than the government’s entire higher education budget.

A string of exam leaks has forced millions of students into re-takes and been linked to dozens of suicides in recent years. The NEET exams are also not the only papers to have been leaked.

The Modi government has been accused of not taking responsibility for the exams fiasco. The CJP began to rally supporters around the issue; calling for the government to be held accountable for exam leaks and for the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to resign.

For many of India’s gen Zs and millennials, the CJP has also given voice to wider frustrations over an education system in crisis and a job market that has been systematically failing them. According to one recent study, almost 40% of India’s graduates below the age of 25 are unemployed.

The CJP’s first offline protest took place in Delhi in early June, calling for the resignation of Pradhan. Dipke returned from the US to lead the demonstration, first in Delhi and then at events across the country.

Later that month, CJP supporters held their second major protest in Delhi, where this time they pledged not to move until Pradhan was gone. The protesters were joined by Sonam Wangchuk, an eminent engineer and education activist from the Indian state of Ladakh, who was last year arrested and detained under terror laws by the government for his activism.

Wangchuk announced he would embark on a Gandhian hunger strike in solidarity with the students and would not eat until the education minister stepped down.

As the protest and Wangchuk’s hunger strike went on into July, they were visited by multiple senior opposition figures. However, the Modi government did not engage with the CJP or Wangchuk and Pradhan dismissed them as the “B-team of terrorists”.

As Wangchuk’s conditioned worsened more than two weeks into his hunger strike, the government faced mounting criticism. After 18 days, the Delhi court ordered for his health to be monitored on a daily basis.

Early on Sunday morning, 20 days into his hunger strike, Delhi police sparked national outrage after they arrived and forcibly removed Wangchuk and took him to a government hospital against his will. The police said it was to protect his health – his wife condemned it as “illegal detention”.

From his hospital bed, Wangchuk called on CJP supporters to march to parliament on Monday and demand Pradhan’s resignation.

The CJP protest on Monday swelled into one of the largest anti-government protests in years. By early morning, thousands of protesters began to flock to the streets of central Delhi, joining hundreds who had already been camped out overnight.

The crowd was largely made up of students and other young people, but parents whose children had been affected by the leaks were also present in high numbers.

Delhi police refused permission for the protesters to march on parliament. Roads across the city were blockaded with barriers, the internet was shut down and protesters were kettled into a designated protest site about a mile away from parliament. However, protesters still continued to arrive in droves, with more than 20,000 people gathered by the early afternoon.

As the crowds tried to push towards parliament, police responded with violence, including baton charges and teargas, prompting criticism from CJP leaders and opposition politicians. Protesters and police were injured in the clashes. Dipke condemned the police response as “absolutely brutal”.

After weeks of ignoring the CJP movement, the Modi government offered a meeting on Monday morning. At a brief 10-minute interaction, three CJP demands were put forward but so far “no commitments were made”, according to the CJP’s spokesperson.

There was no public response to the protest by Pradhan. By late on Monday, even as the police tried to clear the Delhi protest camp, Dipke emphasised that as long as Pradhan remained in his position, they would not be moved. “This peaceful protest is not ending!” read the party post on X.

Kevin Keegan, Liverpool legend and former Newcastle manager, dies aged 75

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:28:43 GMT

Keegan revealed in June 2026 he had stage four cancer

Starred for Liverpool, Hamburg, Newcastle and England

Kevin Keegan, the former England and Newcastle manager who was twice named European Footballer of the Year, has died aged 75. As a player, Keegan illuminated countless matches and in the 1970s proved a stalwart member of Liverpool’s serial domestic and European trophy winning team.

Keegan’s family announced in January that he had cancer and, seven weeks ago, he himself revealed that it was stage four, the most advanced form of the disease. “A double Ballon d’Or winner, Kevin was a much loved husband, father and grandfather,” read a statement. “The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.”

Alan Shearer, who played under Keegan with Newcastle and England, paid his own tribute on social media. “My hero. My manager. My friend,” wrote the former striker. “Sleep easy Boss.”

The Colombian former Newcastle striker Faustino Asprilla wrote: “I am absolutely heartbroken. Kevin wasn’t just a football manager to me. Through his passion, belief and love for the game he inspired so many people, myself included. He taught me that football is about much more than winning.

“It’s about passion, loyalty, hope and never giving up. Those lessons have stayed with me throughout my life and, for that, I will be forever grateful.”

Newcastle released a heartfelt statement describing Keegan as “one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club’s history”. As it explained: “Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.” Prince William said he was “incredibly saddened to hear of the passing of Kevin Keegan. A truly remarkable footballer and manager who inspired generations with his talent, passion and love of the game. Above all he will be remembered as a kind and generous man.”

By late on Monday afternoon, floral tributes were piling up outside St James’ Park as Newcastle fans paid their respects to an enduring hero. Liverpool, meanwhile, said Keegan’s “indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on”.

Keegan started his career at Scunthorpe before being signed for Liverpool by Bill Shankly for £33,000 in 1971. It did not take long for the son of a South Yorkshire miner to become “King Kev”, with his invariably imperious attacking performances helping Shankly’s side win three First Division titles, the FA Cup, the Uefa Cup (twice) and the 1977 European Cup.

By his own admission not a natural talent, Keegan turned himself into one of the world’s best players. “Mighty Mouse” was relentlessly combative, never ducked a challenge, and remained refreshingly humble even as he became a firm Kop favourite. “I learned so much from Shanks,” Keegan said. “He used to say: ‘If I was a road sweeper my street would be the cleanest in the borough.’ I took that to heart.”

Keegan left Liverpool in 1977 for Hamburg, where he became the only British player to twice win the Ballon d’Or. Upon returning from Germany in 1980 he enjoyed further playing stints with Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984. By then he had also won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals in the course of an international career that involved playing at the 1982 World Cup.

1951 Kevin Keegan is born on 14 February in Armthorpe, near Doncaster.

1968 Begins playing career at Scunthorpe United.

1971 Signed by Bill Shankly for Liverpool at age of 20, initially as a midfielder.

1972 Makes England debut against Wales in November.

1973 Liverpool win the league; Keegan scores twice in Uefa Cup final win over Borussia Mönchengladbach.

1974 Scores twice as Liverpool beat Newcastle 3-0 in the FA Cup final. His first England goal comes against Wales.

1976 Liverpool win the league title and Keegan scores in each leg of Uefa Cup final win against Club Brugge. His celebrity is such he appears on the TV show Superstars, and famously crashes his bike during one of the races.

1977 Another league title for Liverpool, who also win their first European Cup, a 3-1 victory over Mönchengladbach. Keegan moves to Hamburg for £500,000, nearly double the German transfer record.

1978 Wins Ballon d’Or.

1979 Wins Ballon d’Or again as Hamburg secure their first German ‌championship title in 19 years, and first in the Bundesliga era.

1980 Captains England at Euros but they are knocked out in the group stage. Leaves Hamburg to join Southampton for two seasons.

1982 Transfers to Newcastle in the Second Division. Plays final match for England, after 63 caps (31 as captain) and 21 goals.

1984 Helps Newcastle secure promotion in his second season, then retires from playing. Across his club career, he scores 204 goals in 592 ‌appearances.

1992 Takes first coaching role as manager of struggling Newcastle in February. Danger of relegation to the Third Division is averted.

1993 Leads them to the First Division title and promotion to the Premier League in his first full season in charge.

1994 Newcastle finish third in Premier League.

1996 Newcastle finish second in the Premier League, ​despite leading for most ​of campaign – by 12 points at one stage. Season includes famous “I would love it if we beat them” comments when discussing rivals Manchester United on Sky Sports.

1997 Leaves Newcastle and takes over at Fulham for two seasons.

1999 Takes charge ​of England national ‌team in February.

2000 Coaches England at Euro 2000 where they beat Germany but still go out in the group stage. Resigns in ​October after a 1–0 loss to Germany in World Cup qualifying.

2001 Takes over at Manchester City.

2008 Returns to Newcastle but lasts eight months after tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley.

Keegan was never one to hold back. He was memorably sent off for scrapping with Leeds’ Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield and harboured a certain volatility allied to a pugnacious intolerance of football’s machinations, real or perceived. “I don’t like people to deceive me and tell me lies,” he told the Guardian in 2018.

Although a private man, Keegan also embraced fame. He was one of the English game’s first players to wear personalised branded football boots, recorded a hit single Head Over Heels in Love, and became an enduring star of the BBC’s Superstars. He was also the public face of 70s aftershave Brut 33 and became close friends with George Best. “I wanted so much to have his ability,” Keegan said. “His skill was unbelievable. I played against [Johan] Cruyff, [Franz] Beckenbauer, [Diego] Maradona but I still say Besty was the best.”

Having hung up his boots at the age of 33, Keegan moved to Spain where his two daughters grew up, initially unaware he had been a footballer. “It was the best decision I made in my life,” he told the Guardian in 2011. “I was at the highest level and the only way was down. I call it the glass mountain – you can’t climb a glass mountain.”

In 1992 he decided to venture into management at Newcastle, guiding them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title, only to miss out to Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United. His finger-jabbing “I will love it” rant from that season has become part of the English game’s lore.

After leaving St James’ Park in January 1997 Keegan took charge of Fulham before becoming England manager in 1999. That 20-month, 18-game tenure would end in despair when, following a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, he resigned after a defeat by Germany at Wembley. The Football Association has announced it will pay tribute to Keegan before England’s Nations League game with Spain at Wembley in September.

A happier spell at Manchester City – who on Monday credited Keegan with establishing them as a Premier League club – followed before an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008. That swansong ended within eight months, however, amid acute tensions with the club’s then owner Mike Ashley and his board. In 2009 a tribunal awarded Keegan £2m damages for constructive dismissal.

Keegan, who was made an OBE in 1982 for services to football, made a fleeting return to public life in June. During an event on Tyneside he talked about his desire to return to St James’ Park to say “goodbye” and joked the club would need to “wait until I die” to erect a statue of him. He was optimistic at the time that gruelling treatment was keeping his cancer at bay.

“Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results,” read Newcastle’s statement. “It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.”

From fidget bags to sticker books: readers’ hard-won hacks for travelling with kids

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 14:00:43 GMT

You told us your tried-and-tested tricks for keeping children entertained. Plus, the best eye masks and natural deodorants, tested

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

If there’s one thing worse than a long journey, it’s a long journey with bored, fractious children. So what helps smooth things along? We asked for your best, tried-and-tested hacks for travelling with kids, from “fidget bags” to lollipops.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

On a long car trip from the UK to France with his kids, reader Tim Leadbeater attached small plastic baskets with string around the pillars of the front headrest: “They held everything from felt tips to half-eaten food, not only preventing stains on covers but also keeping everything reachable for kids in car seats.”

Likewise, Deborah Berzins used to make what she calls a “fidget bag full of little characters, a toy snake, a stretchy man toy, and finger puppets”, which only came out on car journeys so the novelty didn’t wear off.

Another trick suggested by reader Kate is to wrap small, individual toys in old wrapping paper: “Even the oldest crayon, book or tiny Lego figure became an exciting discovery; the unwrapping was a game in itself, and the activity helped pass the time,” she says.

Nettie Hall, who has a no-screen policy, survived a solo trip from London to Cornwall with her three-year-old by arming herself with multiple activities: “I got several sticker books, a simple crown-making kit (sticking gems on a cardboard crown that ties around the head with string), small pots of play-dough, colouring pencils and Orchard Toys packable games,” she says. “Don’t overestimate the attention span of very young children!”

Sophie recommends packing “thousands of snacks”, but this isn’t just to keep her daughter preoccupied. “My daughter is intolerant to loads of things, so this is extra important as we can never guarantee a station shop will have anything she can eat,” she says.

Meanwhile, one reader says she has never boarded a plane or train without the following: a small colouring book for inevitable delays, sticking plasters and antiseptic wipes for inevitable cut knees, and small lollipops or similar for instantly cheering up children with cut knees – and probably sometimes adults too. Happy travels!

Tuchel is clinging to an outdated English style – he must let players take risks

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 13:55:15 GMT

Head coach should ditch a physical approach that has rarely worked and embrace England’s gifted ball players

Only England can claim the bronze medal at the World Cup by beating France in a 10-goal thriller and end up even more annoyed with the manager. Yet emotions are still running high after the collapse against Argentina last week and it is going to take more than winning a game low on jeopardy for the criticism of Thomas Tuchel to die down.

Hiring Tuchel was centred around the promise that he would make the difference in the big games. When that fell down, all that was left was anger. It exposed the core emptiness of the appointment, of a rich federation covering up the flaws in its coaching development by trying to game the system by throwing money at an expensive outsider.

What is the Football Association’s vision? The initial idea was Tuchel providing a short, sharp shock and his tactical acumen helping England to get over the line. Then came a change after a successful qualifying campaign against modest opposition. The FA moved the goalposts by handing Tuchel a contract extension, and suddenly winning the World Cup did not seem quite as pressing.

Yet the idea of Tuchel as a project builder seemed far-fetched during the bitter recriminations after the defeat by Argentina. Criticised for his negative substitutions when England led, the German talked dismissively of English DNA, lamenting the lack of care in possession. Fair enough, you thought, because this has long been a weakness – only, hadn’t Tuchel caused some of the damage by leaving out most of the ball players from his squad? Would it have been different if Adam Wharton, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer had been around in Atlanta? Maybe not, but a lot of money has been spent on developing a different type of English player in recent decades.

Perhaps Tuchel was thinking of an old English DNA. But maybe this is part of the issue with employing a foreign coach whose focus is on winning by any means possible. This is the third time England have been down this road. There is an idea of the manager from abroad as a sophisticate. But Sven-Göran Eriksson was not as tactically adroit as Glenn Hoddle. Eriksson played a traditional 4-4-2 whereas Hoddle was flexible with his formations.

Tuchel, too, has struggled to build an identity. He seems taken with an outdated English style. Tuchel wanted to play like a Premier League team, with pace and physicality, but that has rarely worked for England. They tend to be outpassed in big knockout games, which is why there has been such focus in youth football in developing players more at ease with the dominant Spanish passing style.

Spain have just won another World Cup, their method too much for Argentina in a dour final, and for those watching from afar a big takeaway will surely be that the last two teams standing were led by homegrown coaches.

Luis de la Fuente and Lionel Scaloni have risen through the ranks and are part of a system. They have a feeling for their countries, a sense of the identity. Tuchel has been inserted in the hope he can cover up the FA’s failure to produce its own coaches. No male team led by a foreign manager has secured the World Cup and it should worry the FA when bringing in an outsider with a win-now mentality ends with the senior side using a very different style of play to younger age groups.

There is a view within youth coaching circles that Tuchel has taken England backwards at this tournament. The under-21s have won the past two European Championships by being brave on the ball. They have beaten Spain in consecutive tournaments and the demand from Lee Carsley is that his players take risks in possession. Tuchel finished the semi-final by lobbing balls towards Dan Burn. He played a pragmatic style and his England ended up unable to throw caution to the wind. This World Cup underlines that turning to celebrated coaches from the club game is not a recipe for success.

Brazil appointed Carlo Ancelotti but went out in the last 16. Roberto Martínez failed with Portugal after sticking with Cristiano Ronaldo. Mauricio Pochettino oversaw the USA side being humiliated by Belgium.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Scaloni came through the national setup before winning the World Cup with Argentina in 2022. Similarly De la Fuente won the European Under-19 Championship with Spain in 2015 and the European Under-21 Championship in 2019. He has brought players through and, having earned a promotion, won the senior European title in 2024.

Spain show smooth progression. Players who beat Argentina in the final played youth football for De la Fuente. This is not to say that England’s next step should be to appoint Carsley, who did not seem as if he had the temperament for the senior job when he filled in as caretaker between Gareth Southgate’s departure and Tuchel’s arrival. Even so, Carsley is closer to the Spanish style and has shown it is possible for England teams to be risk-takers.

It is food for thought for the FA as it reviews England’s World Cup. As it stands, Tuchel will get another tournament. There are bridges to build but finishing third is not a sackable offence. In any case there is no other idea at the FA. Tuchel was not produced, he was bought. Hopefully he adapts during the Nations League. There should be a shift away from this physical style. But do not be surprised if the hired gun’s views on English DNA end up making him sound out of touch. It would not happen to Spain. De la Fuente knows their identity. He is part of it.

DeChambeau accused of threatening to call Trump in row over Open penalty

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 13:14:34 GMT

DeChambeau given two-stroke penalty after his second round

Golfer alleged to have used US president’s name during row

Bryson DeChambeau has been accused of threatening to call Donald Trump during a row with senior R&A officials on Friday after the American golfer was handed a two-shot penalty at the Open.

DeChambeau’s alleged use of the US president’s name as he argued his case marks the latest bizarre turn in what was already the dominant story of the 2026 Open. DeChambeau was handed a two-stroke penalty for improving the line of his swing by standing on long grass behind his ball on Royal Birkdale’s fifth hole during round two. The 32-year-old argued his case furiously, including insisting upon returning to the scene of the incident with the R&A’s head of governance and a senior referee.

Upon arrival back at the tournament scoring area and with the R&A unmoved, the chief executive, Mark Darbon, joined the conversation. During that, it is understood DeChambeau said he would phone Trump if the matter was not resolved in his favour. There is no evidence that call actually took place. DeChambeau skipped mainstream media duties throughout the Open. The R&A has not commented on the Trump connection, first reported by the Quadrilateral.

Trump is on regular speaking terms with a number of the world’s most high-profile golfers, including DeChambeau. At last year’s Ryder Cup the pair enjoyed a warm exchange. DeChambeau had said earlier that Trump would “inspire” the US at Bethpage.

DeChambeau’s penalty, which Rory McIlroy later said was entirely correct, moved him out of second place. After Saturday’s round, DeChambeau headed immediately for Darbon’s office to ask for his round two scorecard. The unusual request was politely turned down by the R&A’s chief executive.

DeChambeau has remained in the UK to play in LIV Golf’s stop at the JCB Golf and Country Club from Thursday. His tied-14th finish in the Open was his best in a major tournament in 2026. Dechambeau’s representatives have been approached for comment.
