‘Most people don’t know we’ve set up a doomsday system’: physicist Laura Grego on satellites, nuclear weapons and the battle for our skies

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 13:09:33 GMT

Elon Musk is trying to own it, competing powers are trying to fight in it and nobody seems to be regulating it. So who does space really belong to?

The last time I saw Laura Grego was in a tent in a baking field on the Welsh borders in May. The conversation on stage ranged from the dangers of space debris to how the law of the sea might pertain to outer space; from our sense of the sacred to our interplanetary futures. At one point Grego, a physicist, said intently, “People have to be aware of what is happening in space. Public knowledge has to catch up.” Three weeks later, SpaceX launched on the stock exchange, temporarily making Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire.

So, I ask her now, what is it that we should all know? Well, she says, the average person’s experience of space is about to change. If, so far, that has been “looking at the stars and being full of wonder, full of connection with the universe”, perhaps noticing the occasional streaking object that was not a shooting star, now “there are plans for tens of thousands more satellites, which would really change your relationship with what you see in the sky”. SpaceX, specifically, has just applied to a federal regulator for permission to launch up to 1m of them.

Grego, who is now back in the US and speaking to me on screen from Cambridge, Massachusetts, has an unforced warmth and urgency, and a lack of self-aggrandisement in striking contrast to the gung-ho attitude that seems to accompany so much discussion of space. She became a physicist when she arrived at university and looked for the hardest thing she could find to study, so as to get her time’s worth (“a very midwestern perspective”). Then she became an observational cosmologist, which she found she loved. This merged with her other life as an activist (“anti-war, workers’ rights, racial justice – all the things important for a better society”) when she became research director of the Global Security programme at the Union of Concerned Scientists.

The union, founded at the height of the Vietnam war by American scientists horrified by their government’s misuse of science, aims to direct research energies toward solving environmental and social problems instead; Grego sees herself as working in the tradition of Leo Szilard, who tried to warn the US government against using an atomic bomb on Japan, and of “scientists taking seriously the responsibility to illuminate the dangers”. So she does research, she educates, sometimes she lobbies about specific issues: explaining to the George W Bush administration, for example, that no, their giddy visions of “space weapons, very much inspired by science fiction, maybe movies, things that would zip marines around in space and pew, pew, pew!” would not work. The current administration, which appears to treat war like a video game for which they can make up the rules, is unsurprisingly proving trickier.

There are in fact rules in space. Almost all countries are signed up to the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which requires that space be used for peaceful purposes only, that no one stations nuclear weapons in space, or any weapons on any celestial bodies, and that no one may claim ownership of any celestial body. It is silent on weapons transiting through space, or indeed being put into orbit.

The truth is, Grego says, space has always been a military zone, insofar as the very first satellite, Sputnik 1, sent up in 1957 – “a civilian object in that all it really did was go beep, beep, beep” – was a geopolitical assertion: “Who’s better, who’s on top technologically.” Then there was how it got there. A rocket launcher is not so different from an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM). “And once you have a working ICBM, you could put a nuclear weapon on top of it and send it from the Soviet Union to the United States in half an hour, right?”

It is probably helpful, here, to remember that space is not that far away: the atmosphere begins to peter out about 100km up – roughly the distance from London to Portsmouth, say. “And ICBMs, if you’re sending them 10,000km from one country to another, they pop up above the atmosphere within a few minutes and then they spend most of their time where the lower satellites are. So they spend most of their time in space.”

Because it is so close, and has none of the airspace restrictions we have within the atmosphere, there was quickly another military use to space, which was “overflights of each other’s countries to see what they’re doing. How many nuclear missiles do they have? What are they doing with their troops?” This is an important aspect of enforcing arms control agreements: “Taking pictures every day to see, are you keeping your word?”

But with such range and sophistication comes vulnerability. There is standard military vulnerability: “For a military like the US, which is global, extremely modern, space is the backbone. Space provides long-distance communications, targeting, battle-assessment, weather prediction – even drone warfare runs off satellite signals in some cases.” But satellites themselves are very valuable, and largely undefended, which has been “an uncomfortable position for militaries to be in”.

Then, given that we now use satellites to find our way from A to B, to order a cab or check the weather – not to mention the infinite commercial uses, from airlines to inventory management – there is the economic vulnerability. “You can jam them, you can spoof them, you could cyber-attack them. And that’s not totally uncommon.” In fact, earlier this month Russia was reported to have tried to jam Musk’s Starlink satellites, so as to impede Ukrainian drones.

No country has yet destroyed another country’s satellite intentionally, Grego continues: “That’s been a line we haven’t crossed. But most of the big spacefaring countries, which also happen to be nuclear countries, are testing weapons that you could use against other satellites.” Avant-garde space defence now looks for ways to sidle up to opposition satellites. “If you get that close, you could set your adversary’s satellite spinning. You could spray-paint it. You could blast it with radiation” – effectively, make it “stop working without blasting it into little pieces”. This is an important consideration when all of this stuff is circling the world every 90 minutes, at a speed at which a rogue fragment the size of a marble could take out any satellite in its way.

And finally, there is the nuclear vulnerability. When, last autumn, Kathryn Bigelow’s Netflix thriller A House of Dynamite had 22m views within three days of its release, Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon circulated an internal memo that was obtained by Bloomberg. The movie’s depiction of a US system with under 60% accuracy was, they insisted to their staff, untrue; Trump’s $1.2tn Golden Dome system would be 100% effective.

Grego was asked about the memo live on BBC TV. The movie is in fact correct, she said; just over half of tests have failed. Though actually, she says now, A House of Dynamite – which was well researched, just without asking the Pentagon – portrayed “a strange, very unrealistic case where an adversary might have launched a single weapon without any countermeasures, or any real attempt to disguise it. It’s hard to imagine why a country would do that unless it was an accidental launch.”

But where it was realistic, she adds, was in the timelines. The standard way of protecting ICBMs is to put them in silos – “dig a big hole, pour the concrete, put a shield on top.” But everyone knows where they are because there have been satellites flying over for decades. “And the worry is somebody will pre-emptively attack those ICBMs and leave you without them to retaliate, which would upset the balance of mutually assured destruction. And so a key reason you have these satellites looking is that once you see anything headed in, you can quickly launch those missiles before they’re destroyed on the ground. It’s kind of: use them or lose them.”

The thing is, the whole ICBM trajectory only lasts half an hour, and “you’re compressed by detection, communication. So a president would have less than 10 minutes to decide whether to launch ICBMs or to wait it out … the system is built so that question gets asked right away. And it creates this intense time-pressure” – and on imperfect people, with incomplete information.

She adds: “If the president decided to launch a counterattack, even if the initial attack was launched by accident, certainly the adversary is going to retaliate. That’s a civilisation-ending day – or an afternoon.” I’m so taken aback I laugh out loud. “I know,” she says. “I’m sorry. I’ve had many years to acclimate to this. But most people haven’t. Most people don’t know we’ve set up a system that is essentially a doomsday system. And we can dismantle it. We just have not.”

And not only that, Grego says, but we are upping the ante. “All of the nuclear-armed countries are investing in improving or modernising or expanding their nuclear arsenals.” China tested an ICBM in early July; the US is accusing Russia of building (though not yet deploying) a nuclear weapon that would be based in space and target satellites, “which would be totally counter to the Outer Space Treaty”. Not to mention the possibility of AI autonomous systems that are likely to speed up decision-making times, and have less accountability. “Most of the nuclear-armed countries are involved in some kind of conflict somewhere,” she says. All arms-control treaties have expired, and if countries have learned anything from the Iran war, where the US bombed them in the middle of diplomatic negotiations, it’s that “if you don’t have a weapon right now, you might want to get one so this doesn’t happen to you.” As for the Golden Dome, “it’s a fool’s errand. It’s expensive. It’s strategically unwise, and technically just unachievable.”

Against this backdrop, the other great expansion is, of course, in the commercial use of space, both current and projected. Much of the excitement of the SpaceX IPO was predicated on Musk’s stated intention of launching AI datacentres into space – even though no one has yet made one work, not least because cooling things in a vacuum is not at all straightforward. The main value of the company is currently in Starlink, which already provides internet in more than 160 countries and territories (though not yet in South Africa, which Musk has claimed is “because I’m not black”; South Africa replied he was welcome, provided it could see “compliance with local laws”, which require 30% ownership by local historically disadvantaged communities. Musk’s company has 9,532 satellites in orbit (there are about 17,600 active satellites in total); if permission is granted for the new constellation he wants to build, this will vastly increase. Then there is his stated aim of a colony on Mars.

So one person, with questionable views, is aiming not only to rewrite the night sky but in the process gain unfettered control of our heavens? Grego initially responds quite carefully. “You know, there’s a legal discussion about at what point does that become appropriation, if you’ve put so many satellites in a space? Have you essentially claimed it? I don’t know where that line is.”

What she does know is, “I don’t think we’re talking enough about it in the right places. We’re racing ahead with technical capabilities beyond our legal and normative structures and where the conversation is on Earth” – which clearly has more than a few other things to contend with. A recent opinion piece in this paper noted that even the Artemis mission, with all its wonder and its joy, was in essence a civilisational move, in which the vast majority of people had been relegated to the status of audience, as opposed to active participants in deciding how we would relate to a universe we all share – or even whether we should be leaving Earth in the first place.

Rather like the race for generative AI, or in fact mutually assured destruction, the companies themselves have a momentum that creates facts before anyone has properly thought about what those facts will entail. “Commercial companies are bumping up against what they see are the restrictions on them. Like, ‘If I can’t appropriate, it’s not clear what I can do. But do we all interpret this the same way?’ And that does engender a bit of a race to the moon. You don’t want to be second. You’re not clear that you’re ready to be first, but nobody wants to be second, because there are some places on the moon which are particularly useful, that have near-perpetual sunlight and access to water, like near the south pole. You’re not allowed to claim it for your country but if you’re there building infrastructure” – which is effectively claiming it – “how do we deal with that? And if you have many powerful nuclear-armed countries trying to jostle for the same things in a distant place, that’s another place where you might spark a crisis.”

We only have to look at every environment on Earth, she adds, to “see that the extractive colonialist framework has led to an existential crisis for human beings. And we have a chance to do this better as we move into space. And so we shouldn’t cede that power to the first most powerful company that’s able to do it.” She points to a piece of small print in the Starlink user agreements, about jurisdictions, and governing law. For any disputes about services “provided to, on, or in orbit around the planet Earth or the moon”, Texas state law applies, it says, while “for services provided on Mars, or in transit to Mars … no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities. Accordingly, Disputes will be settled through self-governing principles, established in good faith, at the time of Martian settlement.”

It’s not as though Martian settlement is imminent, but the intent is effectively there in print, to refuse all other jurisdiction but of those who get there first. “I obviously don’t know him [Musk]. I can only see what he says and what he does. But I don’t share a view of humanity that he does. I probably shouldn’t go any further. But I don’t think it’s inclusive. I don’t think it values human life in the same way that I do. I don’t think it prioritises future generations in the way that I would, or human culture. What’s the best of us, not what’s the worst of us. I don’t know the mechanism to make a course correction right now but I do know that it won’t happen unless people demand it.”

There are a couple of levers. Although the Outer Space Treaty did not imagine Musk – or any private actor being able to function so widely in space – it does clearly say that the launch country is responsible for any subsequent activity “in outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies”. So the “United States government could say yes or no, or: ‘To do this, you need to show me a plan for why this is in our interest, not just your interest.’”

There is a United Nations of Outer Space Affairs – but little in the way of mechanisms of enforcement. Any brakes have so far in effect been left to bureaucratic regulatory bodies, Grego says – though from a military point of view it is hopeful that just this week there has been a meeting in Geneva of the UN’s Open-Ended Working Group on Preventing an Arms Race in Outer Space.

One reason Grego really enjoyed talking at the philosophy and music festival in Wales, How the Light Gets In, was the opportunity to think about things on a bigger horizon than her usual diet of research and policy papers. In an ideal world, she argues, we would completely reframe the narrative. Currently the dominant story is “really problematic, which is: space is the final frontier. The US military likes to call it the space domain, and that it needs to be dominated.” It is all about the singular (male) hero, long pointy rockets, speed, to boldly go.

But there are other ways. Not all scientists, but most, she says, “whether they’re looking at very, very small scales or very, very large scales, pretty quickly come to the realisation that human beings are extraordinarily interesting and rare. How do we safeguard that? And how do we steward that? If we think that humanity is something worth saving, then we actually have a lot we need to do to make sure that happens.”

That might include considering whether we should just step back altogether. “I happen to think Earth is a really nice place. It’s beautiful. I love the beaches, the mountains. Mars has none of that. Mars is harsh. The moon is harsh. They’re very difficult places to live. It will take a long time to make them habitable or pleasant. And Earth has so much going for it.

“So that’s really the horizon that I spend my time on. My kids and my grandkids. And I hope that there’s a world, a beautiful world for them, you know?”

‘We didn’t want him to be punchable!’: Matthew Broderick and Alan Ruck on Ferris Bueller’s Day Off

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 12:58:17 GMT

‘Alan and I have neat hair because we’d both just been in a military play. If we’d had crazy 1980s mullets, it wouldn’t have become a timeless classic’

I’d done WarGames and Ladyhawke and was getting sent a lot of “young guy” parts. I was a little concerned at first because Ferris talks to the audience – I’d done that in two plays and didn’t want to it to seem like that’s all I could do. Meanwhile, my agent said: “You’ve been asked to do a John Hughes movie. You’re doing it.” I didn’t know much about John at the time but I kept hearing him being referred to as the “Spielberg of teen films”.

I thought Ferris shouldn’t seem to be trying too hard, that things came easy to him. I wanted to be a little cool and aloof. We didn’t want him to be somebody you wanted to punch in the face. That’s always the danger with guys who get away with everything.

After a test screening, one young woman’s feedback was that she didn’t like Ferris because “he’d make me do things I don’t want to do” so they got rid of a scene where I try to get Sloane [Mia Sara] not to go back home and keep hanging out having fun.

Alan [Ruck, played Cameron] and I have timeless hair-dos because we’d both just been in a military play, Biloxi Blues. Given the date the film was made, had we been able to, we might’ve both had crazy mullets, in which case, it would not have become a timeless classic.

John could be a very exacting director. Often, I’d be doing his ideas as carefully as I could but the scenes where I’m alone in the house talking to the camera? We’d just make stuff up. I picked up the clarinet and started playing just because it was there and I pretended I was playing great. The plan was to replace the sound and make it really good but John saw the footage and said: “I’m not doing that.”

Marilyn Vance [costume designer] and John came up with my outfit. There’s details you don’t even see. My socks had flags of all the nations on them. The rabbit’s foot in my pocket was just there. John thought Ferris’s leather coat should be simple, like James Dean’s red jacket but we went very much the other way. The beret was my idea.

The parade scene was huge. We shot at an actual parade one weekend, then did closeups the next. They had a radio contest inviting people to be in a John Hughes movie and 10,000 people showed up. It felt real. The window washers dancing? The camera guys just noticed them. They were catching whatever they could.

I spent weeks with choreographer Kenny Ortega but blew my knee out doing those back yard running scenes. It made the dancing very spontaneous. John would be far away with a megaphone shouting: “Make something up!” I was scared but once everybody’s cheering you on, I felt like I was the king of the world.

When John was alive, I always thought, “Maybe we’ll do it again?” but too much time passed. What happened to Ferris? He’s pretty charming and creative but he probably turned into his dad. That’s what most of us do.

John Hughes originally thought of Anthony Michael Hall or Emilio Estevez for Ferris but they wanted to move on to different things so he wisely cast Matthew. We were doing this play together, Biloxi Blues. In one scene, he’s writing in his journal and we’re supposed to be asleep. One night, he nudges me. I open my eyes and he shows me his journal. It said: “They offered me Ferris Bueller.”

The casting directors didn’t want to see me because I was 28 and thought I was too old. My agent said: “He plays opposite Broderick every night. They look the same age.” I auditioned and they thought, “This’ll work,” but they didn’t offer it to me right away. Matthew’s manager kept laying the idea in John’s ear, saying: “Matthew would like to work with Alan.” That went a long way to getting me the part. Matthew and I were already friends. We didn’t have to make that up.

I always felt on the outside of life. Besides having Ferris for his best friend, Cameron’s definitely on the outside too, I figured because of his repressive home life. He wasn’t free and easy. That was also easy to tap into.

Matthew has a photographic memory for comedy routines and movie scenes. We were big Richard Pryor fans and he knew every routine. He’d do monologues of Tony Montana from Scarface and crack me up. Biloxi Blues director Gene Saks would get mad at us because we were always screwing around. Matthew used to imitate him backstage, going: “I don’t believe you’re soldiers in world war two!” When John told me to come up with an authoritarian voice for Sloan’s dad, that was me imitating Matthew, imitating Gene. I did it just to see if I could make Matthew laugh – and it did.

I honestly can’t remember what was going on in my head during the gallery scene. I had a number of personal losses and tragedies in my life, as we all do and I tapped into some of that.

We had three cars. One had heavy-duty suspension for stunts. The one we drove was plagued with electrical problems. When we collect it after the parade, we’d do the scene and it wouldn’t start. We did 16 takes. When we sent the third one flying out the window, the whole crew erupted into an enormous cheer.

There was a period where I didn’t want anything to do with the film. I was having trouble getting work and everybody kept talking about Ferris Bueller. I thought that’s as good as it’s going to get for me. As soon as I started working again, I really came to appreciate it. My joke is that Cameron’s father came home and threw him out the window. The rest of that day wasn’t a happy one, but maybe things turned out OK. Maybe now he’s a lawyer in Chicago.

Matthew Broderick and Alan Ruck will reunite in the upcoming movie The Best Is Yet to Come

Vamos España? Why this World Cup victory for Spain feels so different from the others

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 12:52:36 GMT

The success belongs to many more people around the world from Gaza to Latin America – even if the collegiate spirit of the team has yet to be mirrored in our public life

Just past midnight, the cheers erupted from blocks of lit flats in my neighbourhood in central Madrid. Hours later, people of all generations were still out in the streets in the middle of another tropical night, and not only because it was warm, with temperatures hovering close to 30C. In the big pedestrianised square Plaza de Olavide, fans had gathered around screens, some sitting on the ground while children and dogs ran around. A girl played on the swings, her Spanish-flag cape fluttering as she swung back and forth.

Argentinian Lionel Messi jerseys were visible throughout the crowd. Many fans gathered also at a nearby Argentinian bar. Not too surprising when you consider there are more than 400,000 Argentinians living in Spain. Messi, whose life and career are embedded with Barcelona, is a football hero in Spain too.

It was the same across the city and throughout the country. Barcelona had one of the largest public gatherings, with more than 30,000 people watching on a giant screen installed by the city council. Catalonia is the home region of stars including the 19-year-old Lamine Yamal, the national side’s most promising player. There is as much regional variety in Spain’s team as there is in the country. Several come from the Basque Country, once only a reluctant supporter of the national team. One player, Aymeric Laporte, was born in France. Backgrounds are as diverse as the population.

It was hard not to agree with Ferran Torres, who scored the extra-time goal that brought us victory, when he said his achievement belonged to “47 million people, not just me or my teammates”. But it felt as though the success belonged to many more people around the world, from Gaza, where Spain has come to represent solidarity with the Palestinian cause, to Brazil.

The celebratory mood was just as palpable three years ago when we gathered to watch the women’s national team win the World Cup. But the joy was overshadowed by sexual harassment and misogyny after the Jenni Hermoso case.

Sixteen years ago I watched Spain’s first World Cup victory among late-night crowds in Brussels, where I then lived. That night felt joyful, but those were painful times. I was covering the eurozone crisis that was already hitting Spain harder than almost anywhere else, as a burst property bubble and soaring unemployment left many people with a sense of hopelessness.

This win feels somehow more rounded. The country itself is in a better place despite the deep political polarisation and widespread mood of dissatisfaction that often dominates public debate. Spain’s economy has become one of the strongest performers in the developed world and its cities feel more prosperous, confident and dynamic than many in Europe.

The national team is young, diverse and relentlessly professional. The cheers in Lavapiés, one of Madrid’s most diverse neighbourhoods, felt momentous in a country where more than 10 million people, about 20% of the population, were born abroad.

Spain’s players also offered an example of maturity under pressure. The clarity with which Yamal responded to former prime minister Mariano Rajoy’s racist comments about the French national team stood out in contrast to the crudeness of a supposedly experienced politician.

The contrast between football’s power to promote integration, which this team seems to fully understand, with the constant partisan battles dominating public life in Spain couldn’t be sharper.

The message repeated most often by the coach, Luis de la Fuente, and his players is simple and powerful: “We are a team. We embrace diversity while working together towards a common goal.” Spain’s greatest strength on the pitch lies not in individual brilliance but in a cohesiveness that becomes greater than the sum of its parts. Ironically, that sense of shared purpose and collective responsibility is perhaps what Spanish public life is missing the most.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Yet even if the impact of football seems fleeting and insignificant, especially in these challenging times, its extraordinary appeal can inspire a shared spirit. At its best, it fosters solidarity and camaraderie. At its worst, it can fuel violence and disrespect, as Argentina’s team sadly showed before, during and after the match.

Everyone sees what they want to see in the Spanish national team, be it nationalism, diversity or simply great football. Of course, not every message is inclusive, but the variety of fans on the street, regardless of age, origin or gender, is a reminder of the immense power of football to bring together very different people.

I keep thinking these days about the motto of the country that hosted the World Cup final: E pluribus unum – out of many, one. Those words reflected the US founding fathers’ thinking. They believed the Declaration of Independence’s ideals would unite people from very different backgrounds without needing centuries of shared religions, cultures and wars, as in Europe.

Unity in diversity remains a painfully unfulfilled ideal in the US and in much of the world – also in Spain. But at least for a night, amid the chants, klaxons and fireworks, one could hope that somehow it is still possible.

María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario. es, a news outlet in Spain

Sex, beds and grisly executions: what Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey changed, invented – and left out

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 12:17:13 GMT

From missing scenes and characters to a brand new ending, the director has taken some artistic liberties with Homer’s epic poem

Peter Bradshaw’s five-star review and a less enthused classicist’s take Will women also enjoy Nolan’s Odyssey? Christopher Nolan interviewed Why shooting on occupied land feels like a betrayal

Turning a 12,000-line poem that takes a day to read aloud into a three-hour film was always going to require some pruning. So it has proved with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, which dispenses with a number of scenes and characters from Homer’s ancient Greek epic. The director has also changed the emphasis in some of the story’s most famous episodes and made a few of his own additions. Here we run down the most significant alterations.

The godsHomer’s Odyssey opens with a discussion between Zeus and Athena on Olympus; with Zeus’s blessing, Athena plays an active role in guiding Odysseus home, supporting him in vanquishing the suitors and offering encouragement to his son, Telemachus, while adopting multiple disguises. Meanwhile, Poseidon frustrates Odysseus’s progress and Hermes is sent on a couple of key missions. The only god Nolan depicts is Athena (Zendaya), who appears as a vision seen only by Odysseus (Matt Damon) and seems to represent his conscience rather than being a fully realised divine entity.

Nausicaa and the PhaeaciansOne of the Odyssey’s most celebrated scenes is the meeting between Odysseus and the young princess Nausicaa; he has washed up naked on a strange island where she and her maids are playing with a ball. After they handle this awkward situation with delicacy, Odysseus follows Nausicaa to the city of the Phaeacians, where he recounts his tales of the Cyclops, Circe, Scylla and Charybdis before being given safe passage back to Ithaca. Nolan leaves out the Phaeacians entirely and has Odysseus tell those stories to Calypso (Charlize Theron) as recovered memories.

Some major ghostsThe film shows Odysseus meeting his former commander Agamemnon (Benny Safdie) in the realm of the dead (Nolan is correct not to depict it as an underworld). But we don’t see Achilles, the greatest of the Greek warriors, nor Ajax, who in the poem silently rebuffs Odysseus’s attempt at reconciliation. Neither do we meet Odysseus’s mother, whom he tries and fails to embrace three times. Another character omitted is the luckless Elpenor, who plunges to his death after drinking too much and then pleads to be properly buried. It’s easy to see why Nolan wanted to economise on these spiritual encounters, despite their power and resonance in the poem.

The execution of the disloyal womenIt comes as no surprise that Nolan shies away from including the Odyssey’s nastiest scene, in which 12 enslaved women who have been disloyal to the household and slept with the suitors are hanged by Telemachus. But Nolan invents a detail along the same lines when he shows one of those treacherous women, Melantho (Mia Goth), effectively condemned to death by Odysseus’s wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), who shoves her into the carnage while the suitors are being slaughtered. He spares us the grisly spectacle of what happens in the poem to the odious goatherd Melanthius, who has his nose, ears, hands, feet and genitals chopped off.

Penelope’s bed testHomer’s Penelope is no pushover when Odysseus returns, and to satisfy herself that the beggar who has just slaughtered the suitors is, in fact, her husband, she draws him into describing their marital bed, as only he and Penelope know that Odysseus had fashioned it from an olive tree. Nolan omits this detail, which demonstrates how Penelope matches her husband for guile; instead, Odysseus shows her a figurine of Athena to prove his identity.

The wooden horseHomer does not tell the full story of the wooden horse, but it is mentioned on three occasions in the the Odyssey (and not at all in the Iliad). Given that using the horse to break into Troy was Odysseus’s idea and crucial to the Trojan saga, it seems appropriate to include it in the film.

SinonThe character of Sinon (Elliot Page), who is shown in the film unwittingly tricking the Trojans into accepting the wooden horse, does not appear anywhere in Homer. Nolan is drawing on Virgil’s account of the fall of Troy in the second book of the Aeneid. He also invents the backstory of Sinon being made to take the place of Antinous (Robert Pattinson) in the Greek army at Troy.

The people from the seaThere is much talk in the film about the world of the Greek heroes being threatened by “people from the sea”. This is not a preoccupation of Homer’s Odyssey. Nor does any Homeric character say, as Nolan’s Odysseus does, that the Trojan war was really all about “trading routes”. But these nods to the concerns of ancient historians show Nolan has done his research.

CalypsoNolan’s Calypso sedates Odysseus with lotus flowers to make him lose his memories, but somehow develops pity for him and lets him go on his way. The Calypso of the poem doesn’t do drugs but is very much into sex (not something we see in the film), forcing Odysseus to share her bed night after night even though he is desperate to get home. She releases him only after Hermes shows up to tell her that Zeus has decided she must do so; as a mere nymph, she knows she must defer to the authority of Olympus. Once it is clear he can leave, Odysseus is able to enjoy a last bit of lovemaking before heading off on his raft.

The CyclopsNolan’s Cyclops doesn’t speak (much), whereas in the poem he engages in lethally comic banter with Odysseus. The lack of dialogue in the film makes the one-eyed giant scarier, but it means we lose a couple of important details from the poem: the ruse whereby Odysseus identifies himself as Nobody so the other Cyclopes won’t come to the blinded monster’s aid, and the moment when Odysseus recklessly reveals his real name, which the Cyclops can then use to ask his father, Poseidon, to curse Odysseus’s return journey. These changes fit with Nolan’s decision to downplay Odysseus’s abilities as a trickster and foreground his battle-hardened resilience and trauma.

CirceIt is never explained why Homer’s Circe turns some of Odysseus’s comrades into pigs. She turns them back into men because Odysseus has proved immune to her potion (thanks to a herb Hermes has given him) and then agrees to have sex with her. She proves to be a very helpful ally and he stays with her for a whole year. Nolan’s Circe (Samantha Morton) seems to be motivated by anger towards animalistic male behaviour, but then meekly agrees to restore Odysseus’s men to their human bodies after he intuits that he really shouldn’t touch that stew and makes her feel sorry for a bunch of guys who just want to get home.

The ambush and father-son reunionIn the film, a band of villains hired by Antinous attempt to kill Telemachus (Tom Holland) at a temple, only to be thwarted by Odysseus, who has arrived on the scene in disguise. Soon afterwards, Telemachus realises his saviour is his father. In the poem, the ambush is led by Antinous out at sea and is easily (and undramatically) evaded by Telemachus, who then meets his father back in Ithaca in a reunion carefully stage-managed by Athena.

The endingHomer’s Odyssey comes to a notoriously unsatisfactory conclusion. Nolan sensibly discards all the poem’s final scenes: the suitors’ arrival in the realm of the dead; Odysseus’s encounter with his father, Laertes, whom he needlessly upsets by adopting yet another fake persona; and the anticlimactic battle between Odysseus and the relatives of the suitors. In the film, Telemachus becomes king of Ithaca, allowing Odysseus and Penelope to sail off into the sunset on a mission to honour his fallen comrades.

Chris Tryhorn is the author of Homer’s Odyssey, a new version of the original story now available as an ebook

England’s white-ball success risks baking in a divide with future Test setup

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 11:50:57 GMT

Finding a candidate to lead the red-ball side is no easy task, with Ben Stokes gone and Brendon McCullum still around

As England’s men scatter for the Hundred, ready to pull on new colours, ingratiate themselves with their new paymasters and use the word “exciting” repeatedly, the management above them could be forgiven for letting out a sigh of relief.

Not that everything is shipshape going into their month-long recess. Far from it. Test cricket is king in this country, No 1 across all age groups and demographics – as per Richard Gould, chief executive of the England and Wales Cricket Board, in his Ashes review in March – and in that regard the first half of the season still goes down as a bit of a shambles.

The 2-1 defeat by New Zealand forced the removal of Brendon McCullum from one half of his role as head coach, while a strung out Ben Stokes threw himself overboard into retirement and was last seen playing for Durham against Northumberland in front of 300 people at Allendale Cricket Club. Three Tests on from Gould and Rob Key insisting the status quo with just a bit more rigour was the way forward, the team have no coach and no captain.

But the T20 and ODI series victories, against an India side at No 1 in the rankings for both, should not to be sniffed at. McCullum’s retention for the limited-over teams was not universally popular but over the past year he and Harry Brook really do seem to have struck upon something as a leadership pairing.

India admittedly chose to reset their world champion T20 side and a one-sided 4-0 defeat showed they swung the pendulum too far. But England’s 2-1 victory in the one-dayers displayed some serious gumption from 1-0 down, the wins in Cardiff and Lord’s equally hard fought but achieved in wildly contrasting conditions.

Cardiff was a low-scoring dog-fight that owed plenty to the enduring class of Joe Root, whereas Lord’s was a high-scoring gunfight on an unusually flat pitch. That England found a way in both – even if Jasprit Bumrah’s absence from the series decider was a bonus – said a lot about the variety they have cultivated.

For all that England are playing catch-up before the 2027 World Cup after a few years of 50-over neglect, Brook leads a side with bases covered. His batting lineup has touch players, power players, and left-right combinations. Brook also had eight varied bowling options at Lord’s: three quicks, wrist-spin, a left-arm angle, two better than part-time off-spinners and Jacob Bethell tweaking it the other way.

Brook’s use of Bethell in particular goes back to the chemistry struck with McCullum, having run off the field mid-innings for advice and been told that a spinner driving the ball into the surface à la Ravindra Jadeja was the play. The wicket this produced of Rohit Sharma on 138 was gamechanging.

Although, this is where things get tricky and we circle back to the strange place that England find themselves. Because for all that white-ball success has mildly offset the anger caused by the Test team’s further nosedive, it risks baking in a divide that may be hard to square when the vacancies for Test coach and captain are filled.

Right now, England seemingly have only two options for captain. One is Root, who would be doing it out of a sense of duty rather than any desire, and the other is Brook himself. Neither is ideal, while both would need strong guidance on tactics and leadership from the new coach: Root because he did previously – and never quite received it – and Brook because everything would be new to him.

In an ideal world, Stokes would have held the role until the 2027 Ashes, by which time Brook’s education as vice-captain would have been greater and he could slide across post-World Cup. This is far from an ideal world, however, and for all that his early appointment would invite questions about his maturity on and off the field, a personal view is that he is the correct, forward-looking choice.

But as well as the burden that a three-format captaincy would place on Brook, can doing this under two separate coaches work in practice? Whoever is tasked with nursing Brook through the early stages of the Test role, they will need a strong alignment with McCullum so as not to overwhelm him with conflicting methods.

Sign up to The Spin

Subscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s action

after newsletter promotion

Andy Flower, the leading coach in the world, turned down the vacancy last week citing an incompatibility with the two franchise teams to which he is contracted. But for all that they probably are incompatible – both the logistics and the message it would send – one wonders whether he also spotted these limitations.

Attractive though the job is, candidates will look at the setup and surely clock that no one bar Stokes – the one player any coach would want – has left the building. Essentially, the person being asked to put out the fire still raging from that failed Ashes campaign also needs to fit in with the people who caused it.

All of which goes back to that tour review in March, the upshot of which was to keep everyone in situ, hire Marcus North as a selector (not head selector, tellingly), flood training with extra coaching bodies, and offer a nod to county cricket by arranging quarterly meetings with domestic coaches and picking the in-form Emilio Gay. Oh, and Ollie Robinson came back for one Test.

Had more fundamental change come about back then – including an approach for Flower with the promise of a far blanker canvas – there is a chance Stokes might have been reinvigorated at the start of the summer, rather than triggered by walking back into an environment in which he had stopped believing.

Who knows, perhaps Gould and Key will find the ideal candidate to make this split-screen approach work. As good as the two white-ball series wins were, and as much as the next month will be about some fun, disposable, content-generation cricket, they can ill afford another mis-step in the format that is still No 1.

The disturbing rise of ‘gooner’ assaults at Dollar Tree stores: ‘They find it funny to degrade women’

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 11:00:03 GMT

In dark corners of the internet, men are goading each other to masturbate in public – and on female shoppers – and post the footage

This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault.

The woman known in court papers as MR never much liked going to dollar stores. She found them cluttered and chaotic, with too few staff on duty and too many strange people roaming the aisles for comfort.

But in early December 2023 she went anyway, because she was planning a promotional photoshoot for her doggy daycare business in Houston and wanted some cheap Christmas props – reindeer ears and Santa hats – to put on her dogs. She and a friend picked one of the few Dollar Trees in an affluent neighborhood and arrived early, thinking they would be in and out quickly enough.

As she walked the aisles, MR said in an interview, she sensed a man standing close behind her. She turned to confront him and noticed that he was a good six inches taller than her. He was talking in graphic detail about sexual things he wanted to do to her. “You’re so disgusting, get away from me,” she told him, and hurried off to find her friend.

Still, he stayed close, and for a few tense minutes the two of them locked eyes while she waited in line to pay. When at last he left, she thought that was the end of it – until, back outside in the chill of the winter morning, she felt something cold against the back of her leggings.

The man had ejaculated on her.

“I didn’t know how to react. I wanted to kill this man,” said MR, who was 47 at the time, recalling the horror and helplessness she felt as her friend wiped her off with towels. (The Guardian has verified MR’s identity but is not publishing her full name to protect her privacy.)

Hours later, on the advice of a sister who worked in law enforcement, she fished her soiled leggings out of the garbage and took them back to the store to report what had happened. A clerk listened to her account and, not seeming to realize that MR understood Spanish, shouted to a colleague in a backroom: “Tenemos otra.”

“We’ve got another one.”

Over the next several weeks and months, MR would learn not only that there had been reports of similar incidents at the same store in the same timeframe – one that had been shared on social media and at least one other she heard about anecdotally from shopping center employees – but that masturbating in front of female customers at branches of Dollar Tree was fast becoming a national phenomenon, a disturbing new form of sexual assault that men were documenting and bragging about in dark corners of the internet.

It even came with its own specialized vocabulary. Masturbating in public and surreptitiously ejaculating on random women was known as “tagging” or “sharking” – or even “cum-sharking”. Online forums praised perpetrators for being “low inhibition” or “low inhib”, and users contributing to the discussion said they wished they could summon the same fearlessness in themselves.

Dollar Tree cropped up again and again as a favored location for such attacks, according to research conducted by MR’s lawyers and corroborated by police and media reports. While perpetrators have not spelled out the reasons, their choice appears connected to the same problems that made MR hesitant to shop at Dollar Tree in the first place and have led, over the years, to intense federal government scrutiny and millions of dollars in fines: inadequate safety and security, understaffing on the premises, and disorganized aisles filled with unopened boxes that offer shoplifters and other criminals ample opportunity to skulk.

In a statement to the Guardian, Dollar Tree did not address the specifics of what happened to MR but said it was committed to maintaining a safe and secure environment for its staff, customers and visitors. “We take reports of inappropriate, unlawful, or harassing behavior in our stores extremely seriously,” a spokesperson said. “Any incident of this nature is unacceptable, and when we become aware of criminal activity, we cooperate fully with law enforcement and support their investigations.”

As soon as MR spoke to a local TV station in Houston about her story, she and her lawyers heard many similar ones – either via social media or directly from women who recognized what she was talking about and wanted legal representation of their own. “This happened to me in November of last year,” one woman wrote on X. “Same store, same location.” That woman had previously posted images, also on X, of a man she said followed her out of the same Dollar Tree, in Houston’s River Oaks shopping center, and ejaculated in front of her in the parking lot. (Attempts by the Guardian to reach the woman were unsuccessful.)

MR’s lawyers, Anna Greenberg and Ed Blizzard, were soon handling cases in Colorado Springs, San Diego and Miami, and collecting police and media reports on more than a dozen similar instances at Dollar Tree or its former sister chain, Family Dollar, going back to 2017. In some cases, the victims were out shopping with their young children. One perpetrator was a freshly hired sheriff’s deputy. Another was a Dollar Tree employee.

“We couldn’t believe how big the scale was,” Greenberg said.

Almost immediately, the lawyers stumbled on another weird dimension to the cases they were developing: an online subculture of lonely, disaffected men, known as “gooners”, who bond with one other over their shared fascination with obsessive masturbation and compete with each other to see who can keep going for hours or even days at a time.

While most appear to pursue their self-pleasure in private “goon caves” and are not criminals, some gooners, the lawyers found, took pride in public acts of masturbation. In fact, some were committing sharking assaults at Dollar Tree stores and posting the footage online.

Greenberg and Blizzard could not establish how public MR’s assailant had been with his exploits, since he has never been identified. But they did find an individual going by the name “Goon-God”, who had a page on an amateur porn site offering more than 200 sharking videos for $25 – along with a promotional clip that appeared to show an attack on an oblivious Dollar Tree shopper as she pushed a cart along a crowded soap aisle.

Another gooner, who was caught filming himself while masturbating at a Dollar Tree in Fern Park, Florida, told police that he did this regularly “in different locations” and uploaded the videos to an OnlyFans page, according to his arrest report.

MR’s lawyers believe this constitutes a new frontier in sexual assault – what Cecelia Prewett, a consultant to the legal team, describes as a “gamification” of sexual abuse perpetrated and encouraged by isolated men who pool their anger towards women in online forums.

It’s a view broadly shared by criminologists and sociologists who study the intersection between human sexuality and crime – although they note a similar wave of sharking attacks in Japan about 15 years ago that attracted an online audience before subsiding again.

“Masturbating over someone in public is done – and filmed – for the purposes of humiliating women and also receiving attention and accolades from other men,” said Michael Halpin, a sociologist from Dalhousie University in Canada who has studied the relationship between male “incel” culture and gender-based crime. “The [online] community applauds it, supports it, uplifts it and calls for more acts like it.”

Halpin and other researchers say the misogyny is not restricted to people who are involuntarily celibate but extends to a broader community of men who are fueled by a combination of unfulfilled sexual desire, easy access to pornography and the lure of an attention-seeking economy.

“Fame and celebrity are held up by many people as the ultimate form of success – more than wealth,” said Adam Lankford, a University of Alabama criminologist. “To some fringe individuals, this form of provocative behavior, no matter how distasteful, can be seen as a ticket to their own form of attention.”

The degradation may even be the point, said Jamieson Webster, a psychoanalyst who teaches at the New School in New York. “A dollar store is the most abject place, where people who are already at the bottom go because they can’t afford anything else. In some way this is about trying to get a leg up on the lowest rung you can fall to – how to make a dollar on people who only have a dollar,” she said. “There’s something about that that feels so sad and tragic.”

The acts themselves – public masturbation and ejaculating on strangers – long predate the internet, as does their place in the underbelly of popular culture. Jeffrey Dahmer had a history of indecent exposure before he became a serial killer, including an arrest in 1986 for masturbating in front of two 12-year-old boys in Wisconsin. In both the book and film The Silence of the Lambs, a prisoner housed next to Thomas Harris’s fictional serial killer, Hannibal Lecter, flings his semen at FBI agent Clarice Starling in an effort to sexualize and humiliate her.

What has changed in the digital age, Lankford argues, is the accessibility of material apt to arouse people in the most anodyne of settings, such as a traffic intersection or a dollar store.

Long before it developed an association with criminal acts, “gooning” was understood as a pornography-fueled compulsion, sometimes involving multiple screens at once, that can become a substitute for intimate relationships with others. It also tends to come with a heavy dose of self-loathing. Experts say that online forums and video content aimed at gooners often send the message that obsessive masturbation – whether alone or in public – is as much as men like them can aspire to in life. Webster described it as a “disavowed manic state of triumph over something hideous”.

One common trope of the pornography that these gooners consume has men ejaculating over women’s bodies, faces and hair – acts that, Lankford said, have no basis in evolutionary biology and are difficult to interpret as anything other than demeaning to the women.

The Dollar Tree assaults essentially bring these elements together, turning a criminal act into some combination of a dare and a misogynistic joke. “Damn that’s pretty cool,” reads one comment on an incel forum in response to a 2018 sharking video. (The video has since been taken down.) “How did he not get caught there lol,” reads another.

And the phenomenon appears to be growing.

Six months after the attack on MR, a woman at a Dollar Tree in Philadelphia captured her own sharking episode on video and the clip subsequently went viral.

“He fucking nutted on my fucking leg!” the woman can be heard yelling as she chases her assailant out of the store. The man is clearly visible in surveillance photos released by the police.

The Philadelphia rapper Meek Mill reposted the video with the offer of a $2,000 reward for anyone willing to “play manhunt”. Within hours, 35-year-old Gary Miles turned himself in and subsequently pleaded guilty to charges of indecent exposure, open lewdness and indecent assault without the consent of the other party.

Over the following months, the term “dollar store gooner” became a meme on the internet that spread far beyond the closed world of the gooners themselves. A “Dollar Tree gooner” crypto coin launched in January 2025, followed by an unofficial Pokémon card and a song released on SoundCloud by an underground noise band from Tennessee named Mukus.

Around the same time, another episode went viral – not at a dollar store, but at a coffee shop called Bikini Beans in Tempe, Arizona, where a man was filmed masturbating as he ordered from a female barista at the drive-through window. Again, the online response pointed to some constituency of men who find such things entertaining. “They find it funny that the women are getting degraded,” said Halpin, the sociologist. “That’s what they enjoy.”

Within hours of the Arizona video appearing online, the perpetrator, who appeared to have no connection to the online subculture fascinated by him, wrote a note to say he couldn’t face his family and killed himself. The episode raised the complicated question of whether the man should be remembered primarily as a sex criminal or as a victim of public shaming. A group of supporters firmly believing the latter organized a protest at the coffee shop to pay homage to a man they called “goonlord” and dubbed the occasion a “gooneral”.

MR, for her part, was so horrified by her assault that as soon as she got home she walked into the shower fully clothed, only later understanding that she was washing away crucial evidence. She subsequently made extensive efforts to find her assailant and was heartened when a store employee told her there were video surveillance cameras.

But Dollar Tree never produced any footage, never apologized for what happened to her and, when challenged in a lawsuit alleging negligence and failure to provide a secure environment, argued that MR was not entitled to damages under Texas law because she had suffered no physical harm. Without video footage, police and private security officers at the River Oaks shopping center were unable to pursue an investigation.

MR’s lawyers counter that the relevant legal standard is not, in fact, physical harm but “offensive contact”. And, in a testy exchange with a lawyer for Dollar Tree during a sworn deposition, MR vigorously challenged the notion that she had suffered no damage. She described how the incident had rocked her confidence, affected her relationships and made her afraid to go out after dark. “My life is not the same since that incident,” she said. “I totally was caught off guard. I didn’t have a chance to defend myself.”

When the Dollar Tree lawyer asked her what she wanted out of the lawsuit, she replied: “You [have] to take accountability of what is happening in your stores. You’re causing pain to people. I don’t know if it’s because of the bottom line, or what, but it’s happening and you guys need to stop it.”

In its statement to the Guardian, Dollar Tree said it was committed to effective safety and security. “Our efforts include ongoing safety education, regular policy reviews, risk assessment and mitigation activities, investments in physical security measures, and collaboration with local law enforcement,” the spokesperson said.

With MR’s lawsuit, though, the company has attempted to limit the introduction of evidence from assaults in other states and other Dollar Tree outlets as a matter of legal strategy. In an August 2025 email to MR’s lawyers, company attorney Wesley Welmaker described the assault on MR as a “one-off event at Dollar Tree in the River Oaks shopping center”.

In response, Greenberg told the court that MR’s assault was “anything but a ‘one-off event’” and pointed to 10 cases of sexual assault at Dollar Trees she had documented over the previous year and a half, six of them involving ejaculation.

A year later, with the lawsuit still mired in preliminary motions and no trial date in sight, Greenberg’s research team has dug up 63 officially documented sex crimes in all – fewer than five a year before 2020 and as many as 18 a year since the December 2023 attack on MR. Sixteen involved masturbation or ejaculation. The company’s attempts to disavow this, Greenberg said in an interview, amounted to “a plethora of stupid arguments” and only underlined what she saw as a pattern of poor corporate governance.

Dollar Tree, its former sister company Family Dollar (which it sold last summer), and its rival Dollar General have all been under a microscope after multiple reports in recent years of safety violations, improper storage of drugs, rat infestations, poor security, shoplifting and other crimes including sexual assault that have occurred in its stores. Predominantly, the stores serve low-income neighborhoods where there are few alternatives, and critics often accuse them of preferring to endure some degree of criminal behavior occurring in stores and weather fines from the federal government’s workplace watchdog, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha), than pay for fully functioning security systems and boost staffing.

In 2022, an Osha administrator accused Dollar General of valuing “profits more than the safety of the people who work in their stores”. The next year, the Biden administration reached a settlement with Dollar Tree and Family Dollar, under which the companies agreed without admitting liability to pay $1.35m in outstanding fines and overhaul workplace safety arrangements.

At the time, Dollar Tree said it was taking steps to address safety concerns and that the foundations of the company were “continuous associate feedback, engagement and root cause analysis to understand issues and ensure compliance”. When asked by the Guardian about continuing criticisms that Dollar Tree was more interested in the bottom line than in adequate security or staffing at its 9,000 US outlets, the company had no comment.

Greenberg and Blizzard believe the Dollar Tree gooner phenomenon can shed further light on these issues and offer an opportunity to address some of them. In MR’s lawsuit and a similar case in San Diego, their legal filings argue that Dollar Tree should have had more staff and security, should have alerted the police to the sharking episodes on its premises and should have issued a warning to shoppers.

In the San Diego case, Greenberg and Blizzard found eyewitness and photographic evidence that the same perpetrator had masturbated and ejaculated on another woman in the same store one day before – and returned six days later to assault a third victim. “Dollar Tree did nothing,” they and a team of California lawyers allege in court papers. Dollar Tree did not respond to questions about this accusation.

The lawyers saw what they allege to be a similar corporate disregard for shopper safety in a case they read about in Knoxville, Tennessee, where a Dollar Tree employee named Collin Miller was caught on camera as he masturbated in front of customers in November 2024. “The [security] video shows the defendant with his penis exposed as he walks past the register where the victim is checking out,” a police report quoted by a local TV station said. “The video also later shows the defendant rubbing his groin area for several minutes at the register while customers are present in the store.”

Although Miller pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of indecent exposure, he was not fired. And then, eight months later, he was accused of following a family around the store with a camera and taking surreptitious photographs up the 16-year-old daughter’s skirt. Once again, the police investigated and, according to media reports, found 25,000 compromising images of women on his phone. He subsequently pleaded guilty to two counts of unlawful photographing in violation of privacy. Dollar Tree did not respond to questions about the case and Miller’s employment status.

Halpin, the sociologist, said he sees an overarching pattern linking the Dollar Tree masturbation incidents, photographs like Miller’s – known as “creepshots” – and the compulsion of some perpetrators to post evidence of their exploits online.

“They’re not just doing this for personal gratification,” he said. “They want an audience to engage with it, and they want other men potentially to do it too. When these things are posted, they look at view counts, comments and accolades from other men. And there are other people out there who look and think, ‘I want that attention as well.’”

The attention-seeking has a cost. MR said that, two and a half years after her sharking episode, she had found no peace. “I feel like crying,” she said, “and then I get so fucking angry.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

The one change that worked: I tried the ‘no poo’ method – and it transformed my hair

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 10:00:54 GMT

When I gave up washing my hair, the first two weeks were the worst. But I was determined to follow my barber’s advice ...

In 2025 I’d not had a paid-for haircut in about five years, preferring to ask my ex to cut it with kitchen scissors in the bathroom. But now I was in my late 20s and single and I decided that it was time to look more grown up. Not knowing the first thing about looking after my hair, I felt that a trip to an establishment that offered something beyond a short back and sides – a trendy, gentrified place where a trim puts you back a cool £38 – was sorely overdue.

“You need to stop washing your hair,” my barber told me bluntly. As they ruffled through my shapeless, overgrown mop I was warned about using too much shampoo, which can leave your hair dry, lifeless and coarse. I sat in the swivel chair feeling a bit embarrassed. My barber’s words were less a caution and more a diagnosis. I was instructed to drop shampoo immediately for at least two weeks. The dry variety was fine if I got desperate for a clean and I could maybe use a bit of conditioner as a treat. But for the most part, water was my entire regime.

To my mum’s delight and my own teenage dismay, I have thick, ginger hair. Years of heckling and having a name that starts with the letter G have made me and my gingerness inseparable. For better or worse, my hair is usually the first thing someone will notice about me. I wanted to take some pride in my hair, and the knowledge that I’d unwittingly been sapping the life out of it was jarring.

Like most people, I found a daily squirt of shampoo to be as much of a ritual as brushing my teeth. It felt counterintuitive, then, to forgo it completely.

The first two weeks were the worst. Advocates of the “no poo” method – ditching shampoo for water or homemade concoctions due to claims that commercial products cause repeated, unnecessary damage to your locks – often tell you that it gets worse before it gets better. There is a sort of dirty threshold you have to pass before reaping the benefits of poo-less hair, they say.

This was harder than I first imagined. I would step into the shower, dunk my head under the cascading water and immediately reach for the bottle without a second thought. A glob of apple-scented shampoo would ooze on to my scalp and then, suddenly realising what I’d done, I’d have to scrape it off. A few days in and my head was crying out for a lather. But I was determined to follow my barber’s advice.

I carried on, counting the days until I could wash my hair. But slowly I felt no need. Two weeks became three. Three became four. Eventually, I lost track. “I can’t remember the last time I washed my hair,” I said to my best friend, who thought it sounded a bit gross. But my hair had never felt better. It was wavier, bouncier, glossier. The dirty, itchy feeling that had lingered during the first fortnight disappeared, and suddenly I felt as if my hair was finding a natural balance after years of endless shampooing. Until then, I hadn’t realised just how dry my hair had been.

My scalp used to feel irritated, but it was one of those minor issues we all tend to leave unspoken unless they snowball into something more troubling. Shampoo seemed to have been stripping away the natural oils that were supposed to moisturise and protect my hair.

Obviously, everyone’s hair is different. I’m told people with fine or greasy hair don’t last long without needing to shampoo. But for people with my hair type, it’s really not necessary.

More than a year later, my hair is shinier and curlier than ever. A wash at my quarterly haircut does me just fine, and I could probably go even longer. The apple-scented shampoo I bought a year ago remains untouched on my bathroom shelf.

Two new tortoises have hatched. Now we have seven – and it’s chaos

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 10:00:54 GMT

The males have to be separated or they attack each other. The tiny new arrivals are a constant source of anxiety. Yet, despite all this, my husband is considering adopting more

To hatch one unexpected baby tortoise is universally viewed as a blessing; hatch two more and people start asking pointed questions, such as, “Are you running a tortoise sanctuary now?” and “Do you have the horniest tortoises in Yorkshire?”

The answer to both is “apparently”, and it’s chaos. We now have seven tortoises of which at least three are male and therefore – sorry for the gender essentialism, but it’s true – trouble. The two male adults have to be separated or they attack each other and we got confirmation that the previous baby, who hatched in 2024, is also male when we found him trying to have sex with his mother (it’s OK – she is 10 times his size).

We thought it would be cute to take a picture of all seven together last week but within seconds, it descended into violent anarchy with everyone biting and scattering in opposite directions at high speed (tortoise slowness is a myth – they move like Usain Bolt in this heatwave).

Our current strategy is divide and contain: the most violent recidivist has been taken to my stepfather’s yard where the only things he can hurt are hardy perennials. The other adult male is temporarily in the greenhouse. This has confirmed our suspicion that he is really quite dim: he keeps capsizing despite there being absolutely no obstacles in his way and is unable to right himself – I’m constantly having to flip him over when I’m watering the tomatoes. Meanwhile, I am brokering the wayward two-year-old toddler’s adoption and re-education by a lesbian couple who have vowed to try to “raise a good man” (rather them than me).

That leaves the females (serene, unbothered, bankrupting us in chicory) and the two, as yet unsexed, new arrivals. Barely bigger than a 50-pence piece, they are a source of constant anxiety. Back Dot (we took a marker to their shells) keeps trying to escape; Side Dot is dozy and reluctant to eat. The collective noun for tortoises should be a torment, not a creep. Despite all this, I’ve just found my husband reading about Theo, a 40kg teenage African spurred tortoise currently up for adoption, with a furtive, calculating expression. Grounds for divorce!

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

How Elephant and Castle risks becoming London’s gentrification ‘patient zero’

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 09:58:55 GMT

New £500m town centre welcomes its first tenant this month, but displaced traders say promises that they could return have been broken

Diana Sach once employed more than 30 people and catered for hundreds more every day from her Latin American restaurant and delicatessen, famous for its Peruvian empanadas, in south London’s Elephant and Castle district.

Now, she looks longingly at the shiny tall buildings that have replaced the brightly coloured but shabby shopping centre that was her home from home before being demolished in 2021.

“I hoped to be part of it. But there has been delay after delay and now I can’t see how it will happen for me,” says Sach.

The Elephant, which will this month welcome its first commercial tenant – the matcha-serving Blank Street Coffee – and where residents are due to move in later this summer, is part of a £500m redevelopment of the south London landmark once renowned for its urban deprivation.

A modern town square surrounded by tower blocks has replaced the old shopping mall – a brutalist fortress surrounded by spooky underground walkways and tunnels, which was one of Europe’s first large indoor shopping centres when it opened in 1965.

It is the latest step in the multi-billion pound reinvention of the area, which has seen the neighbouring Heygate housing estate demolished and rebuilt as modern towers, with shops and eateries on the ground floor, surrounding a leafy park.

The opening of the Elephant, which includes about 40 shops, restaurants and bars as well as a cinema and gym, a new home for the London College of Communication, 55,000 sq ft of offices and hundreds of flats – all watched over by the former centre’s distinctive statue of a pachy­derm carrying a tower on its back – marks a new start for the area after years of construction.

The regeneration plan has been the subject of wrangling between local people, the council and developers since the 1990s, with residents nervous that their needs would be steamrollered along with the mall in favour of gentrification.

It is part of an ongoing battle across London, and other UK cities, between communities and redevelopers.

Oli Mould, professor of social, cultural and historical geography at Royal Holloway, University of London, says the redevelopment of Elephant and Castle, which began with the razing of Heygate, is almost “‘patient zero’ of London’s gentrification.”

“A lot of these processes happen quite fiercely and quickly in London then spread across the country,” he says.

Mould suggests the new development has created an “identikit homogeneous gentrified place”, which risks “destroying the very thing that makes a community thriving and beautiful in the first place”.

Sach, who came to the UK from Colombia 30 years ago, is not alone in feeling there is no place for her in the Elephant development.

She says the developers, Get Living, and Southwark council have failed to honour promises that her restaurant would find a new home.

She and the 90 displaced Latin American businesses that brought colour to Elephant and Castle were told there would be adequate temporary accommodation for them to maintain their businesses during construction. But only a handful found a new place to trade on the temporary site. For the restaurant and cafe owners, the shoe boxes on offer within a stack of metal containers, now set to be dismantled, proved unviable.

Many closed down as the difficulty in finding an appropriate alternative site, compounded by the impact of Covid, took its toll.

Once the development was completed, the businesses were told a more permanent, low-cost sites would be available in the new Elephant development or new streets nearby.

However, fewer than half of the displaced small businesses are being offered new premises in the neighbourhood, according to a report by local charity Latin Elephant.

Alongside Blank Street Coffee, a Marks & Spencer food store, a Pret a Manger, an Everyman cinema and DistriAndina, a Latin American supermarket currently based in the neighbouring railway arches, are among the first signed tenants.

Only five of the 40 commercial sites are being set aside for the return of local businesses at affordable rents, as well as 10 small spaces within the railway arches.

A food market hall, expected to be run by the Blend Family operator, will have space for 14 small food stalls, but none have been specifically set aside for former tenants of the defunct mall.

It is a similar story above the shops and restaurants, where there are 485 homes to rent across three towers, including just five at social rent tenure, 45 on London living rent (LLR) terms and 124 at discounted market rent. A further phase of the development, yet to be built, will add 116 social rent, 12 LLR and 37 discounted market rent homes.

Get Living says it is “working closely with Southwark council to finalise the affordable retail strategy, with a clear commitment to ensuring that eligible independent traders from the former Elephant and Castle shopping centre are given first priority when applying for discounted market rent units within the Elephant”.

It says the “ambition is to create a vibrant and diverse town centre, and a core part of making that happen is ensuring it continues to support the local and independent businesses that make Elephant and Castle what it is today”.

On a tour of the site, Rick de Blaby, the outgoing boss of Get Living, acknowledges local people have experienced a “decade of destruction”, demolition and rebuilding.

“In the end, the developers have got to show them it was all worthwhile. We have got to make it a place people engage with and come back to time and time again, where they can connect and feel safe,” he says.

John Batteson, Southwark council’s cabinet member for climate emergency, jobs and transport, said he was committed to “keeping the cultural diversity that makes Southwark such a special place”.

He said it was a “cast-iron condition of planning permission” that the developer must provide affordable retail space for local businesses and traders.

However, today it feels as if the independent shops, cafes and restaurants that inhabited the area, bar a few exceptions, have been priced out, making way for a more corporate, orderly vision, similar to many other developments across Britain.

Even those independent businesses that have found appropriate space in the wider Elephant and Castle redevelopment say they are struggling to hang on.

Dario Lopez, an accountant representing the few Latin American businesses that managed to secure premises nearby, says most now fear they will need to leave, despite having taken out large loans to fit out their shops, cafes and restaurants.

Miko, a Venezuelan restaurant, started life as a kiosk in the old shopping centre before taking up residence at the base of a new tower block.

Lopez says Miko’s owner, Lenin Erazo, was offered a lease with zero rent in the first year, rising to £3,000 a month at the end of a five-year period.

Now, he is in dispute with a new landlord, who wants to double the rent to more than £6,000 a month.

“The area is still a building site, and in the first five years the developers have failed to invest in anything that will bring people from outside the area to visit. There are homes, but nothing to increase the footfall for local shops,” he says.

Mould says local authorities and developers looking to revitalise town centres should be wary of what they could lose as well as what can be gained through redevelopments.

“You can address problems without having to displace people with multi-billion pound programmes. If you can make a developer out of the community, that’s better,” he suggests, pointing to efforts by traders in south London’s Brixton to buy their colourful local market.

“It might not make as much money short term, but longer term it keeps cultural vibrancy in the area, which makes it attractive and makes people want to come.”
