The rave secret: why middle-aged women are larging it – and seeing big health benefits

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 09:00:51 GMT

For those who are burned out, perimenopausal, or both, dancing all night can be a panacea. It’s great exercise, lowers stress, boosts energy and provides connection. No wonder so many are doing it

It’s 4am and I’m in a club – the first time I’ve done this in years. I’m 51 and in my sandwich era, meaning I’ve got teenage and elderly loved ones on my mind – a situation that generally calls for early nights. But when you’re responsibilities-maxxing, sometimes you need the opposite. A blowout. A huge, transcendent, resetting release. A rave.

I don’t know what took me so long to get around to it. Misplaced parental guilt? Internalised ageism? Exhaustion? It’s not as though I didn’t know other gen-Xers who have been regularly getting blissfully – ceremonially, even – lost in house, techno or drum’n’bass, and they’re not alone. A 2025 study by the University of Leeds went viral: “Women aged 40-65 are turning to raves for real mental health,” said one of many Instagram posts and press headlines. “Why many women over 40 still go to raves,” read another. But surely the question should be: why the hell wouldn’t they?

Many of those who do never actually stopped. Of the 136 women surveyed for the study, “82% had been attending for more than 20 years”, says one of its authors, Alinka Greasley, professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. “I’m a DJ myself,” she says. “I still go out raving and I’ve been doing so for 26 years.”

But others like me had lapsed, only to return when the need became borderline desperate. There is a small amount of psychological literature looking at why clubbers stop as they get older, with women citing family responsibilities, says Greasley, “or saying: ‘I feel that women of my age shouldn’t be out doing those activities.’” Joanna, 50, started clubbing again six years ago and now goes every few months with old friends. “There’s something about it being completely separate from parenting and work that feels really special,” she says. She realised she had been missing nightlife when her children were very little. “And I love club culture,” she says.

When going raving was first mooted by her friend, Joanna’s internalised ageism reared its head. “I was so resistant, I was almost repulsed by the idea of a woman in her 40s going clubbing – and possibly taking drugs.” This unease at entering spaces that are traditionally associated with youth culture is not unusual. Greasley says that before she and her colleague Alice O’Grady did the study, women O’Grady had previously interviewed “had experienced comments on the dancefloor such as: ‘Whose mum are you?’” And while some said they dressed up for self expression, many dressed down to escape attention in a sea of 18- to 25-year-olds. Other comments included people saying such things as: “Oh, can I take a photo of you?” or: “Wow, I hope I’m still clubbing when I’m your age.” But, says Greasley, “negative attitudes were not a defining part of their participation”. Quite the contrary.

The music itself and dancing were the top draws for the women, followed by socialising with friends. But, “overwhelmingly”, says Greasley, “they were reporting that they did feel a really strong sense of belonging. There’s a strong theme of age being irrelevant, they talk about making friends with people in different generations – predominantly they’re going to spend time with their own friends but also get something from being there, around other people.” A couple of women even said they go with their children “and feel at home”.

Rachel Giddings, a psychotherapist who works with (mostly EDM) artists on their wellbeing and uses psychology to hone their performances, says that while “women often feel lost in society at a certain age, when you go into an inclusive dance space, you can enter a liminal space where time dissolves and everybody is treated as an equal. Doesn’t matter if you’re a CEO, a road sweeper, a woman or a man, if you’re 25 or 55, you can access that space, and that gives you a sense of belonging.”

Joanna says she did feel conspicuously “‘a mum’ at first, and like: ‘Oh, I won’t know how to dance any more.’ But after I had been once, that melted away. There are a lot of young girls out, but you see other people in their 30s, 40s, 50s and actually begin to stop noticing.” On one early outing, she saw a couple in the queue who looked as if they could be in their 60s. “She was wearing a tweed suit – it was almost as if they were in fancy dress, like: ‘Hi, we’re the old couple,’ and I saw them dancing later on, so that made me feel a lot better.” In any case, she says, clubbing now isn’t about trying to get back to her younger self. “I’m seeing where it’s at these days, and I quite like it. It’s something that you can dip in and dip out of.”

My big night out was in a vast club filled with mostly young people, but all the eye contact from strangers was warm, inclusive and full of shared wonder. To be fair, pretty much everyone seemed to be high or drunk or both, but as Giddings points out – with no judgment either way – you can reach that awed, transcendental state without drugs. “These psychological states are absolutely accessible without substances,” she says. When she posts on this topic on social media, she says, “there are thousands of comments where people say: ‘Never had a drug in my life but I feel these feelings,’ or: ‘I’ve done drugs and don’t any more, and feel these feelings.’”

Giddings says part of her mission is to redefine society’s perception of rave culture as naughty or illicit. “When you are going out on the dancefloor, you are doing it because it’s healing, because it’s connective.” People often say clubbing is escapist, “but actually, the reframe is: it’s self-regulation together. We say: ‘I’m escaping from my normal life,’ but we’re actually seeking togetherness, identity, belonging.”

This raving-for-wellbeing narrative, as Giddings points out, also appeals to gen Z – an unprecedentedly health-conscious youth demographic. “At age 14, they’re in my gym on the treadmill next to me,” she says. Even on some fundamental levels, clubbing now is more clean-cut than it was in the 90s. Joanna says when she first started going again, “I was just stunned by needing a photo ID, and the air-con – no sweat dripping from the ceilings. And no one’s smoking [inside], obviously, so your hair and clothes don’t stink.”

Dancing all night undeniably counts as exercise and comes with added mental-health benefits that can be especially helpful when you’re middle-aged, burned out or perimenopausal. Greasley says these include “feeling alive, feeling energised, both at the time and afterwards. And then also a lot of women report that the ability to go out and enjoy nights and to dance for hours has a positive impact on lowering anxiety and depression and low-mood states.” I have often likened the mood swings that come with perimenopause to the “hormonal” moods of adolescence – perhaps for women it’s both of these times that we seek a release the most.

Dancing with others is particularly medicinal. As Greasley says: “People moving together increases social connection and bonding, and that entrainment with other people I think is particularly the case for beat-based music. There is research showing that this physical movement entrainment [when the body synchronises its movements to an external rhythm] leads to feelings of pleasure and social connectedness.” EDM is structured to elicit sweet anticipation building to huge group highs. “You get buildups, you get breaks – the moment where you know that the beat might come back in after a prolonged period – and everybody starts moving together, and that’s what creates these highly pleasurable embodied experiences, and that can create these really powerful emotional experiences and chills within the body.”

“The group becomes one organism,” says Giddings, “so we start to sync into each other’s nervous systems and when you’re waiting for the beat, your heart rate starts to rise, and then boom, it’s that somatic release of energy and we can release that stress we brought with us that we don’t want any more.”

It is also an opportunity for women, she says, “to reclaim their identity outside ‘I’m a carer’, ‘I’m a parent’, ‘I’m a worker’ – I’m not just one dimension but multifaceted and this amazing part of me can be spontaneous and free and connected”.

For those who are put off by late nights, says Greasley, “all sorts of nights are cropping up, targeted at older people. Here in Leeds, I’ve noticed that there are an increasing number of raves starting at 6pm and finishing at midnight. I love going to them myself. You can dance for hours and still be in bed by midnight or 1am.”

This suits the OG acts and DJs who have also got older. EDM clubbing started in the 80s, so, says Greasley, “while it still remains a youth culture, the culture as a whole has aged”. In November, Leftfield performed at an event with the promoters Bugged Out! at Drumsheds – a 15,000-capacity former Ikea store in Edmonton, north London – which ran from 1pm until 10.30pm.

But Joanna says she loves her occasional late nights. “Going out for me, and staying up until 3am or 4am – when I tell some people that, they’re horrified but I find it really energising. Obviously, not all the time, or if you’ve got full-on childcare the next day.”

It took me days to recover from my late night. It was gone 5am by the time I got into bed, ears ringing, body clock thinking it was nearly time to wake up. I slept terribly, but I felt revived in other ways. Being at the rave didn’t make me feel old. I felt as if I’d come home. After all, my generation invented this.

‘We need to talk about how difficult it is’: why one couple are pinning surrogacy hopes on Mexico

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 08:00:51 GMT

Jules Von Hep and Mark Beverlo, who have been trying to become parents since 2020, are now seeking help abroad

Rise in overseas surrogates ‘increases risk of stateless babies’

Why Mexico is at the heart of ethical debate over global surrogacy

Jules Von Hep has wanted a baby ever since he can remember. For many people that dream is straightforward to realise – but, as a gay man, he has always known it would take years of saving and searching.

The only way he can have a biological child is to use a surrogate, which costs tens of thousands of pounds, and it often takes years of searching to find the right match. For Von Hep, it has been an “incredibly painful, incredibly expensive” process.

“I’ve always known that surrogacy is the option I wanted to go down. That, really, has led to the career choices that I’ve made, how I’ve worked, making sure that I was always saving money in the bank for fertility,” he said.

Von Hep and his partner, Mark Beverlo, started trying to become parents in 2020. They signed up with an IVF clinic, bought some donor eggs and submitted themselves to rigorous sperm-testing requirements. They soon found themselves facing rapidly mounting charges, starting from £1,000 for single advisory meetings to £13,000 for a round of embryo creation, including a failed attempt along the way.

They then signed up to an agency, where the waiting list for UK-based women volunteering to be surrogates was two to three years. Von Hep had a look at some unregulated Facebook groups, in which prospective parents pitch themselves to potential surrogates. “I just couldn’t bear the idea of pitching our lives, standing there in front of the house with a dog and saying: ‘This is what we’ve got’.”

Eventually, the surrogacy agency matched the couple with a woman and the embryo transfers began, at a cost of £5,000 a go. When these didn’t work, they opted to attempt insemination at home, sometimes referred to as “turkey basting”.

That approach also failed and Von Hep and his partner decided to give up on surrogacy in the UK. They turned their sights abroad: the most popular destination, Ukraine, was closed off due to the war, leaving the US – too expensive at about £250,000 – Canada and Mexico, in which surrogacy was legalised for same-sex parents in 2021.

At a cost of around £60-90,000, they were lucky to be able to afford to go to Mexico. Although the costs are similar to the UK, which has a non-commercial altruistic model of surrogacy in which a surrogate’s expenses are paid, some Mexican states take a commercial approach.

“The difference doing it commercially is unbelievable. The knowledge that the egg donors are being paid, that everyone is – there’s nothing woolly about the situation,” he said.

The cost includes all medical bills and expenses, plus a fee to carry the pregnancy, which the agency they are working with, My Surrogacy Journey Mexico City (MSJMX), said is usually around MXN$388,000 (£16,914).

“[Our surrogate] has been a surrogate before, and she is also trying to build a business. I think that’s where commercial surrogacy helped. She was very open about it. She said: ‘Yeah, I’m trying to build my business, and this is a great way of earning extra money.’

“For me, that answer was really refreshing. I’m like, OK, perfect. We’re all in this together. Everyone is getting what they need. There’s no murkiness.”

The agency the couple is working with is UK-based and helped them find their surrogate, who they met via video call. It’s also queer-founded, which Von Hep felt made it more supportive and sensitive to their circumstances.

There are concerns in Mexico that the patchwork of regulation – two states have banned it, while three have laws governing the practice – has left women open to abuse. Researchers have raised concerns that poor women could “rent their wombs as a survival strategy” and there have been reports of women coerced into surrogacy by abusive husbands.

MSJMX says that “ensuring the ethical and legal protection of both intended parents and surrogates is one of our highest priorities”, and it only operates in “surrogacy-friendly states” like Mexico City. The agency said it works with “highly experienced, independent human rights specialists and leading surrogacy lawyers in Mexico City who have an exceptional understanding of reproductive legislation and family law”.

The couple have shipped their sperm to Mexico, picked a new egg donor and had embryos fertilised. They are now waiting for the transfer to begin.

If everything goes to plan, once their baby is born, Von Hep and Beverlo will move to Mexico for around three to six months while they arrange their baby’s passport – another potentially fraught process. On their return to the UK, they will have to apply for a parental order with the family courts to become legal parents.

Von Hep and his partner have decided this will be their last attempt to become biological parents. Yet he is feeling tentatively excited that this time it might finally work – so much so he has recommended surrogacy in Mexico to other gay and straight couples he knows who are struggling with fertility.

“It feels like the wild west in the UK. The professionalism from the Mexican clinics – I can’t fault it. It’s unbelievable and it costs the same price,” he said.

Despite his frustration with the system, he is incredibly grateful to the women who carry other people’s babies. “Anyone who is willing to be a surrogate is like an angel on earth. Whether it’s to help a friend, relative or total stranger, it’s one of the most selfless acts of kindness and love I can think of. We wouldn’t be able to even dream of having children of our own if it wasn’t for the benevolence of surrogates,” he said.

But mostly he wants to talk about his surrogacy journey to challenge the taboo, and add his voice to the growing conversation on social media around the difficulties gay men face in becoming parents, from adoption to surrogacy.

“I feel like the conversation around gay men having babies, and the money that it costs, and how difficult it is, needs to be talked about so that it’s not as difficult for the generations under me,” he said.

“The more same-sex relationships are accepted and embraced within this country, the more gay men are going to want to have a family, because this social norm is shifting to embrace same-sex couples.”

Feel guilty after gossiping? You’re clearly not doing it right

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 08:00:50 GMT

Some social media users claim they get a horrible sinking feeling called ‘post-gossip clarity’ after dishing the dirt. May I suggest they try harder?

Many phrases sound more elegant in French and post-coital tristesse is one of them. The English version is direct to the point of rudeness: post-nut clarity. This phenomenon, much discussed on social media, isn’t exactly the sadness à la Française, it’s more the sudden clear-headedness and, often, sense of regret men experience after climax, once the dopamine and arousal chemicals have crashed and their prefrontal cortex – responsible for logic and reasoning – is back online. It’s a calm, rational, remorseful view of the situation.

Now, there is a new offshoot of this sensation for 2026: post-gossip clarity. Ugh! Also originating on socials, it is that horrible, sinking feeling you get when the buzz has worn off after a particularly juicy goss sesh, especially if you got carried away and spilled a little too much tea. This is easily done, especially if you have fully committed to the conversation, which you always should when blessed with killer info.

Let’s not get into whether gossip is better than sex, but there are certainly parallels. During arousal, desire clouds the brain and leaves you unable to concentrate on anything else. If it’s good, it can make you gasp. There is also a certain level of gratitude involved. You don’t want to be selfish; you have to give as well as receive. But when you’re overexcited, it’s hard to hold back, which can lead to premature revelation.

Dishing the dirt well is an art form and perhaps post-gossip clarity is simply an occupational hazard, like an unfortunate side-effect of medication that makes you feel better in every other way. Besides, surely the unpleasantness of the deep wish that you hadn’t said something is more than cancelled out by what you heard in return? If not, maybe you’re doing it wrong.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Top 30: from half a million World Cup photos, why I love these the most

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 07:00:49 GMT

Our picture editor chooses his favourite images from the tournament including Lionel Messi’s cathedral, that delicious diving header from Jude Bellingham and a humbling scene in Gaza

What makes a great World Cup photograph? Now there’s a question with myriad answers. Composition, newsworthiness, emotional resonance, expert timing and luck can all contribute to varying degrees. But one thing they all share is the power to capture attention.

On the Guardian sport picture desk, we have received more than 500,000 World Cup photographs over the past six weeks, with so many gems among them. Here, with much applause to the photographers who created them and a slight bias towards England, are my favourite images of the tournament.

1

An absolute cracker to start with. In this picture, the cavernous Kansas City Stadium sweeps around a small corner of grass on which the world’s most famous footballer stands alone. You can’t really see it’s Lionel Messi, but somehow you can tell it’s him. It feels as though everybody’s eyes are pointed in his direction, like they’re worshipping a deity in an epic footballing cathedral.

2

Technological improvements have led to the creation of high-quality miniature cameras which can be placed inside goalmouths and operated remotely. Seeing the game at such close quarters feels wonderfully dynamic. This frame in particular captures a mad scramble between Brazil and Japan; the wonky angle adds to the sense of chaos.

3

A self-referential choice, but this was a big news story at the time: England played Croatia in their first game and the England manager, Thomas Tuchel, was so furious he couldn’t see the players during the national anthem that he asked Fifa to move the photographers for subsequent games. In fairness to him, you can see why. Four weeks later, Tuchel would garner headlines again after his substitutions in the semi-final against Argentina triggered England’s collapse.

4

At first glance it looks innocuous enough, then you notice Tarik Muharemovic’s right ankle buckling under the pressure applied by Folarin Balogun’s mistimed challenge. Replays of the incident suggested the foul was unintentional, though the Bosnian was lucky to escape injury. Balogun received a red card following a VAR review, but his one-game ban was suspended by Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. With Balogun back in the team, the USA were dumped out of their own tournament by Belgium in the next round.

5

I’ve relished seeing so many photographs from inside the tunnels at this World Cup because the players seem to reveal a little more of themselves away from the public eye. This candid shot of Scotland players Findlay Curtis and Jack Hendry shows them in the wake of their 3-0 loss to Brazil – a defeat that was filled with calamity, and which ultimately led to Scotland’s early exit. They look like they’re outside a head teacher’s office waiting to be reprimanded.

6

I love a good diving header and this one by Jude Bellingham against Mexico was peachy. From a photographic point of view, you seldom get shots from tribune positions like this during a Premier League season, so they have a real novelty value during major tournaments. But it’s more than just novelty: the elevated vantage point helps to remove the surrounding clutter and give a proper fan’s eye view of the goal. I also love the verdant grass, the shocking pink goalkeeper’s jersey and the sense of anticipation because the ball has yet to cross the line. It reminds me of the signed photograph of Coventry’s Keith Houchen, from the 1987 FA Cup final, that hangs proudly on my dad’s office wall.

7

So many hydration breaks, so much Powerade, but only one player managed to look like a Portuguese water dog fresh from a dip in a lake. The Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimarães is pictured here dousing himself in H2O when his side faced Morocco in their opening game at New York New Jersey Stadium. Brazil ultimately went home for an early bath after losing to Norway in the last 16.

8

The mass rowing displays performed by Norway’s fans this summer have been a viral sensation. Seen everywhere from Times Square to Miami Beach, they also became a fixture of the team’s post-match partying, with Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard both banging a fan’s drum as the side progressed to the quarter-finals. The Vikings were stopped by England, but their journey was one of the feelgood stories of the tournament.

9

A gorgeous pool of afternoon sunlight spilling on to the pitch, surrounded by deep shadows. You couldn’t really create better low-key lighting conditions if you tried. The photographer just had to nail the exposure and wait for a subject to pass through. The fact that it’s Kylian Mbappé who’s skating across the turf in his rich blue France top adds a nice splash of colour and gravity to the scene.

10

Luka Modric has spoken in the past about not wanting to let his people down, and of carrying memories of his grandpa, Luka, with him. He appears to be deep in thought here before playing Panama. Perhaps it’s just a fleeting moment – a man simply massaging his temple or visualising the first tackle – or maybe he’s remembering his war-torn roots and the family member he was named after.

11

At the ripe age of 40 and with a club career that has taken him to Cyprus, Moldova, Portugal and Slovakia, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha became the breakout star at this year’s World Cup. His numerous saves against Spain in the group stage earned him global praise as well as 17 million followers on Instagram. Another stellar display against Argentina, in which he memorably denied a quick free-kick by Messi, further enhanced his reputation. I like his expression in this photograph as he soaks up the adulation from the crowd following the Blue Sharks’ remarkable goalless draw with Spain.

12

This photograph shows the power of football while also putting the World Cup into perspective. Palestinian residents in Gaza gathered amid the ruins to watch a screening of Egypt’s game against Argentina. A moment of normality amid the horror and heartache.

13

Erling Haaland’s first goal against Brazil left his old Premier League rival, Gabriel Magalhães, in a heap. In this shot you can see water (or perhaps sweat) flying off the striker’s forehead, his neck fully strained after connecting with the ball. Haaland scored seven goals in five World Cup games: he netted from inside the box, outside the box, with his left foot, right foot and of course his head. Norway have still never been beaten by Brazil after five matches. No other nation can say that.

14

This image was shot before the tournament, as part of Fifa’s official player portraits, but I’ve only recently seen it – and it’s well worth a mention. You don’t see many players with braces, but Lamine Yamal, who only turned 19 this month, wears his with pride. This frame was shot using a 24-70mm lens on a Canon R5 Mark II which has a whopping 45 megapixels, so I suspect it’s been cropped quite hard in post-production to achieve this composition.

15

Some penalty misses are worse than others. Germany’s Jonathan Tah and Manuel Akanji of Switzerland both had Chris Waddle moments as they blew their chances from 12 yards over the bar. Ordinarily I’d say you need to see the crossbar to illustrate that the shot went over, but the way the ball is rocketing skywards – almost as if it could escape the stadium roof – tells the story perfectly.

16

Even when your ego is as big as the sun, sometimes you just need a cuddle. This photograph captures Neymar Jr’s visible distress as he realises his international career is over and his childhood ambitions of lifting the World Cup will never be fulfilled. His teammate Raphina is there to support him. It lacks the humility of Freddie Flintoff consoling his opponent Brett Lee in the Ashes, or the stoicism of Derek Redmond being helped across the finish line by his father at the 1992 Olympics, but it still packs an emotional gut punch.

17

This photograph was flipped 180 degrees by Getty Images before being transmitted to us. Manipulation of this ilk feels almost heretical in the world of photojournalism, but the result is very compelling. It shows Julián Alvarez celebrating his late winner against Switzerland, and it makes me question my fundamental photographic principles. Would I publish it like this in print to illustrate a news story? Absolutely not. Would I include it in an online gallery of images that caught my eye this summer? Evidently so.

18

The stadums in the US have been mind-blowing in scale. Atlanta Stadium, home of the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons and the city’s MLS and NWSL teams, has a maximum capacity of 75,000 people, a climate-controlled environment and a 335-metre display known as the “halo”. This picture from up in the gods looks suitably epic. Initially I assumed the camera was remote-controlled, but it transpires some photographers were actually working up there on the gantry. What a view they had!

19

This is a beautiful example of a photographer using a slow shutter speed while panning gently with the action. I especially like the details within: Anthony Elanga’s facial expression is crisp, and the pink boots leave a painterly trail.

20

Harry Kane’s late strikes against the Democratic Republic of Congo in the last 32 led to an outpouring of emotion from the England captain. I was torn over which frame to select – there are some lovely ones of him sprinting across the turf, flanked by Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon – but this one of him being embraced by Bellingham serves as a perfect reminder of their twin heroics at the tournament. It’s clean, nicely balanced and full of bromance.

21

The guaranteed agony and ecstasy of penalty shootouts always makes for brilliant images. This year, Gustavo Gómez of Paraguay takes the crown for the wildest reaction. After beating Germany during sudden death, Gómez, who scored his own spot-kick, surged across the pitch like a heron taking flight, almost vaulting his teammates José Canale and Orlando Gill as he went to embrace them. He then careered through the photographers behind the goal in pursuit of a mobile phone so that he could document the moment himself.

22

Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, also known as Lumumba Vea, is dubbed a “living statue” because he doesn’t move during games. Instead, the DRC fan poses on a plinth for the entire match, raising his right arm to mimic the statue of Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic, which stands in Kinshasa. Why anyone would go to a football match and not respond to the on-pitch action is beyond me, but Mboladinga insists it’s his patriotic duty.

23

Youri Tielemans scored twice in Belgium’s stunning comeback against Senegal in the last 32. This 89th-minute header might have been a little trickier to control had the defender Moussa Niakhaté competed for the ball instead of diving theatrically to the ground at the first sign of contact. The virtue of modern cameras, many of which shoot 30 frames per second, is that the full sequence of this goal was captured, and we could choose the exact frame when Tielemans’s head connects with the ball.

24

Sasa Kalajdzic overcame three anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the years and months prior to the 2026 World Cup, but the Austrian enjoyed a moment to savour when he netted a 96th-minute equaliser against Algeria to keep his side in the tournament. The game ignited accusations of fixing, because a 3-3 draw ensured both sides went through, but a finale like that – and celebrations like this – cannot be scripted.

25

Australia’s Connor Metcalfe needed three stitches in his eyebrow after being clipped by a stray boot from Andrés Cubas during the Socceroos’ group match with Paraguay. Maybe it’s the slumped shoulders or the shirt pulled up around his neckline, but he looks like a forlorn child who needs a parent to clean him up.

26

You could say this is just another “two men and a ball” photograph (an expression the Guardian’s photographer, Tom Jenkins, uses to describe generic images of sporting action). But I particularly like this one because of the contrast of sporting prowess – the acrobat versus the brick wall – and for the misshapen ball which appears ready to pop. Dan Burn has become a cult figure for England, in the mould of Peter Crouch. Many supporters call the 6ft 7in defender Big Dan Burn, but Bellingham apparently calls him Burninho. There’s no way Raúl Jiménez, the Mexico striker, was ever getting the ball past him.

27

Let’s be honest, Lionel Messi is not very good at penalties. He’s missed four of eight in World Cup matches and 34 of 151 in his career, including shootouts. A botched effort against Egypt, in a match which the African side went on to lead 2-0, could have been a pitiful ending to his gilded international career. Instead, Messi scored the equaliser and drove his team to a remarkable 3-2 win in normal time. This picture, taken after the match, speaks to the weight he carries on his shoulders. Is it relief or guilt? Either way, he looks tortured by expectation.

28

The composition of this photograph is simple but beautiful. The intersecting diagonals, the contrast between light and shade, and the depth within the scene … it makes for rich viewing.

29

Ismaël Koné’s eyes say it all. The Canada midfielder had just broken the tibia and fibula bones in his lower left leg after a challenge by Qatar’s midfielder Assim Madibo, who would receive a red card and a five-match ban. As a photo editor, when incidents like this occur you have to weigh up decency and news value before publishing (I still feel traumatised by the uncensored images I saw of Eduardo’s broken leg in 2008). I think this image conveys the severity of the incident without being unduly graphic. Koné left the pitch on a stretcher but waved to fans as he exited.

30

I’d typically include a celebration photograph from the World Cup final among my favourites from a tournament, but this ‘tackle’ by Enzo Fernández was so bad – and the image of Pau Cubarsi flying through the air so striking – that I couldn’t look beyond it when reviewing the match. Cubarsi looks like he’s falling from space. An absolutely dreadful final sparked into life at this defining moment. Cubarsi rose from the turf to claim the title of ‘best young player’ of the tournament and, more importantly, a World Cup winner’s medal.

Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?

The Guardian Mon, 20 Jul 2026 05:00:48 GMT

A report on the Spectator’s coverage of Muslims makes for grim reading. Conservatism is now focused on this minority to the exclusion of everything else

I start this column already resigned to the tune out, to the glaze over, the click away. This is not to say that I do not have faith in you, dear reader, to keep reading and caring. But I am aware, and this is central to the problem, that it is now normal, when it comes to a certain minority in this country, to speak of them as if they were some sort of plague. Islamophobia has become so common as to be mundane in large parts of the British media. Foremost among the offenders is Britain’s oldest political magazine: the Spectator.

A large and comprehensive report from the Centre for Media Monitoring reviewed 3,733 articles published in the Spectator relating to Islam or Muslims. Released last week, it criticised the publication for “a sustained and systemic pattern of biased coverage of Muslims and Islam”, according to the CMM, “with more than half of all relevant articles rated as biased over an eight-year period”. It is grim, grim reading.

Among the conclusions reached by the report are that articles in the magazine regularly portrayed Muslims as a “problem population”, delegitimised the very notion of Islamophobia, and consistently presented Muslims as exceptional or threatening. The overall effect is of a minority that is not only sectarian and separate, but also, ironically, from within its ghetto, dangerous and aggressively colonising British society.

Articles cited refer to Muslim concerns about racist abuse as “dainty sensibilities” and “handwringing”. Presumably, this precious response includes objections to statements in the magazine panicking that “organised Islam is strong and vociferous” and, in reference to the growing population of Muslims in the country, that “there are now more than double the number of semi-literate, virgin-obsessed potential murderers among [sic] our midst”.

Even the mere existence of Muslims in the UK is presented as something akin to a poisonous foreign presence. “Prominent historians … have noted entirely correctly that Islam seems to have things about it which make it uniquely indigestible to the modern secularised state,” wrote one columnist. “We should have second thoughts about approving mosques,” wrote another contributor.

The coverage depicts a country that is going to the dogs. Politicians quake in the face of Muslims, the left aids and abets them, the courts indulge them. The scale of the onslaught is staggering and relentless. It would be unacceptable to speak of another minority group in such terms, but Muslims occupy a sweet spot that makes them convenient subjects for the forces of reaction. They are racialised, they are immigrants or the descendants of immigrants, some of them dare to practise their own religion. Their unique profile makes it easy to channel racism, anti-immigration sentiment and just plain old petty parochialism. Islamophobia itself has metastasised, becoming a vehicle for the sort of things you can’t say out loud about people of colour in general, but which you can say about Muslims.

In the foreword of the report, the writer and broadcaster Peter Oborne – the magazine’s former political editor – traces the history of the Spectator, and how it went from condemning the anti-immigration Enoch Powell to “steadily rebuilding his reputation”. Oborne cites a piece from earlier this year that says Powell “had a view of the British polity, values and way of life with which many Britons to this day feel they identify, and that is not least what establishes him as one of the country’s greatest conservative influences”. Now, the publication platforms broader far-right politics, in one article praising Tommy Robinson as likable, “intelligent, quick, articulate, well-informed, good-mannered”.

And yet despite such extremism, the Spectator snugly occupies a position of such respectability that its summer party is attended by Labour and Tory politicians and journalists from across the British media, who rub shoulders there with Nigel Farage and the broader Spectator-verse. “The jamboree remains the most sought-after social ticket of the Westminster summer season,” boasted the Spectator in July after this year’s edition. A refutation of the charge that there is a wholesale coddling of Muslims if there ever was one. There is something crudely and unmistakably symbolic in the magazine’s influence. As the country is riven by far-right politics and protests, as mosques are attacked and hate crimes reach new levels, our elected politicians and opinion-makers are comfortable to drink and make merry among those who mainstream and disseminate inflammatory rhetoric.

But something else struck me while reading example after example of quoted texts. It was all tawdry, poorly written, poorly argued stuff. You come away not with the sense that this is an august magazine dedicating its formidable intellectual and journalistic resources towards a problematic minority it is concerned about, but with the sense that it isn’t a serious publication.

Its articles are the sort of content you get from GB News, or a bellicose radio phone-in, or a tabloid on a tear. A convergence has occurred among the rightwing media, a radicalisation that has alighted on anger and scaremongering, which feeds readers’ and viewers’ fears and paranoia. It is a successful commercial strategy, but there is no community here, no solace or even loving depiction of the precious country vandalised. There is little to bind other than hate and outrage, no hold on what it is we are ostensibly saving from Muslims or immigrants or the left. Tuning in, what one hears in concert is: “You have once again woken up in Britain. Welcome to hell.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The result is a climate that is hostile and dangerous not just to Muslims but all who it has been decided are stealthily annexing the country. But there is also a wider degradation that comes with the relentless focus on Muslims. The project of developing a vision of conservatism that goes beyond purification has been abandoned. Interested in, say, how the contemporary movement can reconcile austerity and free-market policies with stagnant wages and productivity and declining public services? In the ideological fissures in modern conservatism and its splintering? Perhaps a rant about Muslim public prayer as an act of “public domination” can shed some light on these crucial questions.

The Spectator and its broader universe constitute what is now mostly a low-brow media attempting to dress up racist audience-baiting as high-end journalism, all of which is met not with alarm and objection by establishment politics, but a “cheers” in the sunshine. It is not that Muslims have turned into a bigger problem for the country, but that the country itself, and its so-called intellectual elites, have become small. In resisting the feeling that this is all just how it is, in not glazing over, we resist becoming small along with them.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Shayne Coplan of Polymarket and Tarek Mansour of Kalshi are young billionaires intent on dominating prediction markets. It’s more than a battle. It’s “bad blood.”

Credit... Illustration by Scott Anderson

Supported by

By David Yaffe-Bellany and William K. Rashbaum

Early one morning in November 2024, Shayne Coplan, the founder of Polymarket, awoke to an unexpected visit. A group of F. B. I. agents burst into his New York apartment with a battering ram, scouring for evidence of illegal betting on his platform.

On social media, Mr. Coplan dismissed the raid as a politically motivated attack by the Biden administration. But privately, he and his advisers voiced suspicions about a different culprit, whom they blame for many of Polymarket’s problems: Tarek Mansour, the chief executive of Kalshi, Mr. Coplan’s biggest rival in the booming business of prediction markets.

Mr. Mansour’s company had indeed played a role. In the months before the F. B. I. raid, Kalshi’s lawyers met with federal prosecutors in Manhattan to raise concerns about Polymarket, according to four people with knowledge of the discussions, which have not been previously reported. The lawyers explained how Polymarket’s platform worked, one of the people said, and highlighted an important fact — that customers could use it from the United States, where it was supposed to be banned.

It was a moment of maximal aggression in a long-simmering feud between Kalshi and Polymarket, two of the tech industry’s hottest start-ups. A clash of ambitious founders is nothing new in Silicon Valley, where ego-driven squabbles are as familiar as corporate puffer vests. Uber and Lyft battled to rule the ride-hailing industry, and the billionaire-on-billionaire mudslinging between Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic has become an intriguing subplot in the artificial intelligence world.

But the competition between the 28-year-old Mr. Coplan and the 30-year-old Mr. Mansour goes far beyond the normal bounds of corporate rivalry. Both are newly minted billionaires, intent on dominating prediction markets, which offer betting odds on sports, politics, culture and nearly everything else. By most accounts, they also despise each other with a fervor that has seeped into how their companies interact at virtually every level, according to interviews with more than 40 people in their circles, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive dynamics.

“It’s just bad blood,” said Dustin Gouker, who writes a newsletter about prediction markets. “It’s become personal.”

The competition has raged in corporate meetings and the halls of Congress, shaped the regulatory debate in Washington and drawn unusual levels of attention and concern. Kalshi and Polymarket have filed competing trademark applications, jockeyed for the same deals, courted the same talent, sniped at each other in the press and engaged in name-calling on social media. They have each forged a business relationship with Donald Trump Jr., a common strategy in President Trump’s transactional Washington.

Both companies have “crossed the line in some ways,” said Noah Zingler-Sternig, a former Kalshi employee who runs a prediction market investment fund. “It can make public perception of the two companies less serious.”

The mutual loathing is not just about market share. It is a deeper rift over character and business ethics. Kalshi presents itself as a responsible actor that waited to secure regulatory permission to operate in the United States; Polymarket forged ahead without a license and still runs its main platform offshore. Kalshi has “know your customer” rules and bans certain sensitive topics; Polymarket lets customers sign up without sharing personal information and bet on things like the timing of Israeli missile strikes.

Mr. Coplan and Mr. Mansour have met over the years but rarely see each other these days, preferring to bad-mouth from afar. A self-described “math nerd” who graduated from M. I. T., Mr. Mansour has compared the prediction market rivalry to the healthy competition between the former pro quarterbacks Tom Brady and Eli Manning. Lately, however, he has also called Polymarket’s actions “illegal” and “immoral,” and pointed out that its overseas site is operated by a business entity in Panama.

“I don’t know what the laws of Panama are on insider trading on prediction markets,” Mr. Mansour said at a conference in Washington in April. “Probably nonexistent.”

Mr. Coplan, a skilled pitchman who dropped out of New York University, seldom mentions Kalshi in public. But he has called the company a “Polymarket copycat” and believes that Mr. Mansour has set out to sabotage him, two people with knowledge of his thinking said. He is convinced that his site is the best prediction market.

“It’s the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now,” Mr. Coplan said on “60 Minutes” last year.

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said the company had learned about the F. B. I. raid from media reports. Kalshi routinely discusses compliance issues with the government, she added, and has been vocal in pointing out “public issues with a company that is endangering consumers and sullying the industry.”

Mr. Mansour has “no personal animosity towards Shayne,” Ms. Diana said. “The only issue Tarek has with Shayne is his reckless approach to an industry that Kalshi has spent years getting regulated.”

A Polymarket spokeswoman shared a one-line statement about Mr. Mansour, a quotation by Ralph Waldo Emerson: “The louder he talked of his honor, the faster we counted our spoons.” She said Polymarket has protocols in place to stop insider trading, resulting in nearly 100 referrals to law enforcement. “We are committed to maintaining accurate, fair and transparent markets,” she said.

As prediction markets transform from a niche pursuit into a cultural phenomenon, both companies face mounting regulatory threats. Kalshi and Polymarket are battling in court with a procession of state attorneys general who say the companies’ sports offerings violate gambling laws. Polymarket is also being investigated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the U. S. regulator that oversees prediction markets.

Kalshi’s warnings about Polymarket have become much more overt. In May, Brian Quintenz, a former C. F. T. C. commissioner who serves on Kalshi’s board, shared a message on X describing Polymarket’s protocols for screening users.

He tagged an account belonging to a potentially interested party: the U. S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York.

A lifelong New Yorker, Mr. Coplan founded Polymarket in 2020, working out of an apartment in Lower Manhattan, where he set up a laptop in a makeshift “bathroom office.” He viewed himself as an upstart, pioneering a technology far outside the mainstream.

He had a formidable rival. A former Citadel trader who had grown up in Lebanon, Mr. Mansour started Kalshi in 2018 with Luana Lopes Lara, an M. I. T. classmate who serves as the firm’s chief operating officer. Mr. Mansour’s colleagues describe him as smart, scrappy and a bit awkward; Mr. Coplan is more easygoing, an art collector and music aficionado who cultivates a studied New York cool.

They have never been particularly friendly. In one stilted early encounter, Mr. Coplan pointed out to Mr. Mansour that both were raised by single mothers, a comment that made Mr. Mansour uncomfortable, a person familiar with the exchange said.

But the two men share a conviction that prediction markets will transform finance and media, harnessing the “wisdom of the crowd” to provide a valuable new source of information. Bets on Polymarket and Kalshi are structured as yes-or-no questions, with topics that range from the weather to the Super Bowl; the amount that users collectively wager determines the odds of a particular outcome.

Before it started offering these bets in 2021, Kalshi sought a license from the C. F. T. C. to run a prediction market. During early discussions with the agency, Kalshi was already raising concerns about Polymarket, three people familiar with the matter said.

The primary messenger was Jeff Bandman, a Kalshi strategist, who urged the C. F. T. C. to look into Mr. Coplan’s firm, pointing out that it was available in the United States without proper authorization, one of the people said. In January 2022, the agency fined Polymarket $1.4 million for operating an unregistered platform; Polymarket agreed to stop accepting bets from customers in the United States.

The ban opened the door for Kalshi to dominate the U. S. market. But first the company would have to fight the government for friendlier rules. Under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., the C. F. T. C. prohibited bets on elections. Kalshi sued the agency in 2023.

While the legal battle tied up Kalshi, Polymarket turned into a mainstream sensation, despite its U. S. ban. With a few clicks, Americans could gain access to the website through virtual private networks, an online tool that disguises a user’s location. Polymarket’s odds became a major talking point before the 2024 presidential election, when the site showed that Mr. Trump had a clearer advantage than polls suggested.

“They didn’t do the regulatory,” Mr. Mansour said on a podcast in June. “They just launched. They didn’t care.”

Shortly before the election, Kalshi defeated the C. F. T. C. in court, paving the way for licensed prediction markets to operate in the United States. Polymarket still lacked that seal of regulatory approval, even as the platform’s surging popularity turned Mr. Coplan into an overnight celebrity.

In 2024, prosecutors in the Southern District of New York pursued an investigation into whether Polymarket was violating the prohibition on U. S. users. The week after Mr. Trump’s election victory, the F. B. I. conducted the raid of Mr. Coplan’s Manhattan apartment and seized his electronic devices.

Kalshi pounced. Keaton Inglis, a Kalshi employee, reached out to the former National Football League star Antonio Brown, directing him to post a message on X calling Mr. Coplan “guilty,” according to screenshots published in Pirate Wires, a tech publication.

Mr. Brown later apologized, saying he had been “doing other business with Kalshi and just tweeted it.” Mr. Mansour also expressed regret. “Some of our team got pretty heated,” he said on a December 2024 podcast.

The raid left Mr. Coplan and his allies deeply suspicious. Rumors about the incident circulated in the media with striking speed. Behind the scenes, Mr. Coplan and other Polymarket insiders speculated that a private investigator, hired by Kalshi or one of its allies, had tailed him, seen the F. B. I. arrive and shared the information with the press, four people familiar with the discussions said.

“This is a complete lie,” Ms. Diana of Kalshi said. “A truly bizarre level of paranoia.”

Last July, Mr. Coplan arrived for a business meeting at Manhatta, a downtown restaurant known for its sweeping 60th-floor views. He had dressed casually, and brought along a bagel in a paper bag.

Mr. Coplan’s dinner date was the billionaire Jeffrey Sprecher, who founded Intercontinental Exchange, the $80 billion giant that owns the New York Stock Exchange. It was a meeting of old and new — and a crucial moment in Polymarket’s rivalry with Kalshi.

Over the years, Kalshi had built a roster of blue-chip investors, including Sequoia Capital, a leading venture capital firm. Mr. Coplan had not always had the same success navigating large institutions. But he and Mr. Mansour both forged relationships with executives at Intercontinental Exchange, which wanted to invest in prediction markets.

Mr. Coplan and Mr. Sprecher hit it off at Manhatta. After considering a possible deal with Kalshi, Intercontinental Exchange instead struck an agreement to invest in Polymarket last fall.

Mr. Mansour was upset when he heard the news, a person familiar with his thinking said. Before the deal was announced, he and one of Kalshi’s investors, Alex Immerman of Andreessen Horowitz, each spoke with Intercontinental Exchange’s executive team, five people with knowledge of the conversations said.

Those people offered conflicting accounts of the talks. But the feedback from Mr. Mansour and Mr. Immerman came across as a last-ditch effort to dissuade Intercontinental Exchange from going through with the deal, three of the people said.

Ms. Diana said Kalshi was “not interested in the deal” with Mr. Sprecher.

In the end, Mr. Sprecher stuck with Mr. Coplan, unveiling a deal to invest up to $2 billion in Polymarket in October. It was part of a string of victories for Polymarket. Last July, the Southern District of New York dropped its investigation into Mr. Coplan, as the Trump administration pulled back on enforcement. That summer, Mr. Coplan also announced an investment from 1789 Capital, the venture firm part-owned by Donald Trump Jr.

“This admin is very pro-innovation, and pro-crypto, and pro-Polymarket, which is amazing,” Mr. Coplan said on “60 Minutes” last fall.

To capitalize on the friendly environment, Polymarket would need a license to operate in the United States. Mr. Coplan planned to buy a company that already had the necessary approval.

He faced a familiar obstacle: Kalshi. Mr. Mansour raised concerns with top C. F. T. C. officials about a pending application from Railbird, a little-known prediction market operator that was rumored to be Mr. Coplan’s acquisition target, five people familiar with the matter said.

Kalshi’s warnings went unheeded. The C. F. T. C. approved Railbird’s application in June 2025, and Mr. Coplan went on to buy a different firm, QCX, for $112 million, after it received a U. S. license around the same time. Polymarket’s main platform was still banned, but the QCX purchase allowed Mr. Coplan to roll out a smaller U. S. app, giving his company access to more customers.

When he announced the QCX acquisition in July, Mr. Coplan posted an image of the American flag on social media.

“I’ve waited a long time to say this,” he wrote. “Polymarket is coming home.”

As the New York Knicks embarked on an epic playoff run this spring, Mr. Mansour posted a photo of himself under the lights at Madison Square Garden. He sat courtside, with a toothy grin, wearing Knicks colors.

Officially, Kalshi was celebrating a new partnership with the Garden, which had christened its sixth-floor concourse the Kalshi Concourse. But close observers picked up on something else: a subtle act of trolling.

Mr. Coplan had posted frequently about the Knicks before he was famous, and had been spotted courtside at the Garden during the regular season. Before Kalshi secured the partnership with the Garden, Polymarket had explored a similar deal but was unwilling to match Kalshi’s offer, a person familiar with the discussions said.

It was a sign that a rivalry once confined to an internet niche had exploded into the mainstream. Over the first six months of the year, Kalshi and Polymarket have drawn more than $150 billion in trades, a 1,200 percent surge that has raised the competitive stakes.

So far, Mr. Mansour is winning.

After a fund-raising round in May, Kalshi was valued at $22 billion — $7 billion more than Polymarket. Last month, Kalshi processed over $33 billion in trades, twice Polymarket’s total, according to The Block, a data provider.

Ms. Diana said it was “laughable” to suggest that Kalshi’s deal with Madison Square Garden had something to do with Mr. Coplan. “We don’t do deals to troll people,” she said.

The skyrocketing interest in prediction markets has also brought heightened political scrutiny, much of it focused on Polymarket. In April, an Army Special Forces soldier was charged with using confidential information to place bets on Polymarket about the capture of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro. The soldier had made more than $400,000, using the company’s offshore platform through a VPN, according to the indictment. (Polymarket’s spokeswoman said the company bans VPNs.)

Kalshi and Polymarket are taking divergent approaches to policing insider trading. Kalshi requires customers to provide detailed personal information, sometimes including employment status, before they place a wager. Polymarket’s platform creates a public record of trades, allowing sleuths to ferret out possible wrongdoing. But while customers on the U. S. app are required to identify themselves, the company’s main site still does not mandate that users reveal their name, employer or other details.

That model is common in the crypto world, where customers “like to kind of live under the table,” said Aj Pleasanton, an influencer who is a paid partner of Polymarket.

Behind the scenes, Mr. Mansour has grown increasingly furious about Polymarket’s business approach and sometimes calls Mr. Coplan’s chief legal officer, Neal Kumar, to express his outrage, two people familiar with the matter said.

The clashes happen so frequently, it can be difficult to keep track of them. In the spring of 2025, influencers on Polymarket’s payroll amplified news that a business partnership Kalshi announced with Elon Musk’s A. I. effort, xAI, had fallen through, according to a person familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by The New York Times.

Later that year, Polymarket hired Max Crowley, an early Uber employee, to serve as vice president of partnerships. After less than two months, Mr. Crowley quit and joined Kalshi, angering Mr. Coplan. Between jobs, he received legal threats from Mr. Coplan and Alex Spiro, a lawyer who has joined Polymarket’s board, though no lawsuit materialized, a person familiar with the matter said.

Polymarket and Kalshi do not collaborate even in areas where their interests clearly align. When Kalshi announced that it was forming an advocacy group to fight state-level regulations on prediction markets, it joined forces with several companies, but not Polymarket.

The next month, Kalshi suffered a setback in one of the state cases — and a new gambling opportunity popped up on Polymarket’s website. It invited customers to wager on how soon Kalshi would have to wind down its sports betting operation in Massachusetts.

Sharon LaFraniere and Nicole Hong contributed reporting. Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

David Yaffe-Bellany writes about the crypto industry for The Times from New York. He can be reached at davidyb@nytimes. com.

William K. Rashbaum is a Times reporter covering municipal and political corruption, the courts and broader law enforcement topics in New York.

Maine Democrats Are Replacing an Oysterman With a Lumberjack. It Might Just Work.

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Matthew Yglesias

Mr. Yglesias, a contributing Opinion writer, writes extensively about politics, economics and more at Slow Boring. He wrote from Brooklin, Maine.

In the span of just a few days, Troy Jackson, the former president of Maine’s state senate, has emerged as the likely replacement for Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee for the U. S. Senate. In his favor: His platform — Medicare for all, abolish ICE, no military aid to Israel — is similar to Mr. Platner’s. Not in his favor: He’s less magnetic, and in June, he finished third in Maine’s Democratic primary for governor.

It would be a mistake, however, to dismiss Mr. Jackson as a bargain bin (or a Marden’s bargain, as they might say in Maine) version of Mr. Platner. Mr. Jackson might be the Graham Platner that Maine Democrats were always looking for.

For starters, he’s a seasoned elected official who has served in both houses of the state legislature. He’s a populist, beloved by the state’s labor unions, but not really an outsider or an insurgent.

He is, in many respects, the Everyman that the Platner marketing team wanted to pitch. Mr. Jackson is from the interior part of the state, not the touristy coast. His blue-collar profession was logging, a traditional Maine natural resource industry, not oyster farming, a recent import from farther south. He’s from a working-class family, unlike Mr. Platner, the prep-school-educated lawyer’s son. And in his district, Mr. Jackson has shown a distinct ability to win the votes of working-class Mainers who’ve traditionally voted for Democrats but flipped to Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage in more recent cycles.

Will this electoral appeal translate to a larger audience?

Mr. Jackson lacks both the in-room and the on-camera charisma that powered Mr. Platner’s meteoric rise.

Mr. Jackson’s electoral success also comes in a very specific context. His hometown, Allagash, is tiny and remote — it’s a longer drive from Portland, Maine, than Portland is from New York City. As I recall from a long wilderness canoe trip I took years ago, it has only one restaurant, the Two Rivers Lunch. (It also serves breakfast.) The towns on the Canadian side of the nearby border are larger than Allagash, and the cultural and economic orientation of the region is often more toward Canada than to the rest of the state. There is a notable Francophone minority in the area, and Mr. Jackson speaks with a distinctive Acadian accent.

Like many constituents in his traditionally Catholic home base, Mr. Jackson used to be anti-abortion and skeptical of same-sex marriage. It worked politically in a district that was swinging to the right, but it put him out of step with mainstream Democrats. As he ascended the ladder of state politics, Mr. Jackson evolved into a more conventional progressive on cultural issues. He retained his own electoral strength locally, but in 2024, the year he was term-limited out, his state senate district went for Mr. Trump, even as Kamala Harris won the state comfortably.

Which is a reminder that for all the focus on Mr. Platner’s supposed ability to appeal to Trump voters, Maine is, overall, a blue state. It’s an idiosyncratic one: much whiter and more sparsely populated than most of the rest of blue America, but still quite secular. About 40 percent of its population lives in solidly blue Greater Portland, and the state didn’t see the Democratic slippage that others did in 2024. The political landscape suggests that all Democrats really need to do to defeat the incumbent Republican, Senator Susan Collins, is persuade enough Democrats who’ve voted three times against Mr. Trump to vote Democratic this fall.

In a sense, Maine is the inverse of other critical 2026 Senate battlegrounds such as North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. Mr. Jackson’s culturally conservative background — which would be a clear asset in a red state — may be a booby trap in some Maine precincts. Ms. Collins can argue in the southern part of the state that she, unlike her opponent, has been a defender of abortion rights her whole career while in the northern interior she can campaign as tough on border security.

Still, the deftness of Mr. Jackson’s dominant performance in recent days reflects a useful set of political skills.

When Mr. Platner dropped out, Maine Democrats didn’t have time to organize a second primary. So they opted for a convention with delegates selected via a series of county caucuses. This semi-open process heavily favored intensive organizing over mass communication. The Jackson team succeeded in mobilizing committed delegates throughout the state in a way that none of his rivals really did, allowing him to crush the opposition after an unimpressive performance in a more conventional gubernatorial primary; his principal opponents rapidly called it quits.

Given Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings, Ms. Collins, like many other Northeastern Republicans, would be facing an uphill battle against any Democratic nominee. Mr. Jackson, though not without his weaknesses, is on paper a very strong opponent. He has the backing of the progressive movement that boosted Mr. Platner — and experience from his time in the legislature building coalitions with more moderate Democrats. A tumultuous July is setting up a general election that should favor a tested Democrat like Mr. Jackson. But after watching her survive nightmarish political moments for Republicans in 2008 and 2020, nobody should count Ms. Collins out.

Matthew Yglesias is the author of “One Billion Americans: The Case for Thinking Bigger.”

Despite ‘False Positive’ Test, Taylor Farms Is Still Focus of Cyclospora Investigation

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Cyclospora Outbreak

Advertisement

Supported by

The F. D. A. said it was continuing to look into the supplier’s role in the outbreak as states reported stark increases in cases.

By Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

The Food and Drug Administration said on Monday that strong evidence still tied Taylor Farms to the continuing cyclospora outbreak, despite the agency’s retraction on Sunday of what it had said was a positive test of a lettuce sample for the parasite.

The announcement followed days of confusion after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce from 27 states, but did not offer more information about how people would be able to tell whether they had bought the contaminated product.

As consumers sorted through the conflicting information, health officials in Michigan announced cases in that state had risen to 6,148 on Monday — a jump of more than 1,000 cases over the weekend — as other states reported further increases.

The F. D. A.’s retraction of the test result only enhanced uncertainty about what’s to come in the largest recorded cyclospora outbreak in U. S. history.

Such a “flip-flop” in messaging was unusual for the agency, said Susan Mayne, a former top F. D. A. official who is now an adjunct professor of epidemiology at Yale’s School of Public Health. In her more than eight years at the F. D. A., Dr. Mayne said, she could not recall a time when such a reversal had happened.

That said, cyclospora is “one of the most difficult pathogens to detect in agricultural products,” said Kalmia Kniel, a microbiologist at the University of Delaware who conducts research on the parasite.

False positives are common in tests for cyclospora, she said, because there are often so few oocysts, or eggs, present in food samples, and other compounds in the food itself may interfere with the test. The test may also pick up DNA from other microbes that are similar to cyclospora, she said.

It is also possible that the F. D. A. tested a part of the lettuce batch where the parasite was not present, said John Guzewich, who worked on food-borne disease outbreaks at the F. D. A. from 1997 to 2011.

Cyclospora only grows in human hosts, and testing human feces is the most accurate way to find it, said Felicia Wu, a professor of food safety, toxicology and risk assessment at Michigan State University.

But investigating the source of an outbreak requires that investigators search for evidence of the parasite in food and water samples. The test the F. D. A. uses to do that is a polymerase chain reaction (or P. C. R.), which is “the best” scientists have to test food samples for the parasite, despite it not being “100 percent,” said Keith R. Schneider, a professor of food safety at the University of Florida.

Testing food samples for a pathogen is just one part of an outbreak investigation, Dr. Mayne said. Investigators also interview sick patients to identify what they ate and drank during the days and weeks before they became ill, and then look for the common denominator (lettuce, in this case). They then try to trace the food in question back to a supplier or grower.

With the current cyclospora outbreak, Dr. Mayne said, investigators have a “robust” amount of this type of evidence linking the cases to Taylor Farms’ lettuce.

Sometimes investigators never get a positive test result for a pathogen in a food they believed caused an outbreak, Dr. Mayne said.

It is possible that the products that caused the illnesses in the current outbreak are “long gone,” having already been eaten or thrown away, Dr. Schneider said. And going back to where the lettuce was grown — to try to get a positive test from the plants themselves or from water samples — may not yield anything because the field has likely already “been harvested and plowed under, as farmers prepare for the next crop to be planted,” he said.

Taylor Farms said in a statement on Sunday that the F. D. A. had “not identified a single positive product test result for cyclospora.” But based on the information provided by the F. D. A., the company has recalled all of the iceberg lettuce it sourced from central Mexico.

The F. D. A. said the investigation was still going on and that the agency was continuing to collect and analyze product samples. For now, lettuce remains the primary culprit.

If Taylor Farms lettuce is in fact the main cause of the outbreak, cases should begin to plateau shortly, with rising numbers now representing older cases that have already resolved, said Donald Schaffner, chair of the department of food science at Rutgers University.

But some experts said the contradictory messages risk further undermining faith in the public health system.

“The big concern I have about the flip-flop is also the impact it has on trust,” Dr. Mayne said. “Changing such an important determination certainly raises questions,” she said. That “is most unfortunate.”

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

G. O. P. Boxed In on Iran War as Trump Sidelines Congress

The New York Times July 20, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Republicans now face a worst-case political scenario of being asked to fund an unpopular war over which they have exercised little oversight.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from Washington

President Trump has yet again circumvented the legislative branch as he orders American forces back into combat in the Middle East, weeks after both chambers of Congress rebuked him for waging war with Iran without authorization.

The collapse of the cease-fire and resumption of hostilities has inflamed a debate on Capitol Hill over war powers just as the administration is seeking tens of billions of dollars to pay for the conflict.

That has presented Republicans with a political worst-case scenario months before midterm elections in which their majorities are at stake: They are being asked to vote to fund an unpopular war over which they have had no meaningful oversight, and which they have never voted to approve.

“The greatest fighting force on the planet, the last great superpower must be fully equipped, and that’s the job of Congress to make sure it’s done,” Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN’s Manu Raju last week at the Capitol. The administration last month requested $87.6 billion in supplemental funding that would include $67.1 billion in extra military spending this year.

Asked whether it wasn’t also the job of Congress to authorize the war, Mr. Johnson replied: “We’re going to supply the needs for America’s national security.”

The position amounts to the latest instance of Republicans ceding power to the executive branch, as they sidestep a debate over the conduct of the war and try to rally support within their ranks for a filibuster-proof, party-line bill to pay for it with no strings attached.

It is all the more remarkable coming weeks after bipartisan majorities in both the House and Senate voted to reassert Congress’s constitutional role over matters of war, a slap on Mr. Trump’s wrist four months into a conflict that he had said would last a matter of weeks.

Democrats who worked for months to rally support for such a reproach have followed it up by refusing to allow consideration of the annual defense policy bill or back legislation to fund the military. They have argued that Congress cannot separate its power of the purse from its constitutional authority over war, demanding that the administration share more information about its strategy and plan for the war before they consider voting to bankroll it.

“If the Republicans want our votes, they should provide a credible strategy,” Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said in an interview last week. “How long it lasts, where does it end, what our goals are. Very simple. They haven’t.”

Even Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, voted with his party to block the defense policy measure, which he had supported in committee, over objections to the handling of the conflict with Iran.

“I cannot vote to proceed to a bill that enables an ongoing war against Iran that Congress never authorized,” Mr. Reed said.

Republicans, by contrast, have largely sidestepped the renewed war powers debate, many of them echoing Mr. Trump’s justification for resuming the fight.

“The fact of the matter is, President Trump is the first president dealing with what has been the status quo for decades — which is Iran attacking everybody’s ships, everybody’s navy, everybody’s anything going through the Strait of Hormuz,” Representative Brian Mast, the Florida Republican who chairs the Foreign Relations Committee, said on Friday during an interview on Fox News. “After this escalation from them, we are now the United States of America that says this is not going to be the status quo. It’s going to change.”

Lawmakers are expected to get one of their first opportunities to publicly press administration officials on the resumption of fighting on Tuesday, when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, are scheduled to appear before the Senate Appropriations Committee to defend the Pentagon’s request for additional military funding this year.

A handful of Republicans have criticized the administration’s lack of transparency and called for additional information, including those who previously joined Democrats in supporting the war powers measure that called on Mr. Trump to end hostilities or seek authorization from Congress.

“If they’re restarting, we should have another briefing,” Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, told reporters. He was one of four G. O. P. senators who broke with their party and supported the measure last month.

Senator Lisa Murkowski, Republican of Alaska, who also backed the measure to limit Mr. Trump’s war powers, likewise said the administration needed to be more forthcoming with Congress.

But the complaints from Republicans have not renewed efforts to restrict the president’s military authority.

Senator John Curtis of Utah, one of the few Republicans who said earlier in the conflict that he would not support military action extending beyond 60 days without congressional authorization, has repeatedly warned his colleagues against repeating mistakes of the past.

“Congress just kept funding the Vietnam War even though there was never a declaration of war,” he said in an interview with the Utah news outlet KSL last week, invoking the conflict that ultimately led Congress to enact the War Powers Resolution. “This is not an anti-president move. This is a ‘Congress, do your job’ move,” he added. “We can’t just sit back and put this on the president’s shoulder. We need to get involved.”

But Mr. Curtis has consistently joined Republicans in voting against war powers resolutions. And Mr. Trump has shown no indication that he plans to work with members of Congress.

He ignored both chambers’ votes directing him to seek authorization for the conflict and last week formally informed Congress that fighting had resumed and that he was again acting under his commander in chief authority with no need to consult with lawmakers. In his notification, the president described the renewed campaign as a “limited, measured” response to new Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz but also said American forces remained prepared to take “further action, as necessary and appropriate,” if Iran continued threatening the United States and its allies.

Sunday evening marked the ninth consecutive night that the United States and Iran traded another wave of strikes. U. S. Central Command said in a statement that American forces “were holding Iran accountable at the commander in chief’s direction.”

At least three U. S. soldiers were killed over the weekend, two in Jordan when an Iranian ballistic missile struck a military base and another during the disposal of an Iranian drone in northern Iraq.

The number of American military personnel killed since the war began at the end of February is now up to 17.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. Trump vowed to avenge the deaths of the soldiers, saying in a social media post that “every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!”

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.
