Aiming for My Fastest Marathon, I Turned to Distance Running’s Mecca

The New York Times July 20, 2026

A New York Times reporter’s quest to beat the personal best he set 14 years ago took him to a Kenyan village, where the biggest benefit he got was not what he expected.

A New York Times reporter’s quest to beat the personal best he set 14 years ago took him to a Kenyan village, where the biggest benefit he got was not what he expected.

The author, in the middle in red, training in Iten, Kenya. Credit... Brian Otieno for The New York Times

Supported by

By John Eligon

Photographs by Brian Otieno

John Eligon spent a week training in Iten, Kenya, which has produced some of the world’s best distance runners, ahead of his 16th marathon, the Cape Town Marathon.

From the moment the race started, my hamstrings began to ache — a dull throbbing that I knew could derail my run.

Just hours earlier, I had woken to an overcast May morning feeling excited to run the Cape Town Marathon. My lungs were strong, and my legs felt lighter than they had before any of my 15 previous marathons. My goal seemed possible: to run the race in 2 hours 50 minutes, more than seven minutes faster than the personal best I had achieved 14 years earlier, at 29.

My attempts to better that time over the years were mostly derailed by leg cramps. No gel, electrolyte drink, potato or salt packet could prevent those crippling moments in races, when it felt like someone was playing tug of war with my hamstrings.

As I reached my 40s, though, I began doing the little things that my younger, more athletic self ignored. I strength trained, foam rolled and stretched more frequently. I gave my muscles more time to recover. I slept more. I ran faster than I expected.

But I had cramped throughout the final 13 miles of the last marathon I raced, in November. I didn’t know how else I could improve at that point. A friend suggested training in Iten, a Kenyan village in the Great Rift Valley, which has produced some of the best marathoners in the world. I spent a week running there in April.

Now as the niggling in my hamstrings so early in the race began to worry me, I thought back on that training. If I wanted to hit my target, I would need to channel the skill I had not known was so crucial to those runners’ success: their mind-set.

On my first morning in Iten, I stood along the main road as packs of runners bounded past along the red dirt paths, like flocks of birds gliding in formation, their strides smooth, their posture straight. They moved with an envious efficiency. Almost every runner looked exceptionally fit.

This is a village where few people run recreationally. Most are hoping to win prize money in major competitions or, like the team I trained with, are trying to win scholarships to run college track in the United States.

“It’s running for their lives,” Richard Mukche, the team’s coach, told me of the ethos in Iten. Nearly 60 percent of the roughly half a million residents of Elgeyo Marakwet, the county that includes Iten, live in poverty.

About 30 years ago, Iten was a speck of a village with just a handful of rural homesteads and a handful of runners. After some of those early runners won international competitions, word spread about the benefits of training in Iten — the high altitude and the serenity — and it grew into a running mecca. It now serves as a base for Olympians and world champions from other countries, who spend weeks or months cloistered in camps that cater to their every training need. Amateur runners like me are a regular presence, helping to sustain the local economy — I paid about $700 for a week of training at a camp complete with meals and massages — as they try to improve their abilities by training with Kenyan runners.

Coach Richard is himself a Kenyan former elite athlete who trained in Iten and ran a 2:16 marathon in his day, which would still clock him in the top 20 finishers of last year’s New York City Marathon. He has been coaching for the past 16 years, mostly 20-somethings shooting for scholarships, but also world-class runners from abroad. Some of his athletes have competed in the Olympics and in major marathons. About six, including his daughter, have earned scholarships.

My first morning, when I joined the roughly 20 Kenyan runners currently under his wing, I was eager to run hard. Could I keep up with them?

But as I would come to learn, much of the training philosophy in Iten is about restraint, rather than excess. Coach Richard drilled in me an almost biblical commandment of Kenyan training: Listen to your body.

My first workout, he said, would be 5 miles at a relaxed pace — “Pole! Pole!” as they call easy runs in Swahili. He wanted my body to adjust to the altitude, which, at a mile and a half above sea level, is a half mile higher than where I live in Johannesburg.

So, I set off at a 8:30-per-mile pace, running past the not-so-subtle reminders of why Iten is a running destination. Past the arch over the main road that says welcome to the “Home Of Champions.” Past the “Champions Barber Shop” and “Champions Wines & Spirits.” By the end, I couldn’t help but feel optimistic — I hadn’t been bothered by the high altitude, which makes it harder to breathe but over time produces red blood cells that make breathing easier at lower elevations.

That evening, when I joined Coach Richard, his team and dozens of others at the Iten Sports Club to watch the Boston Marathon — local hero John Korir blazed his way to victory in course record time — I met Amanal Petros, Germany’s record-holder in the marathon, who was training in Iten for the London Marathon.

Petros has trained at other popular distance running hubs like Flagstaff, Ariz.; Boulder, Colo.; and St. Moritz, Switzerland. In those cities, he said, it takes months to find training partners on his level, while in Iten, he can find a dozen by just going to the main road in the morning.

“There’s nothing here. It’s just animals or runners,” he said. “You focus only on training, on your goal.”

For years after running in high school, I lost my motivation. The constant pursuit of faster times had made running feel like a chore. But then encouraged by a friend, I ran a marathon and then another. I broke three hours for the first and only time at the Chicago Marathon in 2012, clocking 2:57:32.

When I moved to Johannesburg five years ago, I was 38 and had pretty much resigned myself to the fact that my fastest days were behind me. But something changed. Living for the first time at a high altitude — nearly 5,600 feet — in a city with relentless hills, I became more fit than I had ever expected to be at my age.

In 2023, exactly six months before my 41st birthday, I won a half marathon in suburban St. Louis in my fastest time ever, bettering a mark I had set 11 years earlier. I felt like I was keeping mortality at bay. I wanted to see what my body could do.

And so, as day 2 of training in Iten began, I was excited to be able to push myself with the group. Coach Richard had us run 400-meter (one lap) repeats on the track. I felt great from the start, coming in a little over 80 seconds on each. I even talked Coach Richard into letting me do 15 laps, like some of the other runners, rather than the 10 he had assigned me. And when I was done, I wasn’t entirely drained.

“Who still has more energy?” Coach Richard asked us afterward. “In training, it’s better when you finish, you can still do something after. You don’t have to die completely.”

Paying attention to how I felt was the focus of much of my training in Iten. That simple question — how do you feel? — guides most runners in the area. It’s an approach that stands in stark contrast to the emphasis on technology and markers like VO₂ max and average heart rate promoted by most coaches and online influencers these days.

“Eat, sleep, run,” is how Coach Richard described the routine in Iten.

The simplicity is in some ways born out of circumstance. Most athletes here can’t afford the watches, carbon-plated super shoes or electrolyte gels that many privileged runners rely on. Some of the young people I trained with — people who were running at elite speeds — had holes in their shoes and drank water mixed with cheap glucose packets.

When athletes reach world-class levels in the United States and Europe, it’s common for them to follow individualized training plans. They often run alone or with just a few partners.

But there’s a pack mentality in Iten — runners generally run in big groups. In a crowd, a strenuous pace can feel comfortable; you’re syncing your strides with those around you and focusing on staying on the heels of the person ahead of you.

“Enjoy the rhythm, forget the pain,” is how Emmanuel Kipruto, an elite runner and coach in Iten, described group running.

The runners explained to me that the group also encourages discipline. You cannot sleep in when you know you need to meet your teammates in the morning to run. And there is competition within the group. When you see your teammates have success, it pushes you to try to keep up with them.

The ultimate group session in Iten takes place every Thursday when there is a fartlek workout, open to anyone who wants to participate. In fartlek trainings, runners alternate between fast, intense intervals and slow, relaxed ones as a way to build endurance and practice changing speeds.

The workout can attract hundreds of runners, from elites to amateurs. Dozens showed up the day I was there, and the regimen for the day was daunting: 13 repetitions of running one minute easy followed by three minutes hard.

By the end of the first 3-minute interval, I had slipped to the back of the pack. By the second, they had left me in their dust, literally — even the runner I saw hunched over vomiting during the first interval. I called it quits after 10 intervals. The pack was far out of sight, and each breath I took felt like someone was smothering me with a pillow.

It was humbling. The altitude I snickered at on previous days was now exacting its revenge. I felt like an amateur among pros, like a rec league baller trying to dunk on LeBron James.

Coach Richard said he saw progress, though. My body seemed strong, he told me, and that was important so that I could train the next day. I controlled my pace well, which is critical for racing, he said.

“I told you, listen to your body,” he said.

I had come to Iten hoping to find the secret to running success. What I was learning was that the secret was trusting how my body felt — understanding my own boundaries. It was OK to slow down if my body demanded it. But it was also fine to let loose.

Two days after the fartlek session, I prepared for my final run in Iten, nearly 16 miles along Moiben Road, a paved, relatively flat stretch where local runners do most of their long runs. Coach Richard told me to start my run at 75 percent effort, and pick it up if I felt good.

I was a bit uncertain as I set off alongside Vincent Cheruiyot, the team captain assigned to pace me. We settled into a nice rhythm faster than 7:15 per mile, a brisk but far from brutal pace. The running felt comfortable as I focused on the beautiful mountain vistas and watching the elite athletes blow past me, including the 10 kilometer world-record holder, Agnes Jebet Ngetich.

With about three miles to go, my body told me I could handle more. Our pace dipped below 7 minutes per mile. By the time we were on our last mile, the sweat was dripping, my hamstrings were taut, but I knew I could push the pace, matching Vincent next to me stride-for-stride. When we were done, my body felt bent but not broken, my lungs refreshed. Vincent and Coach Richard flashed wide smiles. I felt the progress.

As I prepared to leave Iten, I knew the workouts I had learned were sustainable. I hadn’t trained long enough to experience the full physical benefits, but running is as much a mental challenge as a physical one. I could sense that I had achieved a mental recalibration that I had not been expecting.

“Listen to your body.” That had been Coach Richard’s instruction, and hamstring troubles early in the Cape Town Marathon meant that my body needed me to be conservative. So I relaxed my pace, hoping that I would warm up and the discomfort would go away. By mile six, I felt better.

I was a little behind my goal pace, so I decided to open up my stride. Eleven of my next 13 mile splits came in under my target of 6:29 per mile. I was blowing past other runners and my lungs were at ease.

Then on mile 20, we hit a long, steady, sneaky hill. My pace slowed. I kept my focus straight ahead, and thought about the efficiency of the strides of the Kenyans I ran with in Iten. I tried to mimic that. I pushed, but my body didn’t have more to give. My watch said that 2:50 wasn’t going to happen. But I still could beat my personal best, I thought.

I grit my teeth through those final miles. The sun beat down. I started losing my breath. But I thought back to Iten, when the thin air had me gasping and the steep dirt paths had my legs straining, and I felt more than prepared for this moment. I thought about Emmanuel’s advice to “enjoy the rhythm, forget the pain.”

I saw the finish line and found one last surge.

I crossed in 2:53:50, smashing my previous record by nearly four minutes.

One thing that surprised me about Iten was how comfortable I felt among those elite runners even though I was not nearly as fast as them. The local elites there relish the chance to run with and get to know amateurs who visit from around the world. They don't care how fast you are. Really!

Part of the reason is that they can sometimes turn to visitors they've developed relationships with for material support. Many Kenyans training there come from very modest means and can't often afford expensive running watches or shoes. One young woman I met had gotten a scholarship offer in the U. S. but could not afford the roughly $200 she needed to get an appointment at the US consulate for a visa.

It's become part of the exchange in the Iten experience. They help to pace you and give you tips to make yourself a better runner. And in return, some runners will pay them tips, and sometimes down the line help with bigger asks they may have.

Edwin Okoth contributed reporting from Nairobi, Kenya.

John Eligon is the Johannesburg bureau chief for The Times, covering a wide range of events and trends that influence and shape the lives of ordinary people across southern Africa.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The market for the epic poem is as crowded as a certain Ithacan palace, and publishers have had to get crafty to attract readers to their editions.

Credit... Tony Cenicola/The New York Times

Supported by

By MJ Franklin

MJ Franklin is an editor at the Book Review.

It’s the climax of the “Odyssey.” Odysseus, back in Ithaca at long last, finds his home swarming with suitors vying for the hand of his wife, Penelope, and for his throne. He needs to overthrow the interlopers and reclaim his rightful place. The question is: How?

In their own way, book publishers are fighting a similar battle.

Public interest in the “Odyssey” surged in the lead-up to the release of the director Christopher Nolan’s star-studded adaptation of Homer’s epic last week. So far this year, sales of the “Odyssey” rose by 76 percent compared with last year, according to Circana BookScan, a book industry sales tracker.

Save to your reading list:

For the publishers putting out any of the dozens of translations of the “Odyssey” currently available, that presents both a challenge and an opportunity. Here’s how a few of them are meeting the moment.

The most direct way publishers are elevating their translations of the “Odyssey” is by giving them splashy reissues.

Picador is one such publisher. In May, the imprint, which in the United States is a branch of Farrar, Straus & Giroux, released a new edition of Robert Fitzgerald’s 1961 translation of the “Odyssey.” Nolan’s film directly influenced its rerelease strategy.

“We originally planned to publish our deluxe reissue of the ‘Odyssey’ in fall 2025, but moved it to spring 2026 so we could take advantage of the excitement surrounding Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation,” Sheila O’Shea, the director of publicity and marketing at Farrar, Straus & Giroux and Picador, said in an email. In addition to calibrating the timing, Picador gave the reissue a glitzy new look, with a vibrant green cover, foil stamping, French flaps and deckled edges.

Picador is not alone in applying a fresh coat of paint to the epic. In June, Penguin Classics reissued Robert Fagles’s 1996 translation in a hardcover wrapped in a colorful jacket featuring figures from the poem.

The release date for Nolan’s movie was serendipitous for Penguin Classics, where plans were already underway to mark both the 30th anniversary of Fagles’s translation and the 80th anniversary of the imprint itself, which launched in 1946 with E. V. Rieu’s translation of the “Odyssey.”

“It was beautiful timing, actually,” Elda Rotor, publisher of Penguin Classics, said in a statement. “As filmgoers anticipated his cinematic interpretation of Homer’s epic, at the same time we were preparing to celebrate the Fagles translation.”

Instead of reissues, some imprints are harnessing another tool: celebrity.

Although many of the most popular translations of the “Odyssey” are decades old, two recent translations have gained cultural prominence. In 2017, W. W. Norton & Co. published a translation by the University of Pennsylvania professor Emily Wilson. And last year, the University of Chicago Press released a version translated by the Bard College professor Daniel Mendelsohn.

Classicists are stereotyped as monkish, spending their time cloistered in the ivory tower of academia, but both Wilson and Mendelsohn are surprisingly buzzy media figures. Mendelsohn’s cultural criticism is as acclaimed as his scholarship, and he has written for publications including The New York Times, The New Yorker and The New York Review of Books.

Wilson, who is the first woman to translate the “Odyssey” into English, became a lightning rod for two reasons. First, her provocatively blunt translation ignited a fierce debate about the best way to translate Homer. Second, her work got swept up in the culture wars, as she put it in a recent interview with New York magazine.

“After I published the ‘Odyssey’ translation, it was both celebrated in quite simplistic ways as a work of girl power,” Wilson told New York last month. “It also faced backlash.”

The fact that both translators have garnered a reliable amount of name recognition has, in this moment of “Odyssey” fever, been a boon.

“It may come as no surprise that we are, indeed, promoting Emily Wilson’s translation, but what is more surprising is how much interest is bubbling up spontaneously,” Norton’s chief communications officer, Louise Brockett, said in an email. “There have been Emily Wilson read-alongs; there have been ‘Odyssey’ book clubs.”

Like Wilson, Mendelsohn “has already been a go-to voice for reporters covering the movie who want to know more about the poem and about Homer’s world,” Levi Stahl, the marketing director for the University of Chicago Press, said in an email.

In the lead-up to the movie’s release, Mendelsohn published pieces about the “Odyssey” in The Times and The Free Press, and on Friday, he reviewed the movie for The New York Review of Books. To further connect Mendelsohn’s name with the phenomenon, Stahl added, “we’ve been drawing the connection with our social media and direct-to-consumer outreach since the first trailer.”

Homer’s verse is considered particularly tricky to translate, and there’s no definitive method for bringing his poems into modern English.

“It is very difficult to capture the tone of the poems, which is elevated (clearly very different from everyday speech), yet can be colloquial and emotional at times and is always vivid and immediate,” Egbert Bakker, a professor of Greek language and literature at Yale, said in an email. “The ‘Odyssey’ is one of these works of verbal art that transcends translation.”

Each translator takes a different tack. Picador highlights the lyrical flair of Fitzgerald’s translation, which “continues to stand apart because it combines deep scholarship with the instincts of a practicing poet,” O’Shea said.

Norton stresses the briskness of Wilson’s version. “It feels like the ancient Greek: direct, accessible and compelling,” Brockett said. “Wilson’s is one of the first metrical translations in recent memory, offering the English-language reader or listener the same sense of motion and adventure, in iambic pentameter, that the original listener to this epic poem would have perceived in their era, in their meter.”

At the University of Chicago Press, the team is emphasizing Mendelsohn’s fidelity. “Our translation is the most poetic, accurate and faithful to the original, as Daniel Mendelsohn deliberately replicated Homer’s long lines and attended carefully to the poem’s metaphors, tone, level of diction and word choice,” Stahl said.

And Penguin Classics is leaning on its legacy as a classroom staple. “Fagles’s translation remains one of the most widely taught editions of the ‘Odyssey’ in U. S. higher education, continuing to be assigned by hundreds of instructors and reaching thousands of students each year,” Rotor said.

Moviegoers who are just now giving Homer a go might feel overwhelmed by the glut of translations of the “Odyssey” to choose from. But keep in mind, as David Elmer, a professor of Greek literature at Harvard, puts it: “No translation is perfect, and everyone has their own taste.”

5 Things to Know About the Maine Senate Candidate Troy Jackson

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Jackson, who has emerged as the clear front-runner to replace Graham Platner, is a Republican turned Democrat who is seen as close to Mr. Platner on policy.

By Tim Balk and Beth Reinhard

Troy Jackson, a logger from northern Maine who morphed from Republican to progressive Democrat across a long political career, has emerged as the clear front-runner to replace Graham Platner as the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Jackson, 58, of Allagash.

1. He ran for governor this year. Mr. Jackson, a longtime state lawmaker who once was president of the Maine Senate, sought a return to state government this year, running for governor on a progressive platform that called for expanded health care and child care options for Mainers. Late in the campaign, he received an endorsement from Mr. Platner, then the front-runner in the Democratic primary race for Senate. Mr. Jackson ultimately finished third in the ranked-choice primary for governor.

2. He is supported by progressive groups and politicians. Even before Mr. Jackson formally started his Senate bid, he was backed by progressives, including Representative Ro Khanna, Democrat of California, who had supported Mr. Platner. Mr. Khanna endorsed Mr. Jackson hours before Mr. Platner suspended his campaign. Our Revolution, the liberal group founded by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, backed Mr. Jackson’s bid soon after he set up an exploratory committee. On Sunday, Our Revolution issued a statement saying that Mainers had “voted for a movement to continue” by supporting many pro-Jackson delegates chosen for the nominating convention, which is set for this Saturday.

3. He is seen as close to Mr. Platner on policy. Mr. Jackson and Mr. Platner campaigned together repeatedly before Mr. Platner’s campaign was rocked this month by a rape allegation. (Mr. Platner has denied the allegation but decided to drop out of the Senate race as former allies, including Mr. Jackson, called on him to withdraw.) Many Maine Democrats have been drawn to Mr. Jackson as someone who might carry forward Mr. Platner’s progressive, populist message. Mr. Jackson’s platform calls for universal health care and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It also accuses Israel of carrying out a genocide in the Gaza Strip.

4. His positions have changed over time. As a state lawmaker for much of the past two decades, Mr. Jackson changed positions on prominent social issues. He became a Democrat in 2004 after serving in the State House for two years an independent. (Mr. Jackson ran unsuccessfully for office in 2000 as a Republican but had become an independent by 2002.) Now he is a strong supporter of abortion rights and gay rights. But his voting record once received perfect scores from the anti-abortion group Maine Right to Life, according to the nonpartisan Project Vote Smart. And in 2009, he voted against a bill legalizing same-sex marriage in Maine. By 2023, he had helped pass a bill that allowed women to get abortions late into their pregnancies. And in 2024, his voting record earned a 100 percent rating from Equality Maine, a gay rights advocacy group. “It’s become very clear to me that abortion is health care,” he said in a recent interview. He added that he regretted his previous position on gay marriage. “Now people in L. G. B. T. Q. circles know that I am one of their strongest advocates.”

5. He’s a fifth-generation logger from Maine’s northern reaches. Mr. Jackson was born in Fort Kent, Maine, which sits on the border of Canada. He has long lived in nearby Allagash, a wooded town of 237 people. The town is so far north that Allagash Brewing Company, in Portland, Maine, is closer to Boston than it is to Allagash, Maine. His campaign says that as a logger, he has put in 80-hour weeks in the forest. And his ads show him using a chain saw to chop tall trees. In 1999 he led a group that blockaded roads to protest low wages for loggers. “The only promise I have made,” he told The Bangor Daily News when he ran for office as a Republican in 2000, “is that I will work hard if I am elected.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research, and Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

Beth Reinhard is an investigative reporter for The Times covering politics.

‘Vibecoded’ Apps Are Flooding the App Store. Is That Good for Apple?

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Mobile apps are easy to make with artificial intelligence. That doesn’t mean people are excited to use them.

Mobile apps are easy to make with artificial intelligence. That doesn’t mean people are excited to use them.

Artificial intelligence is feeding a boom in the number of apps available in Apple’s App Store. Credit... Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times

Supported by

By Kalley Huang

Reporting from San Francisco

Marco Pérez had long wanted to read all of the news he was curious about in one place. This year, he used artificial intelligence tools to get the job done fast.

Mr. Pérez, a software engineer in Chicago who had never made a mobile app before, spent five weeks over the winter tinkering with “vibecoding” A. I. tools to create a prototype, and two more preparing the app for Apple’s App Store. The app, InfoDrizzle, has been modestly successful, netting 1,300 downloads and about $500 in profit.

Mr. Pérez’s next app was more popular. In May, after about a week of work, he released Stampa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital postage stamps. Stampa has been downloaded 20,000 times and made about $3,000 in profit.

The two apps were part of a surge of additions to Apple’s App Store over the past year and a half, after years of slower growth — thanks in large part to vibecoding.

Vibecoding emerged as a phenomenon last year as A. I. improved at creating software code. Without knowing anything about programming or writing a line of code, people can describe an idea to an A. I. tool, which can build a custom website or app for them.

“I feel like the mobile app space was really hot 10 years ago and kind of got boring,” Mr. Pérez, 27, said. “Now, it’s the hottest thing again because of A. I. and vibecoding and how that technical barrier is not there anymore.”

But as with many things A. I., just because something is easy to build doesn’t mean people will use it. It is not clear if vibecoding is breathing new life into the App Store or just cluttering it.

Last year, the number of new apps released in the App Store grew 30 percent to about 600,000, according to estimates by Sensor Tower, an app analytics firm. In the first half of this year, new apps doubled to about 560,000.

This boom could be a boon for Apple. The company takes a 30 percent cut of in-app purchases like subscriptions, or 15 percent from smaller developers. Theoretically, the more apps in the App Store, the more revenue for Apple.

But Apple can’t take its cut if consumers don’t download and buy things from apps — and downloads from the App Store haven’t taken off. Last year, they grew 3 percent to 35.4 billion, according to Sensor Tower. In the first half of this year, downloads grew 2 percent to 17.6 billion.

Even if they aren’t being downloaded and used, all of the new apps demand resources and labor from Apple. The company manually reviews apps before they are released or updated in the App Store.

In recent months, app makers have complained in Apple’s developer forums of longer review times. In March, for example, the developer of an app said it had been “waiting for review” for about a month with no communication from Apple.

Peter Ajemian, a spokesman for Apple, said that the app had required additional technical review and received approval shortly after it was resubmitted, and that Apple had been engaged with its developer. He said Apple consistently reviewed 90 percent of app submissions within 48 hours.

Mr. Ajemian added that downloads were only one measure of the App Store’s value.

“We’re thrilled to see a new generation of developers embracing the latest tools to build and ship apps faster than ever,” he said in a statement. “All apps are held to the same high standards for quality, privacy and security that users have come to trust.”

When Apple introduced the App Store in 2008, developers flooded it with new apps. Flappy Bird, the 2013 game in which players tried to fly a bird between pipes without hitting them, earned $50,000 per day at the peak of its popularity. The number of new apps released in the App Store peaked in 2016, at about 890,000, according to Sensor Tower.

As the App Store matured, consumers consolidated around a handful of apps. Last year, Apple collected $34.21 billion of the $114.02 billion in revenue from in-app purchases, according to estimates by Appfigures, an app analytics firm.

Growth in the App Store stagnated after 2017. New releases hit a low in 2022, about 420,000, according to Sensor Tower. But since vibecoding became possible, that has changed. Much as they did in the early days of mobile apps, developers are joining the gold rush.

Mr. Pérez is one of those developers. He is planning on quitting his job at JPMorgan Chase next month to develop apps full time.

“I’m talking to these people all the time who are way, way, way ahead of me,” Mr. Pérez said. “It’s crazy how much money they’re making and the opportunities that are there and how fast you can move. Some of these people have failed, have made five apps, and their sixth app blows up.”

This flood is a mixed bag for Apple. The App Store is “not like a typical storefront, where you have shelf space,” said Phillip Shoemaker, who led the App Store from 2009 to 2016. That means that having a lot of new, vibecoded apps — “stuff that somebody might use once” — isn’t necessarily a problem for Apple, he added.

Instead, Mr. Shoemaker said, the risks for the App Store are having “more junk,” or making it easier for “a bad actor” to slip in something problematic, like inappropriate content.

Apple could also see less upside than expected from the surge. Vibecoded apps might not offer in-app purchases, which tend to be more complicated to set up, and contain ads instead, said Eric Seufert, a mobile advertising analyst who runs Mobile Dev Memo, a blog about the app economy.

“Apple doesn’t benefit from that,” Mr. Seufert said.

But not all app developers are hoping to make money for themselves — much less Apple. David Svensson, who works on revenue operations at a construction technology company, started vibecoding in earnest with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude in February, when his workplace started pushing its employees to use A. I.

Mr. Svensson, 44, now pays for a subscription to the tools and makes “small little apps that solve a specific thing,” like tracking fire risk and bans in Sweden, where he lives.

Over the past five months, Mr. Svensson has released 11 apps in the App Store, where they have been downloaded nearly 2,400 times in total. His most popular app, Utkik, tracks aircraft and watercraft. The app has what Mr. Svensson called “a tip jar,” but he said he otherwise didn’t think about making money from vibecoding, or vibecoding for other people.

“I want to keep it as a passion,” Mr. Svensson said. “If something blows up, sure, that would be super, super nice. But that is not the thought behind this.”

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

China consumes more eggs per capita than almost every other country, so a recent spike in costs is touching a nerve.

A food stall vendor in Shanghai prepares jianbing, a popular savory pancake. Credit... Video by Qilai Shen

Supported by

By Alexandra Stevenson and Murphy Zhao

Reporting from Hong Kong

In China, the humble egg, a longtime supporting act in many dishes, is now center stage.

Around dining room tables, budget-conscious families are griping about its sudden spike in price. In the countryside, befuddled farmers who complained of a glut of eggs last year now fret about scarcity. At food stalls, frustrated cooks are reeling from the one-two punch of egg prices and rising energy costs from the Iran war.

Even state media has taken to using the term “rocket eggs” to describe skyrocketing prices.

Egg prices are up by more than 40 percent from a year ago, according to an index that tracks the top producing provinces. They recently hit a 10-year high by another benchmark that tracks prices at a wholesale market in Guantao, in northern China, catching industry insiders by surprise.

In a country that consumes more eggs per capita than almost any other in the world, the surging price is especially painful. And it has become a paradox in an economy still struggling to shake off widespread deflation, in which industrial overcapacity and reluctant consumers have led to falling prices for several years. (The price of pork, for example, recently hit a 16-year low.)

The war in Iran has pushed up energy prices and stoked nascent inflation, but this has been accompanied by a slowdown in economic growth, an unwelcome combination.

The price of eggs is the kind of issue that can hit a nerve, and not only in China. The United States had its own egg crisis not long ago, because of supply chain snarls and an avian influenza outbreak. Eggs became a talking point during the 2024 presidential election campaign, with Donald J. Trump using the rising cost of groceries to berate his opponents.

In China, the problem began with overenthusiastic poultry farmers.

Two years ago, farmers started expanding after several bumper years, adding more egg-laying hens from 2024 to 2025 than ever before, according to Aspen Li, an analyst who studies the egg market. Suddenly, there were too many eggs and the price plunged. Farmers then found themselves short of money to feed all their chickens.

So they culled them, at a rate that experts considered excessive. Eventually, there were not enough egg-laying hens to meet demand, sending prices to levels that Mr. Li said were “even higher than my expectations.”

At the same time, demand has been particularly strong, which economists attribute to various factors like hungry teenagers studying for a high-stakes national exam and the summer celebration known as Dragon Boat Festival.

And some pin the blame for climbing costs on one person: President Trump. The war in Iran has made cooking gas pricier. Owners at one restaurant in the coastal town of Tianjin stuck a sign in their storefront window to explain that they were raising the price of jianbing, a crepe of eggs, greens and deep fried crackers, by the equivalent of seven cents because of “Trump driving up prices.”

Axuan Bu, 25, who runs two stalls called “Jianbing Man” in the eastern city of Jinhua, says he can’t pass the cost of his savory egg pancakes on to his regular clients. “If you raise the price, people just won’t buy them anymore,” he said.

Mr. Bu goes through 360 eggs every two to three days and he’s seen the price tick upward by a few cents each time he restocks. A carton, which once cost $25, is now $35. To make things worse, the gas canisters he needs to heat his pan have also risen, to $22 each from $16, a purchase he has to make every five days.

“You bustle around month after month and by the end of it, there’s simply nothing left,” he said.

Unlike meat, eggs aren’t easily substituted, said Hellen Zhang in the eastern province of Jiangsu, who together with her boyfriend consumes as many as seven eggs a day — boiled for breakfast, scrambled in dishes with tomatoes for lunch and as batter for rice cakes.

It accounts for a tenth of their monthly food bill, Ms. Zhang said. “But no matter how expensive eggs get, you still have to eat,” she said. “Prices go up, but you can’t skip your protein.”

Harriet Hua, from the southern province of Guangdong, noticed that the price of eggs started creeping up in April on the grocery-buying platform she uses, known as Pinduoduo. They have since risen by 20 percent.

“My first reaction was, ‘Oh my god, why is it so expensive?’ So I stopped buying them, thinking I’d wait for the price to drop,” said Ms. Hua, who normally buys a batch of 30 eggs each month. While she was jobless for six months, even the smallest price increase was painful.

“The price never did drop,” said Ms. Hua, who landed a new job last month. “Eventually I just had to buy them anyway.”

Alexandra Stevenson is the Shanghai bureau chief for The Times, reporting on China’s economy and society.

Here’s What Greeks Think of Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey.’ (It’s Their Story, After All.)

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Before its release, some in the country were highly skeptical about the new depiction of a beloved tale. But many who saw it over opening weekend came back with positive reviews.

By Niki Kitsantonis

Reporting from Athens

Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” drew criticism in Greece in the weeks leading up to the film’s release, particularly over the casting of the Black actor Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy, amid a broader debate about how one of the world’s most enduring myths should be retold.

But after movie-goers saw the film over its opening weekend in Greece, where Homer’s epic remains deeply embedded in cultural identity, the response appeared to be largely enthusiastic.

As crowds left cinemas in Athens after three hours of the IMAX-filmed epic on Friday night, many said they were excited that a work written nearly three millenniums ago had inspired a major global production, bringing to the screen scenes they first encountered in the classroom.

“I was captivated,” said Costas Anastassiadis, 55. “It took me back 45 years, when we were reading the story at school.”

Despite the film’s scale and technological ambition, he said the effects had served rather than overshadowed the story. “This hero doesn’t need graphics or C. G. I.,” he said. “The text transcends everything.”

On Nolan’s decision to cast Nyong’o as Helen of Troy, Anastassiadis said he felt it “strengthened the universality” of Homer’s work. Others dismissed the debate — in which lawmakers traded shots over several months — as overblown, noting that the actress was only onscreen for a few minutes.

Critics in Greece were mixed in their reviews of the film, which took in about $264.1 million worldwide over its opening weekend. The leading Kathimerini daily said that Nolan had met a Homeric challenge, “fusing an epic that has echoed across the centuries with postmodern artistic sensibilities.” Athinorama, a leading Greek culture and entertainment publication, praised the film’s visual ambition but argued that it shied away from the philosophical and narrative complexity of Homer’s original.

Evgenia Makrygianni, an associate professor of Ancient Greek literature at the University of Athens, said “The Odyssey” remained closely linked to modern Greek identity through the Homeric idea of “nostos” — the longing for home and return that drives Odysseus’s journey.

“It connects with Greece’s own historical experiences — war, exile, economic hardship and migration,” she said. “Odysseus symbolizes resilience, determination and the strength to persevere through adversity.”

Classical works remain alive because each generation finds new meanings in them, Makrygianni added, with contemporary creators reinterpreting Odysseus as a traveler, an immigrant, someone seeking to belong. “Homer himself does not change — his readers do,” she said.

At the Athens screening, viewers seemed to largely accept the absence of Greek actors, accustomed to foreign performers assuming Greek roles in major productions like “300” and “Troy.” For some, the stronger connection came through the landscapes: The sea, light and rugged terrain of Greece, where Nolan filmed parts of the movie, made Homer’s world feel instantly recognizable.

Some were impressed by Nolan’s portrayal of Odysseus not simply as a cunning hero, but as a man transformed by war and forced to confront its consequences.

Vangelis Dravopoulos, 17, said the film gave him a new perspective on the poem he had studied three years earlier. “It was amazing to see all the scenes — the Cyclops, the giants,” he said. “At school, the focus was on the hubris of Odysseus and his perseverance. In the film, he realized what he’d done wrong.”

His friend Stylianos Koginis, also 17, welcomed Nolan putting his own stamp on the story. “That’s what cinema should be,” he said, adding, “The spirit of Odysseus was there.” He said he was particularly struck that Athena, who accompanies Odysseus on his journey, was played by Zendaya, who also played a young woman executed during the battle of Troy. “It wasn’t the goddess accompanying him, it was his regrets,” Koginis said.

Not all viewers believed that Nolan’s production captured the complexity of Homer’s poem.

Christina Georgiou, 36, said the film was visually striking but lacked depth. “It was very Hollywood, with drawn-out battle scenes and over-the-top costumes,” she said. “Basically, it glossed over the richness and turned an epic into a morality tale.”

Beyond questions of artistic interpretation, the film also attracted political criticism before its release, particularly from the far right. Reports that Greece had supported the production with subsidies of more than 6 million euros, about $6.9 million, prompted objections from the nationalist Niki party, which argued that public funds had been used to support a “woke” reinterpretation of Greek heritage.

Culture Minister Lina Mendoni rejected the criticism, telling Lifo magazine that “it is not the state’s role to dictate to a creator how they should artistically interpret a work or a myth.”

Makrygianni, the classics professor, said the controversy surrounding the film was proof of Homer’s enduring relevance. “When a work continues to provoke discussion about who has the right to tell its story and how its heroes should be portrayed,” she said, “it still carries profound symbolic power.”

For Vangelis, the student, the film was an emotional reminder of the continuing significance of one of Greece’s defining works. “I feel proud that all this happened in our country,” he said, “and that people are still talking about ‘The Odyssey’ thousands of years later.”

In Maine Senate Race, Democrats Go From Chaos to Coronation

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Troy Jackson’s emergence as the clear front-runner to replace Graham Platner spares the party some challenges but points to some new ones.

By Reid J. Epstein

A process to choose a new Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine that began as a messy free-for-all has turned into a coronation for Troy Jackson, a progressive in the mold of Graham Platner, who was forced from the race 12 days ago.

Over the weekend Mr. Jackson’s supporters swept the county meetings to select delegates to the state convention, according to the slate released by his campaign, seizing command of the two-week sprint to choose an opponent for Senator Susan Collins, the state’s five-term Republican incumbent.

The gatherings provided quick clarity to a state convention that could have been chaotic and spared Maine Democrats myriad risks inherent with standing up a nomination process in less than three weeks.

Mr. Jackson, a former state lawmaker, built such an imposing advantage on Saturday that he delivered what amounted to a victory speech on Sunday morning before the day’s delegates were selected.

“Those delegates were not handed to us,” he told supporters gathered at the York County party meeting in Sanford, Maine. “We earned them because hundreds of hundreds of people organized their neighbors, made the calls, had the conversations and showed up.”

Yet Mr. Jackson’s triumph also points to some new challenges Democrats might confront.

Mr. Jackson, who has never been known as a smooth orator, ran a lackluster campaign for governor, placing third last month. He is a progressive in the mold of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, on track to face the most moderate Republican in the Senate. He has little experience raising the huge sums required to run a battleground Senate campaign and has in the past disparaged some of Maine’s biggest Democratic donors.

And Maine Democrats, after watching their first Senate nominee’s campaign implode, are on the verge of hitching themselves to another man who has not faced a serious vetting in the national glare of a battleground Senate campaign.

The Maine Democratic Party has until July 27 to formally declare a replacement for Mr. Platner with the secretary of state.

At the state convention, set for this Saturday in Bangor, the new nominee will be decided. Delegates, who ran on their support for Mr. Jackson, are not required to vote for any specific candidate.

Still, Mr. Jackson’s organizational dominance over the weekend means that, barring yet another political calamity for Democrats in Maine or another unexpected twist, they are well on their way to nominating him as their Senate candidate.

Such was the scale of Mr. Jackson’s victories at the Saturday meetings that before any Sunday sessions began, his chief progressive rival, Shenna Bellows, the Maine secretary of state, ended her campaign. By dinnertime, the top moderate in the race, Dr. Nirav Shah, the state’s former public health director, also suspended his campaign and endorsed Mr. Jackson, as did Dan Kleban, a local beer magnate, and Jordan Wood, a former congressional aide.

“When Graham Platner stepped aside, Maine Democrats had eighteen days to do what usually takes a year,” said Bev Uhlenhake, a former Maine Democratic Party chairwoman. “They built a process from scratch with full transparency. No backroom deal. No delay. Just a party that showed up when it mattered focused on one imperative — beating Susan Collins.”

Democrats seeking Maine’s Senate nomination have until Monday night to submit signatures to qualify for the convention ballot. Dr. Shah’s campaign submitted his petitions last week, and he intends to remain on the ballot at the convention, an aide said Sunday, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe internal conversations.

Mr. Jackson, a former president of the Maine Senate, had significant structural advantages heading into the weekend meetings.

He was the only Senate candidate with significant endorsements from labor unions, which in Maine do not represent large numbers of voters but which brought a political organization others could not match on the abbreviated timeline for selecting a nominee to replace Mr. Platner.

And while Mr. Platner did not make an endorsement in the race, Mr. Jackson was most ideologically aligned with him. During his run for governor, Mr. Jackson won endorsements from Mr. Sanders and Maine’s chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Some Democrats hope Mr. Jackson’s quick rise heralds an end to a tumultuous chapter in Maine politics. Mr. Platner, an oyster farmer and political neophyte who was drafted into a Senate campaign that briefly turned him into a national progressive icon, survived news cycles about his offensive online posts, his tattoo that resembled a Nazi symbol and accusations that he had been physically threatening to a former girlfriend.

A rape allegation made by another former girlfriend to Politico and during a CNN interview on July 6 — which Mr. Platner has denied — caused his support to evaporate. There was just a week before the deadline for Mr. Platner to withdraw his name from the ballot.

Maine Democrats designed their replacement process to provide maximum democracy on an abridged schedule. In the end, it served as an exercise in old-school machine politics, with Mr. Jackson’s supporters from labor unions using a superior organization to elect delegates from his slates.

“Unions are very good at disciplined organizing, and this was highly, highly disciplined organizing,” said Matt Schlobohm, the executive director of the Maine AFL-CIO, a federation of more than 200 unions in the state. “We were pulling from a core set of 300 volunteers who had just gone and knocked on doors for Troy in the primary.”

Mr. Jackson’s top rivals cleared the field for him and declared it time for Democrats to coalesce around him.

“This has been an unprecedented nominating process, compressed into days instead of months, and I’m grateful to every volunteer who worked around the clock for this movement,” Ms. Bellows said. “That energy is exactly what we need to beat Susan Collins in November — and Democrats don’t have a day to waste in unifying around that shared goal.”

Dr. Shah pleaded with Democrats to unite behind Mr. Jackson.

“Susan Collins will not be defeated without a united Democratic Party,” he said. “We cannot unite without treating one another with respect. No matter whom you supported in this race, I urge us all to remember that in the weeks ahead.”

Never in modern political history had a state party tried to run a competitive nominating contest on such a short timeline.

When President Joseph R. Biden Jr. ended his 2024 re-election campaign, Democratic National Committee members anointed Vice President Kamala Harris to replace him without opposition. Senate candidates who have died or quit their campaigns after winning primaries have been replaced by state party committees.

Just this month, when Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died, President Trump urged the state’s Republican governor to appoint Mr. Graham’s sister to the seat (the governor agreed) and endorsed her in a special election to replace him on the November ballot.

Ms. Collins is the only incumbent Senate Republican running for re-election this year in a state that Mr. Trump lost in 2024. The speed at which Mr. Jackson consolidated support shocked his rivals and supporters of other candidates in the race.

Kristen O’Neill, a teacher from Portland who backed Mr. Platner and then volunteered for Ms. Bellows, said the condensed process left her without time to research any of the delegates and alternates on her ballot in Cumberland County.

“How was I supposed to vote for 173 people without putting hours and hours of work into it?” she said. “What happened was that these slates were created and we were told to support a candidate. The whole system just did not work.”

Bayliss Wagner contributed reporting from Topsham, Maine, Sydney Cromwell from Sanford, Maine, and Tim Balk from Dover, Mass.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Cinephiles Took Their Own Odysseys to Watch ‘The Odyssey’

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

To see Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of an epic journey in his preferred IMAX 70mm format, admirers packed their bags and took out their passports.

By Malia Mendez

Even before buying his movie tickets for the opening weekend of “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan’s long-awaited epic, Zach Weible reserved his hotel room.

He could have driven just over an hour to catch an IMAX screening in Orlando. But instead he took a car, bus and train nearly 300 miles from Ocala, Fla., to Fort Lauderdale to watch the film twice in IMAX 70-millimeter, which he called “cinema in its purest form.”

Weible did not encounter a furious Cyclops or narcotic lotus plant on his journey, but he did travel to great lengths to see the movie. And just to see it. Weible is deaf, and IMAX 70mm does not support modern closed captioning systems.

“It’s a trade-off I’m willing to accept,” Weible said in an interview over Google Chat. “The visual experience is too great to miss out on.”

Many cinephiles made their own odysseys to view Nolan’s take on the ancient story about the Greek king Odysseus’ yearslong journey back to his throne, a spectacle with the hype of being a modern “Ben-Hur” or “Lawrence of Arabia.” They traveled on busy thoroughfares and across international borders to reach the 41 theaters worldwide that can screen “The Odyssey” in the director’s preferred format.

“The Odyssey,” the first feature film to be shot entirely on IMAX cameras, can be viewed in nearly 1,900 large-screen IMAX theaters globally. It is the much rarer IMAX 70mm version, which uses film instead of digital projection, that Nolan fans said they just could not miss.

“We are dedicated and willing to go through such lengths,” Weible said, because “we are confident in this man’s track record in delivering an unforgettable experience.”

Nolan won his first Oscars for the 2023 biopic “Oppenheimer,” about the scientist behind the atomic bomb, and has been entertaining audiences for decades with temporal-bending films like “Memento,” “Inception” and “Interstellar.” He has also amassed a legion of fans who cannot get enough of his analog inclinations.

To see “The Odyssey” as big as possible as soon as possible, several pulled out their passports.

Aldo Ruggiero flew from Italy to catch a screening at the British Film Institute’s IMAX theater in London. To his mother’s bafflement, Nickolas Hogan and a group of his friends drove 12 hours from Brookings, S. D., to see the movie in Regina, Saskatchewan. David Erazo, who plans his trips to the United States around movie releases, took a plane from Honduras to Florida.

And for the second time to see a Nolan film, Daniel Reveles drove from just outside Seattle to Langley, British Columbia.

When he made the trip three summers ago for “Oppenheimer,” Reveles was stopped by a Canadian border agent who could not comprehend why he was not seeing the movie in Seattle.

“It was definitely a moment where I questioned my sanity,” Reveles said.

Before Nolan popularized the use of IMAX cameras to record blockbuster action sequences, they were primarily used for nature and space documentaries. The ultra-high-resolution footage transported viewers atop Mount Everest and into NASA space shuttles. But the cameras were thought to be too heavy, loud and expensive to use on a standard Hollywood movie set.

For “The Odyssey,” Nolan challenged IMAX to solve two of those problems: The quieter, lighter Keighley camera was born.

But although it is now easier to make a movie in IMAX 70mm, actually viewing it in that format remains challenging. Like the archipelago of islands visited by Odysseus, the 25 compatible theaters in the United States are often separated by vast expanses.

There are eight IMAX 70mm venues in California, but 36 states do not have any at all. The closest option for an “Odyssey” fan in Kansas City, Mo., is a seven-hour drive to Indianapolis or Woodridge, Ill. Someone in Roanoke, Va., must flip a coin between Chattanooga, Tenn., and King of Prussia, Pa.

Around 27 hours after stepping out of his home in Ocala, Weible arrived at his hotel in Fort Lauderdale with scenes from “Miami Vice” flashing through his head.

Weible’s obstacles, unlike those Odysseus faced, were more laughable than lethal: a language barrier, an ill-timed restaurant closure. He slept for only about four hours but woke up with the energy of a kid on Christmas morning.

From his seat at the theater, Weible felt the bass frequencies of the raging waters tossing the Ithacans’ ship, the battle theme swelling as Odysseus confronted a room of insurgents.

When the credits rolled, Weible clutched his IMAX camera popcorn bucket as triumphantly as Odysseus wielded his bow. The journey had been well worth it.

As “The Odyssey” sells out IMAX 70mm theaters nationwide, fans are hoping that a renaissance is imminent. In preparation for the movie, Cinemark added the bulky film projection systems to three of its theaters.

In June, Kinepolis Brussels announced one such upgrade that led Deniz Cansi to cancel his plan to fly from Copenhagen to London and drive 11 hours to Belgium instead. A fervent collector of 35mm film trailers and Blu-ray discs, Cansi said he did not care what it would cost to see “The Odyssey” in IMAX 70mm.

Nolan describes it as 3-D without the glasses. Cansi finds it harder to articulate.

“It cannot be compared to anything else,” he said.

After a transnational road trip that included three electric-vehicle charging stops across Germany, Cansi reached Brussels. He bought a banana and a bottle of water for the morning and turned in for the night.

By 4:30 a. m., Cansi was too wired to fall back asleep. When he entered the theater around 9 a. m., he caught snippets of French, Dutch, German and English. Fifteen minutes after “The Odyssey” ended, Cansi began watching it for a second time.

“The word epic can’t even describe what this movie is,” he said. In one scene, it felt as though a giant Laestrygonian might reach through the screen and pluck him from his seat.

For many Nolan fans, part of the director’s charm is his attention to technical details.

Sergio Estrada drove with his three children from their home in El Paso, Texas, to see “The Odyssey” in Tempe, Ariz. The six-hour drive was nothing, he said, as sheer anticipation granted him a patience rivaling Penelope’s.

Estrada said he felt as awe-struck seeing Nolan’s earlier movies as he did upon his first exposure to classical European sculpture as a teenager.

“The muscle or the rolls in somebody’s stomach, or the folds in their hands, just looked so real,” he said. It is the same with IMAX 70mm.

Estrada and his fellow enthusiasts said that premium formats offered theaters an edge in the competition with streaming. At home, siren sounds beckoned: a buzzing phone, a purring cat, chatty roommates.

Before he headed back to Ocala, Weible stopped in Orlando for his third screening of “The Odyssey” — this time, with closed captions. With home finally on the horizon, he hoped that the next time Nolan released a movie, he would not have to journey so far.

Malia Mendez is a Culture reporter for The Times and part of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

How to Disable Music Videos in Spotify

Wired July 19, 2026

Spotify, it’s fair to say, has made some weird user-experience choices.

There are a number of panels in the app, and the layout is confusing. The service constantly tracks your activity. The app also seems to have an odd hostility to playing actual albums. This all works to create a general feeling that Spotify’s designers are trying to push you into using the service in a particular way.

It’s understandable, then, that some people are annoyed with the way music videos have been added to the platform. For the most part, they would start to play by default, in the background, whenever an artist had uploaded a video for the song. Some music videos have very different audio from the original tracks, particularly if they include sketches or sound effects, which can prove distracting if you prefer the album version of the song. And even if you enjoy music videos (which I do), the decision to have videos play by default—using up bandwidth and battery power—upset a lot of people.

There are a few other quirks. On Spotify’s desktop app, the videos are barely visible; they stay contained in the tiny album art panel until you manage to find the hidden, extremely small Now playing button that enlarges them. Also, the selection of videos that are on the platform, and the ones that are mysteriously absent, seems totally random. Because of this, I check YouTube first when I really want to watch a music video.

The most annoying thing, though, had been a lack of any obvious way to disable all videos. That changed recently—there’s now a toggle in the settings to disable music videos in Spotify entirely, alongside controls that disable the Canvas feature (animated album art) and video podcasts.

On mobile you can do this by tapping your user profile icon in the top-left to bring up the side panel. Then tap Settings and privacy, followed by Content and display.

In the Videos and Canvas section you will see three toggles: one for music videos, one for Canvas, and one for all other videos. This last toggle disables video podcasts, meaning you’ll get the audio-only version of podcasts instead. Turn all these off, and Spotify will use a lot less bandwidth.

On the desktop app, it’s a little different. Click your user profile icon in the top-right corner, then click Settings. Scroll down to the Videos and Canvas section to find the options to disable music videos and Canvas.

I tested this and it worked. The music video icon in playlists and albums disappeared, as did the collection of music videos on Artist pages. The only remnant of the disabled feature is a Switch to video button in the Now Playing sidebar, which appears below the album art. Click it and you’ll be told the video can’t play unless you turn videos back on in the settings. Odd, for sure, but for the most part turning this off means you don’t have to think about music videos in Spotify anymore.

I sincerely wish that Spotify would roll out music videos with more care. Sometimes I really do want to see a video—just not every time I play a track. Playlists of music videos might be welcome if they ran separately from the audio-only playlists. I just don’t want to get a music video when I’m looking for the album version of a song, and I don’t think I’m alone in that. I can only hope that Spotify’s future interface design choices will keep things more clearly separated.

I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated July 2026: I added power banks from Nimble, Baseus, Cuktech, and Pisen, removed some older power banks, and updated prices.

Anker

Anker

Amazon

Best Buy

This is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

You don’t always need big capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy new range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

Maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display shows battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method (Qi wireless charging is less efficient). You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (Programmable Power Supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours (WH). If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have onboard.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, however, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

The chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:

Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely source of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when it overheats. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

How We Test Power Banks

I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.
